Chromosomal translocations

question: Which of the following is a receptor tyrosine kinase, rather than a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - SNAIL

Explanation:

SNAIL is a transcription factor that promotes Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) by downregulating epithelial markers and upregulating mesenchymal markers, thereby facilitating tumor invasion and metastasis.

  • Epithelial cells lose their polarity and adhesion properties and acquire mesenchymal traits (enhancing motility and invasiveness).
  • Dissociation of cancer cells is often due to loss of intercellular adhesion.
  • E-cadherin mediates epithelial cell-cell adhesion; its loss facilitates EMT.
  • EMT is controlled by transcription factors SNAIL and TWIST.
  • Involves downregulation of epithelial markers (E-cadherin) and upregulation of mesenchymal markers (vimentin, smooth muscle actin).
  • EMT contributes to a promigratory phenotype, aiding metastasis in carcinomas like breast and prostate cancers.

Incorrect Options:

E-cadherin (Option A): A cell adhesion molecule; its loss occurs during EMT but it does not drive the transition.

Vimentin (Option C): A mesenchymal marker upregulated during EMT, not a transcriptional regulator.

Smooth muscle actin (Option D): Another mesenchymal marker; indicates EMT but does not initiate it.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar’s Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 274
question: Which gene plays a key role in promoting epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in carcinomas?

correctAnswer: B. Loss of TP53 function and overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Loss of TP53 function and overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins

Explanation:

  • Loss of TP53 and overexpression of BCL2 block apoptosis and allow tumor survival.
  • The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway is the main regulator of apoptosis in cancer.
  • BH3-only proteins (BIM, BAD, BID, PUMA) promote apoptosis by neutralizing anti-apoptotic BCL2 members.
  • Loss of p53 or BCL2 overexpression allows resistance to chemotherapy and radiation.

Incorrect Options:

Overexpression of BAX and BAK (Option A): Promotes apoptosis rather than preventing it.

Increased caspase-9 activation (Option C): Caspase-9 activation triggers apoptosis, so this does not help cancer cells evade death.

Enhanced cytochrome c release (Option D): Promotes apoptosis; cancer cells inhibit this process to survive.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar’s Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 270-271

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - E-cadherin

Explanation:

Loss-of-function mutations in E-cadherin (CDH1 gene) are strongly associated with diffuse gastric carcinoma and lobular breast carcinoma.

  • Role: Maintains cell–cell adhesion; binds β-catenin; mediates contact inhibition of growth.
  • Pathogenesis: Loss of adhesion → increased motility and invasiveness; β-catenin release → nuclear translocation → activation of Wnt target genes → increased proliferation
  • Syndromes (Germline Mutations): Familial gastric carcinoma (autosomal dominant)
  • Associated Sporadic Tumors: Gastric carcinoma (diffuse type), lobular breast carcinoma, esophageal carcinoma, colon carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, prostate carcinoma.

Incorrect Options:

p63 (Option A) is important for epithelial differentiation, not cell adhesion in gastric cancer.

p53 (Option B) regulates apoptosis and DNA repair, not adhesion.

Integrin (Option D) mediates cell-extracellular matrix interactions, not the main defect here.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive abdominal discomfort and weight loss. Endoscopy reveals a gastric mass, and biopsy confirms diffuse gastric carcinoma. Which protein responsible for maintaining cell-to-cell adhesion and inhibiting cell motility is most likely mutated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Peutz-Jeghers syndrome

Explanation:

In Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome, STK11 germline loss-of-function mutations cause hamartomatous GI polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and increased cancer risk.

  • Gene: STK11 (also called LKB1 – Liver kinase B1)
  • Protein function: Activator of the AMPK family of kinases; suppresses cell growth under low nutrient and energy conditions.
  • Pathogenesis: Germline loss-of-function mutations → failure to suppress growth under nutrient/energy stress → tumorigenesis.
  • Features: Hamartomatous GI polyps, GI cancers, mucocutaneous pigmentation, increased risk of pancreatic carcinoma, and other carcinomas.

Incorrect Options:

HNPCC (Option A) is associated with mismatch repair gene mutations and colorectal cancer, without mucocutaneous pigmentation.

Gorlin syndrome (Option B) is caused by PTCH1 mutations, characterized by basal cell carcinomas and jaw cysts.

von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (Option C) is caused by VHL gene mutations, associated with hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma.

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page no. 259
question: A 19-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and melena. On physical examination, she has dark-blue to brown macules on her lips and buccal mucosa. Genetic testing reveals germline loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Germline loss-of-function mutation in PTCH1
explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Germline loss-of-function mutation in PTCH1

Explanation:

PTCH1 mutations cause Gorlin Syndrome (nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome), resulting in multiple basal cell carcinomas, jaw keratocysts, and skeletal anomalies.

  • Gene: PTCH (Patched)
  • Pathogenesis: Germline loss-of-function mutations → constitutive Hedgehog pathway activation → tumor formation
  • Protein function:
    • Tumor suppressor
    • Regulates cell proliferation by controlling Hedgehog signaling
  • Features: Basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma, various benign tumors

Incorrect Options:

Germline loss-of-function mutation in STK11 (Option A): Causes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Germline missense mutation in SDHB (Option B) is associated with hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome.

Germline loss-of-function mutation in WT1 (Option C) is linked to Wilms tumor.

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page no. 259
question: Which of the following is the etiology of Gorlin syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Merlin

Explanation:

Merlin is the NF2 gene product, involved in cytoskeletal stability and tumor suppression; mutation causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas (neurofibromatosis type 2).

  • Gene: NF2; Chromosome 22q12
  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • Protein function:
    • Tumor suppressor
    • Cytoskeletal stability
    • Activator of the Hippo signaling pathway
    • Integrates cytoskeletal signals
  • Features: Bilateral acoustic schwannomas, meningiomas, and other schwannomas
  • Associated Disorders: Neurofibromatosis type 2

Incorrect Options:

Neurofibromin (Option A): NF1 gene product, regulates RAS, associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.

PATCHED (Option C): Receptor in Hedgehog signaling, associated with basal cell nevus syndrome.

RB protein (Option D): Regulator of G1/S cell cycle, associated with retinoblastoma.

question: A 25-year-old woman experiences progressive balance issues and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Imaging reveals tumors affecting both vestibular nerves. This clinical picture is characteristic of a hereditary condition involving a mutation in which protein that plays a role in linking the cytoskeleton to the cell membrane?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - PTEN

Explanation:

The scenario is Cowden Syndrome caused by a Germline loss-of-function mutation of the PTEN gene.

  • Gene: PTEN (Phosphatase and Tensin Homologue) - Chromosome 10q23
  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • Pathogenesis: Germline loss-of-function mutations → dysregulated PI3K/AKT pathway → uncontrolled cell growth
  • Clinical features:
    • Benign follicular appendage tumors (trichilemmomas), lipomas
    • Hamartomatous/inflammatory intestinal polyps, ganglioneuromas; generally no increased risk of GI cancers
    • Benign growths in the CNS
    • Increased risk of breast, endometrial, and thyroid carcinoma; diverse cancers, particularly carcinomas and lymphoid tumors

Incorrect Options:

CDKN2A (Option A) is associated with familial melanoma and pancreatic cancer.

SMAD2 (Option B) is involved in TGF-β signaling, not this syndrome.

APC (Option C) is associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), but not with skin lesions or breast/endometrial cancers.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - p53 is induced by DNA damage

Explanation:

  • p53 is a tumor suppressor protein that is altered in the majority of human cancers (Option A ruled out)
  • It is activated in response to DNA damage (Option B) and plays a crucial role in maintaining genomic stability.
  • It causes cell cycle arrest by upregulating the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, allowing time for DNA repair (Option C ruled out)
  • It can induce apoptosis by upregulating BAX and other pro-apoptotic genes when the damage is irreparable (Option D ruled out)

question: Which of the following statements about p53 is true?

correctAnswer: B. In familial cases, one defective RB allele is inherited in the germline, and the second hit occurs somatically
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - In familial cases, one defective RB allele is inherited in the germline, and the second hit occurs somatically

Explanation:

Knudson’s hypothesis states that:

  • Two loss-of-function mutations (“hits”) of both RB alleles are required to cause retinoblastoma.
  • In familial cases, one defective RB allele is inherited (first hit), and the second hit occurs somatically in a retinoblast.
  • In sporadic cases, both RB alleles undergo independent somatic mutations in the same cell.
  • This explains why retinoblastoma is more common in familial cases and rare in sporadic cases.

Incorrect Options:

Both familial and sporadic cases require two somatic mutations in the same retinoblast (Option A): Familial cases inherit the first hit germline.

Sporadic cases are caused by inheritance of one defective RB allele and a spontaneous second hit (Option C): Sporadic cases involve two independent somatic mutations, not inheritance.

Only one mutation is sufficient to cause retinoblastoma in any case (Option D): Both alleles must be inactivated.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page no. 258

Correct Option D - Mantle cell lymphoma

Explanation:

Mantle Cell Lymphoma characteristically shows t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation, leading to overexpression of cyclin D1, promoting cell cycle progression.

  • Cyclin D1 is a cell cycle regulator proto-oncogene
  • It is involved in translocation in mantle cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma
  • It can undergo amplification in breast and esophageal cancers.

Incorrect Options:

Chronic myeloid leukemia (Option A): Associated with BCR-ABL translocation, not cyclin D1.

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Option B): A broad group; cyclin D1 translocation specifically occurs in the mantle cell subtype.

question: Which of the following cancers is typically associated with a translocation involving cyclin D1?

correctAnswer: B. Proteins that regulate gene activity within the nucleus
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Proteins that regulate gene activity within the nucleus

Explanation:

MYC codes for nuclear regulatory proteins that act as transcription factors and master regulators of cell growth. Specifically, MYC influences the expression of genes involved in:

  • Cell cycle progression - e.g., D cyclins.
  • Ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis - upregulates rRNA genes and rRNA processing.
  • Metabolism - upregulates glycolytic enzymes and glutamine metabolism factors (metabolic reprogramming / Warburg effect).
  • Telomerase expression - contributing to replicative immortality.
  • Stemness/pluripotency - reprogramming somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells.

Incorrect Options:

Proteins that control the cell division cycle (Option A): MYC activates them but does not encode them.

Proteins involved in transmitting signals inside the cell (Option C): MYC regulates signaling indirectly, does not encode them.

Proteins that act as receptors for growth-promoting signals (Option D): MYC acts downstream of these, does not encode them.

question: Which type of proteins are produced as a result of MYC gene expression?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D- Loss of heterozygosity:

  • Retinoblastomas are malignant ocular tumors of young children.
  • In hereditary retinoblastoma, an affected child inherits one defective Rb allele and one normal gene; this heterozygous state is sufficient to prevent the development of retinoblastoma.
  • If the remaining normal Rb allele is inactivated by deletion or mutation, the loss of its suppressor function results in the appearance of a neoplasm.
  • Loss of heterozygosity is the term for this genetic process.

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Balanced translocation:

  • Sometimes a section from one chromosome of a particular pair changes places with a section from a chromosome of another pair.
  • When the two breaks do not pass through a gene, and there is no gain or loss of material when the chromosomes are looked at under a microscope, it is called a balanced translocation.
  • When one couple member carries a balanced chromosome translocation, the risk of miscarriage is approximately doubled.
  • One partner has a balanced translocation in 3-5% of couples with recurrent miscarriages.

Option B- Expansion of trinucleotide repeat:

  • The mutation, referred to as “trinucleotide repeat (TNR) expansion," occurs when the number of triplets in a mutated gene exceeds the number found in a normal gene.
  • Additionally, the number of triplets in the disease gene continues to increase as the disease gene is inherited.
  • Slippage in DNA replication can cause trinucleotide repeats to grow.
  • Therefore, with each cell division, the number of repeats can rise. Expanded repeats can lengthen and are also inherited.

Option C- Gene amplification:

  • Gene amplification refers to various organic and synthetic mechanisms that increase a gene's copy number "without a commensurate rise in other genes."
  • A rise in the gene's copy number. Additionally, there can be an increase in the RNA and protein produced by that gene.
  • An increase in the number of copies of a gene in a genome is called gene amplification.
  • In response to signals from other cells or the environment, cancer cells, for instance, occasionally make extra copies of a gene or genes.


Reference:

Robbins 10th ed, Pg 291
question: Which of the following genetic events best describes the carcinogenesis mechanism in a patient with retinoblastoma?

correctAnswer: A. Constitutive activation of a GTP-binding protein leading to continuous MAP kinase signalling
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • RAS is a proto-oncogene that encodes a GTP-binding protein (G-protein) involved in transmitting growth signals from the cell membrane to the nucleus.
  • When mutated, RAS becomes constitutively active (locked in the GTP-bound form), leading to continuous downstream signalling through the MAP kinase pathway, causing uncontrolled cell proliferation - a key event in oncogenesis.

Incorrect Options:

Enhanced DNA repair leading to genomic instability (Option B): RAS mutations do not enhance DNA repair; rather, they promote proliferation, not repair. Genomic instability arises from defects in DNA repair genes (e.g., BRCA1, MSH2).

Inactivation of a tumour suppressor gene resulting in loss of cell cycle checkpoint control (Option C): This describes tumour suppressor genes like RB or TP53, not RAS, which is an oncogene (gain-of-function mutation).

Increased activity of tyrosine kinase receptors through gene amplification (Option D): Seen in HER2/neu or EGFR oncogenes, not RAS. RAS acts downstream of these receptors.



Reference:

Robbins & Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Pages 287.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The only false statement given is 'Light microscopy reveals secretory granules'. Electron microscopy reveals secretory granules.

Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) are neoplasms that arise from cells of the endocrine (hormonal) and nervous systems. They most commonly, but not only, occur in the intestine, where they are often called carcinoid tumours.

  • Microscopic Features:
    • Uniform, small-to-medium round cells (Statement 4)

[[figure-1]]

  • Moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm
  • Characteristic “salt and pepper” (stippling) chromatin (Statement 1)

[[figure-2]]

  • Electron Microscopy features:
    • Presence of electron-dense neurosecretory granules (Statement 3)

[[figure-3]]

  • Immunohistochemistry:
    • NETs are characteristically positive for:
      • Chromogranin A (CgA)
      • Synaptophysin
      • Neuron-specific enolase (NSE)
      • CD56

[[figure-4]]

  • High-grade NET (small-cell carcinoma) typically have a high mitotic rate and a very high Ki-67 index (>20%)

Although there are many kinds of NETs, they are treated as a group of tissues because the cells of these neoplasms share common features, including a similar histological appearance, having special secretory granules, and often producing biogenic amines and polypeptide hormones (Statement 2).



Reference:

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Page 719, 777.

All of the following are correct about neuroendocrine tumours except?

explanationHtml:
• The Warburg effect is a distinct metabolic feature of cancer cells, where, even in the presence of sufficient oxygen, cancer cells demonstrate a distinctive form of cellular metabolism characterised by high glucose uptake levels (Option A ruled out) and increased glucose conversion to lactose (fermentation) via glycolysis.
  • This shift does not increase ATP production but provides key metabolic intermediates needed for rapid cell growth and division. (Option C ruled out)
  • Otto Warburg was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1931 for this theory.
  • The Warburg effect is the basis of positive emission tomography (PET).
    • Patients are injected with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a non-metabolizable glucose derivative preferentially taken up into tumour cells (due to glucose hunger), which can be detected by PET scan.

It prevents apoptosis and makes the cancer immortal (Option D): While Warburg metabolism can be linked to cellular survival and resistance to certain forms of stress, its primary function is not directly about preventing apoptosis or making the cell immortal. Instead, it helps meet the increased metabolic demands of rapidly proliferating cancer cells.

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the standard antibody-based technique used to detect specific proteins (antigens) in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections while preserving tissue architecture.

  • Extracellular matrix (ECM): Collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans

question: Which of the following statements regarding Hepatitis A infection is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hepatitis A causes only an acute, self-limited hepatitis and does not establish chronic infection or a carrier state.

  • The virus is transmitted primarily by the feco–oral route, typically through contaminated food or water.
  • After an incubation period of about 2–6 weeks, patients develop an acute illness characterised by jaundice, elevated transaminases, malaise, and anorexia.
  • Once the immune system clears the virus, protective anti-HAV IgG antibodies develop, providing lifelong immunity.
  • Because HAV does not integrate into host hepatocyte DNA and does not persist within hepatocytes, it lacks the biological capacity to produce chronic hepatitis.

Hepatitis B (Option A): May progress to chronic hepatitis, particularly when infection occurs early in life. Chronic HBV infection can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Hepatitis C (Option B): Has a high chronicity rate (approximately 75–85%), making it a major cause of chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide.

Hepatitis D (Option C): A defective RNA virus that requires HBV for replication. HDV superinfection in HBV carriers often results in severe chronic hepatitis and rapid progression to cirrhosis.

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 756

[[figure-1]]

  • This phenomenon reflects immune complex formation against nuclear antigens in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and was historically used as a diagnostic test.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects B lymphocytes via the CD21 receptor and induces their proliferation and survival by activating signaling pathways such as NF-κB and JAK/STAT.

  • EBV acts as a polyclonal B-cell mitogen, leading to expansion of multiple B-cell clones.
  • This nonspecific activation of B cells can result in the production of a wide range of antibodies, including potentially autoreactive antibodies, thereby contributing to breakdown of self-tolerance and development of autoimmunity.

Molecular mimicry (Option A) is a general mechanism of autoimmunity but is not the primary mechanism associated with EBV in this context.

PTPN22 encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates T-cell receptor signaling, and disease-associated variants may impair this regulatory function, leading to excessive activation of self-reactive lymphocytes and loss of immune tolerance.

FOXP3 (Option A) mutations cause immune dysregulation syndromes such as IPEX due to defective regulatory T cells, but these are rare monogenic disorders and not broadly associated with common autoimmune diseases.

NOD2 (Option C) is primarily associated with Crohn’s disease, involving innate immune dysfunction and abnormal responses to gut microbes rather than generalized autoimmunity.

explanationHtml:
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease predominantly driven by CD4⁺ T cells (Th1 and Th17), which initiate and sustain synovial inflammation through cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-17, IL-6, and IFN-γ.

  • These cytokines activate macrophages and synovial fibroblasts, leading to chronic inflammation, angiogenesis, and formation of pannus, an invasive granulation tissue that progressively destroys articular cartilage and subchondral bone.
  • In addition, autoantibodies, notably rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) form immune complexes that further amplify inflammation via complement activation.
  • Thus, rheumatoid arthritis is a T-cell-dominant autoimmune disease with significant contribution from humoral immunity, representing a mixed (Type IV + Type III) mechanism of tissue injury.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option A) is an antibody-mediated (Type II hypersensitivity) disorder caused by IgG antibodies against desmogleins, leading to loss of cell adhesion (acantholysis) and blister formation.

Pernicious anemia (Option B) is primarily antibody-mediated, involving antibodies against intrinsic factor and parietal cells, causing vitamin B12 deficiency; associated T-cell-mediated gastric mucosal damage may also contribute.

Goodpasture syndrome (Option D) is a classic Type II hypersensitivity disease in which antibodies against basement membrane (type IV collagen) trigger complement activation and inflammation, leading to glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 187, 190

Papain cleaves the immunoglobulin molecule at the hinge region above the interchain disulfide bonds, separating the antigen-binding arms from the constant region.

Polysaccharide and lipid antigens are T-cell-independent antigens that activate B cells without T-cell help.

  • Because these responses lack CD40L and cytokine-mediated signals from helper T cells, there is minimal or no class switching, and the predominant antibody produced is IgM.
  • In contrast, protein antigens induce T cell-dependent responses, which involve helper T cells and lead to isotype switching with production of IgG, IgA, or IgE, as well as affinity maturation.

IgG (Option A): Produced after class switching in T cell-dependent responses.

IgD (Option C): Primarily expressed on the surface of naive B cells and not secreted in significant amounts.

IL-4 is the principal cytokine that induces class switch recombination to IgE in B cells.

  • It is produced by Th2 helper T cells and plays a central role in type 2 immune responses and allergic diseases.
  • IL-4–mediated IgE production leads to sensitisation of mast cells and is a key mechanism in type I hypersensitivity reactions.
  • IL-13 may also promote IgE production, but IL-4 is the primary cytokine responsible for class switching.

IL-1 (Option A): A pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in innate immune responses; it does not induce IgE class switching.

IL-2 (Option B): Primarily promotes T-cell proliferation and survival, without a direct role in IgE production.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The principal costimulators for T-cell activation are the B7 proteins—CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2), which are expressed on antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and bind to CD28 on naive T cells.

  • Activation of T cells requires two signals:
    • Signal 1: Recognition of antigen presented by MHC molecules via the T-cell receptor (TCR)
    • Signal 2 (costimulation): Interaction of CD80/CD86 on APCs with CD28 on T cells
  • Costimulatory molecules are induced on APCs during innate immune responses to microbes, ensuring that adaptive immune responses are generated appropriately.
  • In the absence of costimulation, T cells become anergic (functionally unresponsive).

CD28 and CD86 (Option A): CD28 is expressed on T cells, not on APCs.

CD80 only (Option B): Both CD80 and CD86 function as costimulators; CD80 alone is not sufficient as the best answer.

CD28 and CD80 (Option C): CD28 is present on T cells, whereas CD80 is on APCs; both are not expressed on APCs.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 177
question: On antigen-presenting cells, which of the following molecules provide the necessary costimulatory signals to activate T cells?

correctAnswer: C. They can target virus-infected cells
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Both natural killer (NK) cells (innate immunity) and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) (adaptive immunity) are capable of killing virus-infected cells.

  • NK cells recognise target cells with reduced MHC class I expression and do not require antigen-specific recognition.
  • CTLs (CD8+ T cells) recognise viral peptides presented on MHC class I molecules and require antigen-specific activation.
  • Thus, while their mechanisms differ, both cell types share the ability to eliminate virus-infected cells.

They are restricted by MHC class I molecules (Option A): Only CTLs are MHC class I–restricted; NK cells are not restricted and instead detect decreased MHC class I expression.

They need antibodies to mediate their effect (Option B): NK cells can mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), but CTLs do not use antibodies and kill target cells directly.

Their activity is antigen-specific (Option D): CTLs are antigen-specific, whereas NK cells are not and act through innate immune recognition.



Reference:
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.09325
  • Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 647

question: Which feature is shared by both natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs)?

explanationHtml:
Gain-of-function mutations in NOD-like receptors (NLRs) lead to inappropriate activation of the inflammasome, resulting in increased production of interleukin-1 (IL-1) and inflammation.

  • These mutations cause autoinflammatory syndromes, which are characterised by innate immune dysregulation and occur without involvement of adaptive immunity.
  • Although certain mutations (e.g., NOD2) may be associated with granulomatous inflammation, the primary classification of these conditions is autoinflammatory rather than granulomatous or autoimmune.

Malignancy (Option A): NOD-like receptor (NLR) gain-of-function mutations are not primarily associated with neoplastic transformation; they mainly cause dysregulated innate immune activation and inflammation.

Granulomatous disease (Option B): Granulomatous inflammation can occur (e.g., NOD2 in Blau syndrome), but these conditions are primarily classified as autoinflammatory syndromes rather than granulomatous diseases.

Autoimmune disorders (Option D): Autoimmune diseases involve adaptive immunity (T and B cells), whereas autoinflammatory syndromes result from innate immune dysregulation, particularly involving inflammasome activation and IL-1 production.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 67
question: Activation of NOD-like receptors by gain-of-function mutations is most likely to result in which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: D. NK cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is a mechanism in which target cells coated with IgG antibodies are recognised by immune effector cells via Fc receptors (FcγR) and are lysed without phagocytosis.
  • Natural killer (NK) cells are the primary and most important mediators of ADCC.
  • Macrophages also play a significant role.
  • In addition, neutrophils and eosinophils can participate in ADCC through Fc receptor–mediated mechanisms.
  • Thus, ADCC is mediated by multiple immune cells, with NK cells being the principal effectors.


Reference:
  • Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 186
  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibody-dependent_cellular_cytotoxicity

correctAnswer: A. Rupture of a saccular aneurysm
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Saccular aneurysm rupture is the most common cause of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage, classically presenting with a thunderclap headache.

Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH) - Ruptured Saccular (Berry) Aneurysm:

  • Most common cause of spontaneous SAH: Rupture of a saccular (berry)
  • Other causes: AV malformations, extension of intracerebral haemorrhage, hematologic disorders, tumours, trauma
  • Saccular Aneurysm:
    • Most common intracranial aneurysm
    • 90% occur at branch points in the anterior circulation of the Circle of Willis

[[figure-1]]

  • Common sites:
    • Anterior communicating artery (most common)
    • Posterior communicating artery
    • Middle cerebral artery
  • Risk factors:
    • Developmental defect → absence of smooth muscle & internal elastic lamina
    • Hemodynamic stress at branch points
    • Risk factors: hypertension, smoking, family history
  • Associated disorders:
    • Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease
    • Ehler-Danlos-Syndrome Type IV
    • Marfan Syndrome
    • Neurofibromatosis Type 1

Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage (Option B): Parenchymal bleed (e.g., basal ganglia), not primary SAH.

Arteriovenous malformation (Option C): Less common cause; often in younger patients.

Traumatic subdural hematoma (Option D): Trauma-related, crescent-shaped bleed, not diffuse SAH.

question: A 24-year-old woman presents with high-grade fever, chills, and left flank pain for 2 days. She also reports dysuria and increased urinary frequency. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Which of the following urinary findings would most strongly indicate renal involvement?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin, especially over pressure points, which is characteristic of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease).

  • Elevated ACTH leads to increased POMC-derived MSH, causing hyperpigmentation.
  • The presence of low cortisol, high ACTH, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia confirms primary adrenal failure due to a deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone.

Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Addison's Disease):

  • Progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex.
  • Symptoms appear when >90% of the cortex is destroyed.
  • Clinical features:
    • Fatigue, weakness, weight loss
    • Nausea, vomiting
    • Hyperpigmentation (↑ACTH → ↑MSH)
    • Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension

Secondary adrenal insufficiency (Option B): ACTH is low, and hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia are absent.

Cushing syndrome (Option C): Characterised by excess cortisol.

Primary hyperaldosteronism (Option D): Causes hypertension and hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 1019, 1020

question: A 42-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, nausea, and dizziness. Examination shows findings as shown in the image. Laboratory tests reveal low serum cortisol, elevated ACTH, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The described lesion is classic for Kaposi sarcoma (KS), the most common neoplasm in patients with AIDS.

  • Clinically, it presents as violaceous plaques and nodules, and histologically shows:
    • Proliferation of spindle-shaped cells
    • Irregular, slit-like vascular spaces
    • Extravasated red blood cells and hemosiderin deposition
    • Chronic inflammatory infiltrate
  • Kaposi sarcoma is strongly associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), which is necessary but not sufficient for tumour development.
  • In AIDS patients, HIV-induced immunosuppression acts as a cofactor, allowing widespread HHV-8 infection and tumour progression.
  • HHV-8 establishes latent infection and produces viral proteins that:
    • Promote cell proliferation (e.g., viral cyclin D homologues)
    • Inhibit tumour suppressors such as p53
    • Stimulate angiogenesis and inflammation, contributing to lesion formation
  • KS lesions are unique in that many are polyclonal or oligoclonal, especially in early stages, reflecting a proliferation driven by cytokines and angiogenic factors rather than purely malignant transformation.

[[figure-1]]

Epstein-Barr virus (Option B) is associated with B-cell lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma, primary CNS lymphoma), not Kaposi sarcoma.

Cytomegalovirus (Option C) causes opportunistic infections such as retinitis, pneumonitis, and gastrointestinal ulcers, not vascular tumours.

Human papillomavirus (Option D) is associated with epithelial neoplasms, including cervical and anogenital cancers, not vascular tumours like Kaposi sarcoma.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 227-228
question: A 52-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple raised, violaceous plaques and nodules over both legs. The lesions have gradually increased in number over the past few months. Skin biopsy shows a dermal lesion composed of irregular, slit-like vascular spaces lined and surrounded by plump, spindle-shaped cells. The stroma contains extravasated red blood cells, hemosiderin deposits, areas of haemorrhage, and a mixed mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate. Occasional mitotic figures are seen. Which of the following infectious agents is associated with this tumour?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hematoxylin bodies are not seen in HIV lymphadenopathy. They represent denatured nuclear material bound by autoantibodies and are characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
  • HIV-associated lymphadenopathy demonstrates dynamic, stage-dependent morphologic changes reflecting progressive immune dysfunction.

In early HIV infection, there is marked follicular hyperplasia (Option A) characterised by:

  • Enlarged, irregular (“serpiginous”) germinal centres
  • Attenuation of mantle zones
  • Germinal centres encroaching into interfollicular T-cell areas
  • Underlying mechanism: polyclonal B-cell activation

As the disease progresses, this hyperplastic phase evolves into lymphoid involution, with:

  • Destruction and eventual hyalinization of germinal centres (Option B)
  • Disruption of the follicular dendritic cell (FDC) network
  • Marked lymphocyte depletion
  • “Burnt-out” lymph nodes that may contain opportunistic pathogens with minimal inflammatory response

Expansion of monocytoid B cells in the sinuses (Option D) may occur as a reactive change in lymph nodes and can be seen in chronic immune stimulation.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 200, 229

options.text: Expansion of monocytoid B cells in the sinuses

question: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with persistent, painless swelling of multiple lymph nodes. A lymph node biopsy is performed. Which of the following histopathological findings is least likely to be observed in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In patients with HIV/AIDS and other forms of immunosuppression, the most common primary brain tumour is primary CNS lymphoma, which is typically a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

  • These tumours are often multifocal, involve deep periventricular regions, and show a characteristic tendency for perivascular infiltration.
  • In immunosuppressed individuals, the malignant B cells are commonly latently infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which plays a key role in tumour pathogenesis.
  • These lymphomas are aggressive and have a worse prognosis compared to similar tumours in immunocompetent individuals.
  • A critical clinical point is that opportunistic infections (especially toxoplasmosis) are more common than tumours in AIDS patients and may present as ring-enhancing lesions, often mimicking CNS lymphoma.

Other listed tumors such as oligodendroglioma, ependymoma, and pilocytic astrocytoma, are not associated with HIV-related immunosuppression.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 1182
question: In patients with HIV/AIDS, which of the following is the most frequently observed brain tumour?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HIV infects cells by binding to the CD4 receptor and chemokine co-receptors CCR5 or CXCR4, which determine viral tropism:

  • R5 (CCR5-using) strains → infect monocytes/macrophages and dendritic cells (M-tropic)
  • X4 (CXCR4-using) strains → infect CD4+ T cells (T-tropic)

The major target cells include:

  • CD4+ helper T cells (Option A) → primary targets; progressive depletion leads to immunodeficiency
  • Macrophages (Option D) → infected due to low-level CD4 expression; serve as long-lived viral reservoirs
  • Dendritic cells (Option C) → capture HIV at mucosal sites and transfer it to T cells, facilitating infection

In contrast, neutrophils (Option B) lack CD4 receptors and the required chemokine co-receptors, and therefore are not directly infected by HIV, making them the least likely target.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 220
question: Which of the following immune cells is least likely to be directly infected by HIV during the course of the disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked immunodeficiency caused by mutations in the WAS gene, which encodes a protein involved in linking cell surface receptors to the actin cytoskeleton, thereby affecting lymphocyte activation, migration, and immune synapse formation.

  • It is characterised by the triad of:
    • Eczema
    • Recurrent infections
    • Thrombocytopenia with small platelets (microthrombocytopenia)
  • The characteristic immunoglobulin profile is:
    • IgE ↑ (Statement 1: correct)
    • IgA ↑ (Statement 2: correct)
    • IgM ↓ (Statement 3: incorrect)
    • IgG usually normal (Statement 4: correct)
  • Patients also have defective antibody responses, particularly to polysaccharide antigens, and progressive defects in T-cell function.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 218
question:
A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent eczema, recurrent pneumonia and otitis media since infancy, and easy bruising. Laboratory investigations show thrombocytopenia with small platelets and abnormal immunoglobulin levels. Which of the following statements regarding his condition is correct?

  1. Serum IgE is elevated
  2. Serum IgA is elevated
  3. Serum IgM is normal
  4. Serum IgG is normal

correctAnswer: D. B-cell count is usually within the normal range
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is characterised by hypogammaglobulinemia due to impaired differentiation of B cells into plasma cells, resulting in defective antibody production.

  • Despite this functional defect, most patients have normal or near-normal numbers of circulating B cells in peripheral blood and lymphoid tissues.
  • The primary abnormality lies in the failure of B cells to mature into antibody-secreting plasma cells, rather than a deficiency in B-cell numbers.
  • This leads to recurrent sinopulmonary infections, along with increased susceptibility to certain viral and gastrointestinal infections, and a higher risk of autoimmune diseases and lymphoid malignancies.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 217

options.text: B-cell count is usually within the normal range

question: In patients diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), which of the following best describes the typical finding in peripheral B-cell numbers?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP) is characterised by an inability to eliminate Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), leading to severe or fatal infectious mononucleosis and an increased risk of B-cell lymphomas.

  • The disorder is most commonly caused by mutations in the SH2D1A gene, which encodes the SLAM-associated protein (SAP).
  • SAP is required for effective T-cell and natural killer (NK) cell activation, particularly in response to EBV-infected B cells.
  • Its deficiency results in impaired cytotoxic function and uncontrolled lymphoproliferation.
  • SAP is also essential for the development of T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, and its absence leads to defective germinal centre formation and impaired production of high-affinity antibodies.

WAS gene (Option B) mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

LYST gene (Option C) mutations cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

FOXP3 gene (Option D) mutations cause IPEX syndrome, characterised by regulatory T-cell dysfunction and autoimmunity.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 218
question: Mutation in which of the following is responsible for the development of X-linked lymphoproliferative disorder, characterised by an abnormal immune response to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and is characterised by markedly reduced or absent serum and secretory IgA, leading to impaired mucosal immunity. It is frequently associated with deficiencies in IgG subclasses, most consistently IgG2.

  • IgG2 plays a critical role in immune responses against polysaccharide antigens of encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Deficiency of IgG2 results in impaired opsonisation and clearance of these organisms, contributing to recurrent sinopulmonary infections, a hallmark clinical feature in symptomatic patients.
  • Although deficiencies of other IgG subclasses (such as IgG3 or IgG4) may occasionally be seen, these associations are variable and less consistent, making IgG2 deficiency the most reliable and clinically significant finding.


Reference:
  • https://primaryimmune.org/understanding-primary-immunodeficiency/types-of-pi/selective-iga-deficiency
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3099256/
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1905297
question: Individuals with selective IgA deficiency most commonly show reduced levels of which IgG subclass?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) results from genetic defects that impair T-cell development, leading to combined defects in both cell-mediated and humoral immunity. Several genes are commonly involved:

  • IL-7Rα (Option A) mutations impair T-cell development, causing an autosomal recessive form of SCID (T⁻ B⁺ NK⁺).
  • RAG1 and RAG2 (Option B) are required for V(D)J recombination; mutations prevent normal T- and B-cell maturation, resulting in SCID (T⁻ B⁻).
  • JAK3 (Option C) is involved in signalling through the common γ-chain cytokine receptor; mutations lead to SCID (T⁻ B⁺ NK⁻).

In contrast, BTK (Option D) mutations cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA), characterised by defective B-cell maturation with normal T-cell function. Therefore, BTK is not associated with SCID.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 215-216
question: Which of the following genes is not typically associated with the development of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of disorders characterised by profound defects in both cell-mediated (T-cell) and humoral (B-cell) immunity, leading to severe, recurrent infections early in life, including opportunistic infections such as candidiasis.

  • The most common form is X-linked SCID, caused by mutations in the common γ-chain (IL2RG) of cytokine receptors, resulting in defective T-cell development (Statement 1).
  • Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is the most common autosomal recessive cause of SCID but is not the most common overall cause (Statement 2).
  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the mainstay of treatment and can restore immune function (Statement 3).
  • Because T cells are essential for B-cell activation, SCID results in combined defects in both humoral and cell-mediated immunity (Statement 4).


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 215-216
question:
A 7-month-old infant presents with persistent oral thrush and extensive diaper rash. History reveals multiple serious infections since birth, requiring repeated hospital admissions. Oral examination shows easily scrapable white patches. Thymic biopsy demonstrates underdeveloped Hassall’s corpuscles. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

  1. The most common form of SCID is X-linked
  2. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) enzyme deficiency is the most common cause
  3. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the preferred treatment
  4. It is due to defects in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hereditary angioedema is caused by a deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), an autosomal dominant disorder.

  • This leads to unregulated activation of the kallikrein-kinin system and increased production of bradykinin, resulting in increased vascular permeability and recurrent, non-urticarial edema of the skin and mucosal surfaces, including the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Episodes are often triggered by minor trauma or emotional stress.

C2 (Option B) deficiency is associated with increased susceptibility to infections and SLE-like autoimmune disease, not angioedema.

C3 (Option C) deficiency leads to severe recurrent pyogenic infections due to impaired opsonisation.

Deficiencies of terminal complement components C5-C9 (Option D) impair formation of the membrane attack complex and predispose to recurrent Neisseria infections.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 214-215
question: A young adult develops recurrent episodes of facial and lip swelling accompanied by abdominal pain and vomiting following minor stress or trauma. There is no associated urticaria. Which of the following complement deficiencies is most likely responsible?

correctAnswer: A. C1 esterase inhibitor - Hereditary angioedema
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) causes hereditary angioedema, an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of oedema involving the skin, mucous membranes, and airways. This results from unregulated activation of the kallikrein system and increased bradykinin production, leading to increased vascular permeability.

Complement deficient

Disorder

C1 esterase inhibitor

Hereditary angioedema

C3 (Option B)

Recurrent pyogenic infections with encapsulated bacteria (like pneumococci)

Factor H (Option C)

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and thrombotic microangiopathy

C6-C9 (Option D)

Recurrent Neisseria (gonococcal and meningococcal) infections

C2, C4, or C1q

SLE


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 214
question: Which of the following complement deficiencies is correctly matched with its associated disorder?

correctAnswer: D. It is due to defects in leukocytic superoxide production
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is caused by inherited defects in components of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, leading to impaired generation of superoxide (O₂•) and reactive oxygen species.

  • This defect results in impaired intracellular killing of microbes, particularly catalase-positive organisms such as Serratia marcescens.
  • The nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test is negative due to failure of the oxidative burst.
  • Most cases are X-linked (gp91phox deficiency), while others are autosomal recessive (e.g., p47phox, p67phox); it is not inherited in an autosomal dominant manner (Option A).
  • The disease is a defect of innate immunity affecting phagocytes, not a lymphocyte-mediated process (Option B) and does not primarily involve the adaptive immune system (Option C).
  • The impaired neutrophil response leads to chronic inflammation with macrophage-rich granuloma formation.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 48, 214

options.text: It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner
Primarily affects the adaptive immune system
It is due to defects in leukocytic superoxide production

question: A 6-month-old infant presents with persistent fever and rapid breathing for 1 week. History reveals multiple previous infections. Blood culture grows Serratia marcescens. Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test is negative. Which of the following statements about this condition is true?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Kidneys and liver

Explanation:

  • Secondary (AA) amyloidosis is systemic and typically associated with chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, IBD).
  • Caused by the deposition of serum amyloid A (SAA) protein secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions.
  • Kidneys are the most commonly affected organ, often leading to proteinuria and renal dysfunction.
  • Liver and spleen may also be involved, but deposition in the heart and brain is rare in AA amyloidosis.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 232
question: Which of the following sites is most commonly affected in secondary (AA) amyloidosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Aβ2-m

Explanation:

  • β2-microglobulin amyloidosis occurs in patients on long-term hemodialysis due to the accumulation of β2-microglobulin, which is poorly cleared by older dialysis membranes.
  • Clinical manifestations are usually musculoskeletal, including joint, tendon, ligament, and muscle involvement, with carpal tunnel syndrome being relatively common.
  • The incidence of this complication has decreased with modern dialysis filters that better remove β2-microglobulin.

Incorrect Options:

AA amyloid (Option A): Derived from serum amyloid A during chronic inflammation; associated with chronic infections or autoimmune diseases, not dialysis.

AL amyloid (Option B): Composed of immunoglobulin light chains; seen in plasma cell dyscrasias like multiple myeloma, not in long-term dialysis patients.

ATTR (Option D): Transthyretin-derived amyloid; associated with hereditary amyloidosis and senile cardiac amyloidosis, not dialysis-related disease.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 233
question: A 58-year-old man with end-stage renal disease has been receiving hemodialysis for 6 years. He now presents with joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, and shoulder stiffness. Laboratory tests show normal inflammatory markers and no evidence of plasma cell disorder. Which type of amyloid is most likely responsible for his symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP)

Explanation:

  • In type 2 diabetes, amyloid deposits are localized to the islets of Langerhans.
  • The protein responsible is IAPP (amylin), co-secreted with insulin by β-cells.
  • These deposits contribute to β-cell dysfunction, worsening hyperglycemia.

AL amyloid (Option A) is from plasma cell disorders, AA amyloid (Option B) is secondary to chronic inflammation, and β2-microglobulin (Option D) occurs in long-term hemodialysis.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 233
question: Which type of amyloid is commonly deposited in the pancreas of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Calcitonin

Explanation:

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from C-cells of the thyroid.
  • These cells secrete calcitonin, which can form amyloid deposits (sometimes called ACal deposits) within the tumor.
  • These deposits are localized and serve as a helpful diagnostic feature.

Thyroglobulin (Option A) is secreted by follicular cells, parathyroid hormone (Option C) by parathyroid glands, and IAPP (Option D) is related to pancreatic islets.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 233
question: In medullary thyroid carcinoma, amyloid deposits are primarily derived from which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Kidneys

Explanation:

  • AL amyloidosis is caused by deposition of immunoglobulin light chains produced by clonal plasma cells.
  • The kidneys are most frequently involved, often presenting with proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome.
  • Other commonly affected organs include the heart (restrictive cardiomyopathy), liver, and peripheral nerves, but the kidneys are the primary target.
  • Pancreatic involvement is rare in AL amyloidosis; localized islet amyloid in diabetes involves IAPP, not AL protein.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 231-232
question: Which of the following organs is most commonly affected in AL (primary) amyloidosis?

correctAnswer: B. Modest increase in plasma cells producing monoclonal light chains
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Modest increase in plasma cells producing monoclonal light chains

Explanation:

  • In AL amyloidosis, most patients do not have overt multiple myeloma.
  • Bone marrow typically shows a modest increase in plasma cells that secrete monoclonal immunoglobulins or free light chains (kappa or lambda).
  • These light chains deposit in tissues as amyloid, causing systemic manifestations.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 231-232

options.text: Extensive osteolytic lesions with &gt;30% plasma cells
Modest increase in plasma cells producing monoclonal light chains
Normal plasma cell count with no monoclonal proteins

question: In primary (AL) amyloidosis, the typical bone marrow finding is?

correctAnswer: B. Abdominal fat pad aspiration stained with Congo red
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Abdominal fat pad aspiration stained with Congo red

Explanation:

  • Abdominal fat pad aspiration is minimally invasive and can detect systemic amyloid deposits with Congo red staining.

Amyloidosis Investigation:

  1. Tissue Biopsy (gold standard)
    • Kidney (if renal manifestations present)
    • Rectal or gingival tissue
    • Abdominal fat aspirate stained with Congo red (specific but less sensitive)
  2. Serum and Urine Studies (especially in AL amyloidosis)
    • Protein electrophoresis
    • Immunoelectrophoresis to detect monoclonal proteins or free light chains
  3. Bone Marrow Aspirate
    • Shows monoclonal plasmacytosis, even if overt multiple myeloma is absent
  4. Imaging / Scintigraphy
    • Radiolabeled serum amyloid P component scintigraphy
    • Rapid, specific, shows extent of amyloid deposition and can monitor treatment response


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 234

options.text: Abdominal fat pad aspiration stained with Congo red

question: Which of the following is the preferred initial investigation for suspected systemic amyloidosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Congo red

Explanation:

  • Congo red is the standard stain for detecting amyloid in kidney tissue, including glomeruli, vessels, and interstitium.
  • When viewed under polarized light, amyloid shows apple-green birefringence, confirming the diagnosis.
  • Other stains may show structural changes but cannot specifically identify amyloid.

Incorrect Options:

Hematoxylin and eosin (Option A): Shows eosinophilic deposits but is nonspecific for amyloid.

Masson’s trichrome (Option C): Highlights collagen and fibrosis, not amyloid.

Periodic acid–Schiff (Option D): Stains basement membranes and carbohydrates, not specific for amyloid.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 234
question: Which of the following stains is most commonly used to detect amyloid deposits in kidney biopsies?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Apple-green birefringence

Explanation:

  • Congo red stain is the standard for detecting amyloid in tissues such as kidney, rectal mucosa, fat pad, or gingiva.
  • Under polarized light, amyloid deposits exhibit apple-green birefringence, which is considered diagnostic.
  • The test is specific but less sensitive, so negative results do not completely exclude amyloidosis.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 234

options.text: Orange-red color under light microscope only

question: When stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light, amyloid deposits in tissue typically show?

correctAnswer: B. CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes and CD4⁺ helper T cells
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes and CD4⁺ helper T cells

Explanation:

  • Acute cellular rejection is mediated mainly by T cells:
    • CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) directly kill graft cells expressing alloantigens.
    • CD4⁺ helper T cells secrete cytokines that recruit and activate other inflammatory cells, causing tissue damage.
  • Acute antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection involves antibodies binding to graft endothelium, activating complement.
  • Hyperacute rejection is mediated by preformed antibodies (often IgM) causing immediate endothelial injury.
  • Chronic rejection involves T cells and alloantibodies promoting fibrosis and graft arteriosclerosis over months to years.

Incorrect Options:

B cells producing preformed antibodies (Option A): These are primarily involved in hyperacute rejection, not acute cellular rejection.

Natural killer (NK) cells only (Option C): NK cells may play a minor role but are not the primary mediators of acute cellular rejection.

Macrophages without T cell involvement (Option D): Macrophages are involved in inflammation, but they require activation by T cells; they don’t mediate acute rejection independently.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page. 209-210

Explanation:

Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS) is caused by a deletion on the long arm (q arm) of the paternal chromosome 15q11-q13, leading to the loss of genes that are normally expressed from the paternal allele. This occurs through genomic imprinting, in which the maternal allele is normally silenced and the paternal allele is essential for normal function.

(Option A): Caused by a maternal deletion of chromosome 15q11-q13 (opposite of Prader-Willi Syndrome). Features include severe intellectual disability, ataxia, happy demeanor (frequent laughter), seizures, and microcephaly. UBE3A gene is affected.

(Option C): Caused by a deletion of chromosome 5p (5p- syndrome). Features include high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features.

(Option D): Caused by MECP2 gene mutations on the X chromosome (affects females almost exclusively). Features include neurodevelopmental regression, loss of purposeful hand movements (hand-wringing), ataxia, and seizures.

question: A pathology report of a heart specimen describes "brisk interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils" and "coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclei. What is the most likely age of this infarct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Myocardial free wall rupture most commonly occurs 3-7 days after MI, when necrotic myocardium undergoes maximal enzymatic degradation and is replaced by soft, friable granulation tissue, making the wall prone to tearing.


Mechanical Complication of MI: Myocardial Rupture:

  • Occurs in 1-3% of myocardial infarctions - frequently fatal
  • Types of Rupture:
    • Left Ventricular Free Wall Rupture (Most common):
      • Hemopericardium, cardiac tamponade
      • Often rapidly fatal
    • Ventricular Septal Rupture
    • Papillary Muscle Rupture
  • Timing:
    • Most common 3-7 days post-MI
    • Occurs when:
      • Necrotic myocardium undergoes maximal lysis
      • Infarcted area becomes soft, friable granulation tissue
  • Risk Factors (Especially for Free Wall Rupture):
    • Age > 60 years
    • Female sex
    • First MI
    • Anterior or lateral wall infarction
    • Absence of left ventricular hypertrophy


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 502

question: A 68-year-old woman is admitted with an acute anterior wall myocardial infarction. On hospital day 5, she suddenly develops hypotension and pulseless electrical activity. Bedside echocardiography shows a large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. At what time after myocardial infarction does this complication most commonly occur?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Microvascular injury typically occurs after more than 1 hour of sustained severe ischemia.


Timeline of Ischemic Events in Cardiac Myocytes:

The progression from initial oxygen deprivation to permanent tissue death follows a specific chronological order:

  • Immediate Response (Seconds): ATP depletion begins almost instantly after blood flow is interrupted.
  • Early Functional Loss (<2 minutes): The heart muscle loses its ability to contract within 2 minutes. (Option B)
  • Progression of ATP Loss:
    • 10 minutes: ATP levels drop to 50% of normal. (Option A)
    • 40 minutes: ATP levels drop to a critical 10% of normal.
  • The Point of No Return (20–40 minutes): Irreversible cell injury (necrosis) typically sets in during this window. (Option C)
  • Vascular Damage (>1 hour): Damage to the microscopic blood vessels (microvascular injury) occurs after an hour of sustained ischemia.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 495

question: A 62-year-old man presents with severe substernal chest pain that began 90 minutes ago. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads. Which of the following events is most likely occurring at this time in ischemic cardiac myocytes?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

After menopause, a decline in estrogen levels is associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction due to loss of its protective cardiovascular effects (favourable lipid profile, anti-inflammatory and vasodilatory effects).


Myocardial Infarction (MI):

  • Death of cardiac muscle due to prolonged ischemia
  • Commonly called a heart attack
  • Major cause: Atherosclerosis (most common underlying cause)
  • Sex differences:
    • Males: Higher risk in middle age
    • Females: Relatively protected during reproductive years (estrogen effect)
    • Postmenopause: Risk increases → IHD becomes the leading cause of death in older women
  • Hormone replacement therapy:
    • Not protective
    • May increase risk (possible prothrombotic effect)


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 494

question: Which hormone is associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction in post-menopausal women?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

After menopause, declining estrogen levels are associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction (MI) due to loss of estrogen's cardiovascular protective effects, including:

  • Favorable lipid profile (↑ HDL, ↓ LDL)
  • Improved endothelial function and vasodilation (↑ nitric oxide)
  • Anti-inflammatory and anti-atherogenic effects.


Myocardial Infarction (MI):

  • Death of cardiac muscle due to prolonged myocardial ischemia
  • Commonly known as a heart attack
  • Most common underlying cause: Atherosclerotic coronary artery disease
  • Sex differences:
    • Males: Higher risk of coronary artery disease in middle age
    • Females: Relatively protected during reproductive years due to estrogen effects
    • Postmenopausal women: Risk of ischemic heart disease increases due to loss of estrogen protection
  • Hormone replacement therapy:
    • Not recommended solely for prevention of cardiovascular disease
    • May increase cardiovascular risk in some women
    • Possible mechanism: Prothrombotic effect → increased risk of thrombosis.

Progesterone (Option A): Primarily involved in preparing and maintaining the endometrium for pregnancy; it does not provide the major cardioprotective effects associated with estrogen and is not responsible for increased MI risk after menopause.

Prolactin (Option C): A pituitary hormone involved in milk production (lactation); it has no significant role in the increased risk of myocardial infarction after menopause.

Oxytocin (Option D): A posterior pituitary hormone involved in uterine contractions during labor and milk ejection during breastfeeding; it is not associated with cardiovascular protection or postmenopausal MI risk.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 494

correctAnswer: B. Right ventricular hypertrophy and dilatation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In patients with chronic lung disease (like COPD or interstitial fibrosis), the right ventricle must pump against increased pulmonary vascular resistance. This leads to Cor Pulmonale.

  • Initially, the right ventricle undergoes hypertrophy (thickening of the wall) to compensate for the pressure.
  • Eventually, the ventricle fails and undergoes dilatation, leading to the clinical signs of systemic venous congestion like pedal oedema, raised Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP), and hepatomegaly.


Left ventricular hypertrophy (Option A): This is the response to systemic hypertension or aortic stenosis. In isolated right heart failure, the left ventricle is typically normal in size or may even be compressed by the bulging interventricular septum.


Mitral stenosis (Option C): While this can lead to right-sided heart failure, it is a left-sided valvular disease. The question specifies "isolated" right heart failure caused by chronic lung disease.


Decreased systemic vascular resistance (Option D): Decreased resistance (as seen in septic shock) would actually decrease the afterload on the left heart. It is increased pulmonary vascular resistance that drives right-sided failure in this scenario.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 484
lessonTitle: Ischemic Heart Disease and Myocardial Infarction
question: A patient with chronic lung disease presents with pedal oedema, raised JVP, and hepatomegaly. He is diagnosed with isolated right heart failure. What is the structural cause of his right-sided heart failure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Isolated right-sided heart failure most commonly results from pulmonary disorders causing pulmonary hypertension (cor pulmonale). This condition directly increases the pressure the right ventricle must work against without primarily involving the left side of the heart.


Right-Sided Heart Failure (RHF):

  • Causes:
    • Most common: Left-sided heart failure
    • Isolated RHF → Cor pulmonale (due to lung disease)
      • Parenchymal lung disease
      • Primary pulmonary hypertension
      • Recurrent pulmonary thromboembolism
      • Pulmonary vasoconstriction (OSA, high altitude)

  • Key Differences from Left-Sided HF:

    • Minimal pulmonary congestion
    • Marked systemic & portal venous congestion.

Systemic hypertension (Option A) causes pressure overload of the left ventricle, resulting in left ventricular hypertrophy and eventually left-sided heart failure, rather than isolated right-sided heart failure.

Mitral valve stenosis (Option B) increases left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures, which may eventually lead to pulmonary hypertension and secondary right-sided heart failure. However, it is not a primary cause of isolated right-sided heart failure.

Aortic regurgitation (Option D) causes left ventricular volume overload, leading to left ventricular dilatation and left-sided heart failure. It does not primarily affect the right ventricle.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 484

question: Which of the following is a cause of isolated right-sided heart failure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chronic hypertension causes left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and increased myocardial stiffness, leading to impaired relaxation and diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF).
  • Therefore, hypertension is the most common cause of left-sided diastolic heart failure (HFpEF).

Left-sided heart failure causes:

  • Common causes overall:
    • Ischemic heart disease → most common cause of left-sided heart failure overall (especially HFrEF)
    • Hypertension
    • Aortic/mitral valvular disease
    • Primary myocardial diseases
  • Types:
    • 1. Systolic heart failure (HFrEF)
      • ↓ Ejection fraction
      • Impaired myocardial contractility
      • Commonly due to ischemic heart disease (Option C ruled out)
    • 2. Diastolic heart failure (HFpEF)
      • Preserved ejection fraction
      • Stiff, noncompliant LV with impaired relaxation
      • Most commonly due to hypertension
      • Other causes: ageing, myocardial fibrosis, amyloidosis (Option B ruled out)

Constrictive pericarditis (Option D) can cause restrictive filling and mimic diastolic dysfunction but is not the common cause.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 484

question: A 68-year-old patient presents with exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows preserved ejection fraction with impaired left ventricular relaxation. He is diagnosed with left-sided diastolic heart failure (HFpEF). Which of the following is the most common cause of left-sided diastolic heart failure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct answer is Hemosiderin-laden macrophages. These pigment-containing alveolar macrophages are classically known as heart failure cells, formed due to chronic pulmonary congestion with RBC extravasation and iron accumulation.

[[figure-1]]

  • In left-sided heart failure, the weakened left ventricle causes blood to back up into the pulmonary vasculature, leading to pulmonary hypertension and congestion.
  • The high pressure causes small amounts of blood (RBCs) to leak into the alveoli. Alveolar macrophages phagocytose these RBCs and break down the haemoglobin into hemosiderin, a golden-brown pigment.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page

question: A patient with long-standing left-sided heart failure develops progressive dyspnea. Sputum cytology shows findings as shown in the image. What are these cells most appropriately termed?

correctAnswer: C. Decreased left atrial cavity size
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Ageing is associated with increased left atrial size, not decreased.


Effects of Ageing on the Heart:

  • ↑ Prevalence of heart disease with age
  • Major contributors: atherosclerosis, valvular degeneration, myocardial stiffening
  • Chambers:
    • ↑ Left atrial size
    • ↓ Left ventricular cavity size (Option D)
    • Sigmoid septum (basal septal bulge)
  • Valves:
    • Aortic & mitral calcification
    • Leaflet thickening
    • Lambl excrescences
  • Myocardium:
    • ↓ Myocytes, ↑ fibrosis
    • Lipofuscin (brown atrophy) (Option A)
    • Transthyretin amyloid → stiffness (Option B)
  • Coronaries:
    • Tortuosity, calcification
    • Atherosclerosis
  • Aorta:
    • Dilated, tortuous
    • Elastic fragmentation
    • Calcification


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 481

question: A histologic examination of the heart in an elderly individual reveals several age-related changes. Which of the following is not typically seen in the ageing heart?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct answer is Fibrosa, spongiosa, ventricularis. While blood vessels have the traditional intima/media/adventitia layers, cardiac valves have a specialised three-layer architecture designed for mechanical durability and flexibility.


Normal cardiac valves consist of three layers:

[[figure-1]]

  • Fibrosa - Dense collagen; mechanical strength
  • Spongiosa - Loose connective tissue core
  • Ventricularis/Atrialis - Elastin-rich; recoil


Endocardium, myocardium, epicardium (Option C): These are the layers of the heart wall itself, representing the inner lining, the muscle layer, and the outer covering.


Tunica interna, tunica externa (Option D): These are alternate names for the layers of a blood vessel wall.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 480

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis occurs because zone 3 hepatocytes are the least oxygenated and have high CYP450 activity, making them vulnerable to ischemic and toxic injury.

Centrilobular Necrosis (Zone 3 Necrosis):

Necrosis localised to the centrilobular region (acinar zone 3) of the hepatic lobule, surrounding the central vein.

  • Located at the distal end of hepatic blood flow
  • Receives the least oxygen supply
  • High concentration of CYP450 enzymes → increased susceptibility to toxic injury
  • Microscopic features:
    • Coagulative hepatocyte necrosis
    • Pyknotic/karyorrhectic nuclei
    • Sharp demarcation between viable and necrotic hepatocytes
    • Apoptotic bodies at the interface
    • Sinusoidal dilation and congestion (prominent in right-sided heart failure)
  • Causes:
    • Ischemia/shock (circulatory failure)
    • Venous outflow obstruction (e.g., right-sided heart failure)
    • Drug and toxin injury (metabolically activated toxins)
    • Ischemia-reperfusion injury
    • Alcoholic hepatitis

Which of the following conditions are associated with centrilobular necrosis?

  1. Ischemic shock
  2. Acetaminophen toxicity

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mitral > Aortic > Tricuspid > Pulmonary is correct because the mitral valve is affected in nearly all cases of chronic rheumatic heart disease, followed by the aortic valve. Tricuspid involvement is uncommon, and pulmonary valve involvement is rare.

Chronic Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD):

  • Mitral Valve (Most Commonly Affected):
    • Leaflet thickening
    • Commissural fusion
    • Thickened, shortened, fused chordae tendineae
    • Leads to mitral stenosis (“fish-mouth” valve)

[[figure-1]]

  • Valve involvement pattern:
    • Mitral alone → ~65%
    • Mitral + aortic → ~25%
    • Tricuspid → uncommon
    • Pulmonary → rare
