Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 510
question: Which of the following correctly lists the valves in order from most commonly to least commonly affected in chronic rheumatic heart disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chronic rheumatic heart disease is characterised by organised inflammation that leads to fibrous thickening of the valve leaflets and commissural fusion.

  • This fusion, often accompanied by calcification, creates the rigid, stenotic, "fish-mouth" deformity typical of the mitral valve in these patients.

[[figure-1]]

  • Gross Features:
    • Commissural fusion + fibrous bridging
    • Leaflet thickening and calcification
    • Classic “fish-mouth” stenosis

Vegetation formation (Option A): Seen in acute rheumatic carditis or infective endocarditis; does not produce chronic stenosis.

Myxomatous degeneration (Option B): Associated with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, not stenosis.

Fibrofatty replacement (Option D): Characteristic of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, not valvular disease.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 511
question: A 40-year-old woman with a history of Acute rheumatic fever in childhood had long-standing exertional dyspnea and palpitations. At autopsy, the mitral valve shows findings as shown. Which pathological process is primarily responsible for this deformity?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely organism is Staphylococcus aureus, as it is highly virulent and can infect previously normal valves, causing acute, rapidly destructive infective endocarditis.

Infective Endocarditis - Pathogenesis:

  • Predisposing Cardiac Lesions:
    • Rheumatic heart disease (historically most common)
    • Mitral valve prolapse
    • Degenerative calcific stenosis
    • Bicuspid aortic valve
    • Prosthetic valves
    • Congenital heart disease
  • Common Causative Organisms:
    • Native, damaged valves (50–60%): Viridans streptococci (Option A) (oral flora)
    • Most common overall: Staphylococcus aureus
      • Infects normal or abnormal valves
      • Most common in IV drug users
    • Others:
      • Enterococci
      • HACEK group (oral commensals) (Option D)
      • Gram-negative bacilli
      • Fungi (rare)
    • Prosthetic valve endocarditis:
      • Early (<2 months): S. aureus, S. epidermidis (skin flora)
      • Late (>1 year): Streptococci, S. aureus


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 512
question: Which organism is most commonly responsible for infective endocarditis in a previously normal valve?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hepatitis E is the most common cause of sporadic acute viral hepatitis in India, particularly among young adults living in areas with poor sanitation. The virus is primarily transmitted via the feco–oral route, most commonly through contaminated drinking water, leading to sporadic cases as well as large waterborne outbreaks.

Hepatitis E (HEV):

  • Transmission:
    • Feco-oral, water-borne
    • Zoonotic (pigs)
  • Self-limited acute hepatitis
  • Severe in pregnancy (mortality ~20%)
  • Chronic in immunocompromised

Hepatitis A virus (Option A): Also transmitted via the fecal–oral route and a common cause of acute hepatitis, especially in children, but hepatitis E is the more common cause of sporadic acute hepatitis in young adults in India.

Hepatitis B virus (Option B): Primarily transmitted through blood, sexual contact, or perinatally and more commonly associated with chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, rather than sporadic waterborne outbreaks.

Hepatitis C virus (Option C): Usually transmitted through blood exposure and most often presents as a chronic infection, with symptomatic acute hepatitis being relatively uncommon.

question: A 32-year-old man from rural India presents with 1 week of jaundice, anorexia, low-grade fever, and elevated ALT/AST levels. He has no history of blood transfusion or intravenous drug use. Serology is pending. What is the most common cause of sporadic acute viral hepatitis in India?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in genes encoding TGF-β receptors (TGFBR1/TGFBR2) or related signalling molecules, leading to abnormal TGF-β signalling and aggressive aortic aneurysm formation.

Loeys-Dietz Syndrome:

  • Rare connective tissue disorder with widespread vascular involvement.
  • Characterised by arterial aneurysms, dissections, and arterial tortuosity.
  • Often more aggressive than in Marfan syndrome.
  • Genetics:
    • Autosomal dominant in most cases.
    • Caused by pathogenic variants in:
      • TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB2, TGFB3
    • Rare autosomal recessive form from IPO8 variants
  • Features:
    • Vascular (most important):
      • Early, aggressive aortic aneurysm & dissection
      • Arterial tortuosity
      • Rupture at smaller sizes
    • Craniofacial: Hypertelorism, bifid uvula / cleft palate
    • Skeletal: Pectus deformity, scoliosis, joint laxity

Type III collagen synthesis (Option A): Seen in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV.

Fibrillin-1 protein (Option B): Defective in Marfan syndrome.

Elastin cross-linking (Option D): Seen in disorders affecting elastic tissue, but not the primary defect in Loeys-Dietz syndrome.



Reference:
  1. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 459
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1133/
question: A 12-year-old child presents with hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and early-onset ascending aortic aneurysm. Family history reveals a sudden aortic rupture at a young age. Genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Which of the following is defective in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Intrauterine mumps infection is classically associated with endocardial fibroelastosis in infants.

Endocardial Fibroelastosis (EFE):

  • Rare pediatric heart disease
  • Fibroelastic thickening of the left ventricular endocardium
  • Most common in children < 2 years
  • ~1/3 cases associated with:
    • Aortic valve obstruction
    • Other congenital heart defects
  • Etiology:
    • Viral infections (e.g., intrauterine mumps)
    • Tafazzin gene mutation (mitochondrial membrane protein defect)
  • Pathology:
    • Diffuse LV endocardial thickening
    • Leads to reduced compliance → diastolic dysfunction
  • Rapid, progressive heart failure
  • May result in early death if diffuse and severe

Rubella (Option A): Associated with congenital heart defects such as patent ductus arteriosus and pulmonary artery stenosis, but not classically with endocardial fibroelastosis.

Epstein-Barr virus (Option C): Not associated with endocardial fibroelastosis. Primarily causes infectious mononucleosis and certain lymphoproliferative disorders.

Cytomegalovirus (Option D): Can cause congenital infection and myocarditis, but is not the classic association described for endocardial fibroelastosis.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 522
question: A 6-month-old infant presents with progressive heart failure. Echocardiography shows diffuse fibroelastic thickening of the left ventricular endocardium with reduced ventricular compliance. There is a history of intrauterine viral exposure. Which infection is most commonly associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Restrictive cardiomyopathy.

  • The clinical triad of endomyocardial fibrosis, mural thrombi, and marked eosinophilia is characteristic of Loeffler endomyocarditis, a major cause of the restrictive phenotype.
  • This condition is characterised by a primary decrease in ventricular compliance, resulting in impaired ventricular filling during diastole.

Loeffler endomyocarditis:

  • Endomyocardial fibrosis + large mural thrombi
  • Marked peripheral eosinophilia
  • Eosinophilic infiltration of multiple organs
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Eosinophil major basic protein → necrosis → thrombus → fibrosis
  • May be associated with myeloid neoplasm
  • Responds to tyrosine kinase inhibitors

Dilated cardiomyopathy (Option A): Ventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction, not fibrosis from eosinophilia.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Option B): Asymmetric septal hypertrophy without eosinophilia or mural thrombus.

Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy (Option D): Fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricle, not eosinophil-mediated fibrosis.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 522
question: A 32-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea. Labs show marked eosinophilia. Imaging shows endomyocardial fibrosis with mural thrombus. Which type of cardiomyopathy is most likely?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Naxos disease presents with the classic triad: woolly hair (from birth), palmoplantar keratoderma, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.

Naxos disease:

Rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis combining:

  • Woolly hair + Palmoplantar keratoderma + Cardiomyopathy.
  • Caused by mutations affecting desmosomal proteins, especially:
    • Plakoglobin gene - classic Naxos.
    • Desmoplakin gene mutations - seen in a Carvajal syndrome variant with left-ventricular involvement.

Clinical features:

[[figure-1]]

  • Hair: Woolly, sparse, curly hair present from birth.
  • Skin: Diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma emerging in infancy.
  • Heart:
    • Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) typically develops by adolescence, with high penetrance.
    • Early asymptomatic ventricular changes can occur in childhood

Management:

  • Close cardiac follow-up with ECG and imaging.
  • Preventive strategies include:
    • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in symptomatic or high-risk patients

Carvajal syndrome (Option A) also presents with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma, but it predominantly involves left ventricular cardiomyopathy rather than right ventricular disease.

Noonan syndrome (Option C) is associated with facial dysmorphism, short stature, and pulmonary valve stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not woolly hair with palmoplantar keratoderma.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (Option D): Isolated ARVC lacks the characteristic cutaneous findings (woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma) seen in Naxos disease.

https://ijdvl.com/naxos-disease-a-rare-occurrence-of-cardiomyopathy-with-woolly-hair-and-palmoplantar-keratoderma/
question: A 13-year-old boy presents with recurrent syncope and palpitations. He has tightly curled woolly hair since birth and diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma since early childhood. ECG shows T-wave inversion in V1-V3, and echocardiography reveals right ventricular dilatation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dilated cardiomyopathy can result from metabolic and nutritional deficiencies that impair myocardial energy production.

Metabolic Causes of DCM:

  • Nutritional deficiency:
    • Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Deficiency: This leads to "Wet Beriberi," characterised by high-output heart failure and significant ventricular dilatation.
    • Selenium Deficiency: Associated with Keshan disease, a specific form of dilated cardiomyopathy originally identified in regions with selenium-poor soil.
    • Carnitine Deficiency: Carnitine is essential for transporting fatty acids into the mitochondria for energy production; a deficiency impairs myocardial metabolism, frequently resulting in a dilated phenotype.
  • Electrolyte deficiency: calcium, phosphate, magnesium
  • Endocrine disorders: thyroid disease, pheochromocytoma
  • Diabetes, obesity
  • Hemochromatosis


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1959
question:
Which of the following deficiencies is associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy?

  1. Thiamine deficiency
  2. Selenium deficiency
  3. Vitamin B12 deficiency
  4. Carnitine deficiency

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Alcohol abuse is a well-established risk factor for dilated cardiomyopathy. Chronic alcohol consumption causes direct myocardial toxicity (via ethanol and acetaldehyde), leading to progressive ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction.

Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM):

  • Four-chamber dilation with systolic dysfunction
  • Most common cardiomyopathy (age 20-50 yrs)
  • Causes:
    • Genetic:
      • Most common: Titin (TTN) mutation
      • Others: Lamin A/C, dystrophin
      • AD > X-linked > mitochondrial
    • Myocarditis: Often viral (e.g., Coxsackie B)
    • Toxins:
      • Alcohol (acetaldehyde toxicity, thiamine deficiency)
      • Chemotherapy (doxorubicin)
      • Heavy metals (cobalt)
    • Peripartum cardiomyopathy:
      • Late pregnancy / ≤5 months postpartum
      • Antiangiogenic factors implicated
    • Iron overload: Hemochromatosis or transfusion-related
    • Catecholamine excess / Stress:
      • Pheochromocytoma, cocaine
      • Takotsubo (“broken heart syndrome”)

Hypertension (Option A): Typically causes left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction rather than primary dilated cardiomyopathy.

Hyperlipidemia (Option C): Predisposes to atherosclerosis and ischemic heart disease, not primary DCM.

Rheumatic fever (Option D): Leads to valvular heart disease, particularly mitral stenosis, not dilated cardiomyopathy.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 516
question: A 48-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and echocardiographic evidence of dilated cardiomyopathy; which of the following is the most likely risk factor?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the least common of the three major pathologic patterns of cardiomyopathy. Among the primary categories, dilated cardiomyopathy is the most common (~90% of cases), while restrictive cardiomyopathy is the rarest.

Cardiomyopathies are intrinsic myocardial diseases causing cardiac dysfunction.

  • Primary → Predominantly confined to the myocardium
  • Secondary → Cardiac manifestation of a systemic disorder
  • Etiology:
    • Inflammatory disorders → Myocarditis
    • Immunologic diseases → Sarcoidosis
    • Metabolic disorders → Hemochromatosis
    • Muscular dystrophies
    • Genetic disorders affecting myocardial fibres
  • Major patterns:
    • Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) (Option A):
      • Most common (~90%)
    • Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) (Option B)
    • Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM)
      • Least common


Peripartum cardiomyopathy (Option D): A subtype of dilated cardiomyopathy occurring in late pregnancy or the early postpartum period; more common than restrictive cardiomyopathy.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 516
question: Which of the following is the least common type of cardiomyopathy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Kawasaki disease, also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, is an acute febrile medium-vessel vasculitis that primarily affects children younger than 5 years.

Kawasaki disease:

  • Clinical (Mucocutaneous LN syndrome):
    • Persistent high fever
    • Bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis
    • Strawberry tongue
    • Polymorphous rash with desquamation
    • Erythema of palms and soles
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy

[[figure-1]]

  • Complications:
    • Coronary arteritis → aneurysm, thrombosis, MI, rupture
    • ~20% untreated patients develop cardiac complications
  • Treatment:
    • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) + aspirin
    • Markedly reduces coronary complications

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option B): Medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis; does not present with mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.

Takayasu arteritis (Option C): Large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis in patients <50 years; characterised by weak pulses, not mucocutaneous features.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (Option D): IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis; presents with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 468
question: A 3-year-old child presents with persistent high fever, bilateral conjunctival erythema, strawberry tongue, erythema of palms and soles, desquamating rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy. This presentation is classically referred to as which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of anti-endothelial cell antibodies (AECA) is a classic association for Kawasaki disease and is thought to contribute to the vascular damage seen in the coronary arteries.

Kawasaki disease:

  • Acute febrile medium-vessel vasculitis
  • 80% <5 years old
  • Transmural inflammation
  • Self-limited but clinically significant due to coronary artery involvement
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Likely triggered by a viral infection in genetically susceptible children
    • Delayed-type hypersensitivity →
      • Cytokine release
      • Polyclonal B-cell activation
      • Autoantibodies to endothelial & smooth muscle cells

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option A): A medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis often associated with immune complex deposition and hepatitis B infection, not classically associated with AECA.

Takayasu arteritis (Option C): A large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis that is primarily T-cell mediated, not characteristically associated with AECA.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option D): Associated with c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA), not anti-endothelial cell antibodies.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 468
question: Anti-endothelial cell antibodies are most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: B. It commonly involves the aortic arch
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Takayasu arteritis classically affects the aortic arch and its major branches, leading to diminished upper limb pulses (“pulseless disease”).

Takayasu arteritis:

  • Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis (Option D)
  • Affects the aorta (especially the aortic arch) & major branches
  • Occurs mainly in patients <50 years
  • Also called “pulseless disease”
  • T-cell-mediated autoimmune aetiology (Option C)
  • Common vessels:
    • Aortic arch (most common)
    • Great vessels
    • Pulmonary arteries (~50%)
    • Coronary & renal arteries
    • May involve the entire aorta
  • Morphology:
    • Transmural thickening of the vessel wall
    • Intimal hyperplasia → luminal narrowing/obliteration
    • Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells
    • Patchy medial necrosis
    • Late stage: fibrosis of all layers
    • Aortic root dilation → aortic regurgitation (occasionally)
  • Clinical features:
    • Weak/absent upper limb pulses (“pulseless disease”)
    • ↓ BP in arms
    • Visual & neurologic symptoms
    • Renal artery stenosis (Option A) → hypertension


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 465, 466

question: A 27-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weak upper limb pulses, and visual disturbances. Imaging reveals narrowing of major branches of the aorta. She is diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis. Which of the following statements is correct?

correctAnswer: C. A negative biopsy does not exclude the diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a temporal headache, jaw claudication, and vision loss in an elderly patient with an elevated ESR is classic of Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis.

  • Giant cell arteritis has segmental (skip) lesions, so that biopsy may miss affected areas. If clinical suspicion is high, treatment (corticosteroids) is started immediately to prevent permanent blindness, even if the biopsy is initially negative.

Giant cell arteritis:

  • Chronic granulomatous vasculitis of large- and medium-sized arteries
  • Commonly involves the temporal, vertebral, and ophthalmic arteries
  • Can involve the aorta (giant cell aortitis) (Option D)
  • Risk: sudden irreversible blindness
  • Morphology:
    • Patchy lesions → biopsy ≥1 cm required (Option B)
    • Intimal thickening → luminal narrowing
    • Granulomatous inflammation in the media
    • Fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina
    • Multinucleated giant cells (~75%)
    • Healed lesions → fibrosis & medial scarring
  • Clinical features:
    • Age >50 years
    • Fever, fatigue, weight loss
    • Temporal headache & scalp tenderness
    • Jaw claudication
    • Ocular symptoms → diplopia or vision loss
  • Diagnosis:
    • Temporal artery biopsy (negative biopsy does not exclude due to patchy involvement) (Option A and C)
  • Treatment:
    • Immediate corticosteroids
    • Anti-TNF therapy in resistant cases
    • Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) in refractory or steroid-dependent cases


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 464, 465

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with new-onset temporal headache, jaw claudication, and transient vision loss. ESR is elevated. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this condition?

correctAnswer: C. It can also involve veins
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Giant cell arteritis is a large- and medium-sized arterial vasculitis and does not involve veins.

Giant cell arteritis:

  • Chronic granulomatous vasculitis of large- and medium-sized arteries
  • Commonly involves the temporal, vertebral, and ophthalmic arteries
  • Risk: sudden irreversible blindness (Option D)
  • Pathogenesis:
    • T-cell-mediated immune response to the vessel wall antigen
    • Key cytokines: IFN-γ, IL-17
    • Associated with MHC class II haplotypes
  • Morphology:
    • Patchy lesions → biopsy ≥1 cm required
    • Intimal thickening → luminal narrowing
    • Granulomatous inflammation in the media (Option B)
    • Fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina
    • Multinucleated giant cells (~75%)
    • Healed lesions → fibrosis & medial scarring
  • Clinical features:
    • Age >50 years (Option A)
    • Fever, fatigue, weight loss
    • Temporal headache & scalp tenderness
    • Jaw claudication
    • Ocular symptoms → diplopia or vision loss
  • Diagnosis:
    • Temporal artery biopsy (negative biopsy does not exclude due to patchy involvement)
  • Treatment:
    • Immediate corticosteroids
    • Anti-TNF therapy in resistant cases
    • Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) in refractory or steroid-dependent cases


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 464, 465

A 72-year-old woman presents with temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and transient visual disturbances. ESR is markedly elevated. Temporal artery biopsy confirms Giant cell arteritis.

Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Thyroidization of tubules is a classic feature of chronic pyelonephritis due to long-standing tubulointerstitial scarring.

Chronic Pyelonephritis - Morphology:

  • Gross:
    • Irregular, asymmetric scarring (if bilateral)
    • Coarse corticomedullary scars
    • Dilated, blunted, deformed calyces
    • Scars commonly at the upper & lower poles (reflux sites)
    • Unlike chronic GN → not diffuse/symmetric
  • Microscopy:
    • Tubular atrophy + dilation
    • “Thyroidization” (protein casts in dilated tubules)
    • Interstitial inflammation + fibrosis
    • Glomeruli:
      • Periglomerular fibrosis
      • Ischemic changes
      • Secondary hypertensive changes

Acute pyelonephritis (Option B): Shows acute neutrophilic tubulitis and interstitial suppuration, not thyroidization or chronic fibrosis.

Minimal change disease (Option C): Light microscopy is normal; electron microscopy shows podocyte foot process effacement without tubular atrophy or fibrosis.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (Option D): Characterised by crescent formation in glomeruli due to severe glomerular injury, not chronic tubulointerstitial scarring with thyroidization.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 844
question: A 52-year-old man with recurrent UTIs presents with hypertension and renal insufficiency. Imaging shows asymmetric kidneys with polar scars. Biopsy reveals findings as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical presentation, the patient has Primary Hyperaldosteronism

  • The most common cause (~60%) is bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia, involving bilateral hyperplasia of zona glomerulosa cells leading to autonomous aldosterone secretion.
    • ↓ Renin (suppressed RAAS)
    • ↑ Aldosterone → Na⁺ retention → volume expansion → hypertension
    • K⁺ loss → hypokalemia

Primary Hyperaldosteronism

  • Autonomous excess aldosterone secretion
  • Causes:
    • Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (~60%) → most common
    • Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Option B) = Conn syndrome
    • Familial hyperaldosteronism (Option D)
    • Rare: adrenocortical carcinoma (Option C)
  • Clinical features:
    • Hypertension (most common)
    • Hypokalemia (not always present) → weakness, paresthesia
    • Sodium and water retention → ↑ECF volume
  • Diagnosis:
    • ↑ Aldosterone / ↓ Renin ratio


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 1015-1017

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Postmortem clots often have a characteristic yellow-red, gelatinous "chicken fat" appearance due to sedimentation of fibrin and serum. They are typically not adherent to the vessel or heart wall and lack lines of Zahn seen in true thrombi.

Antemortem venous thrombus (Option B): Antemortem venous thrombi are generally firm, occlusive, and have a red colour due to trapped red blood cells.

Antemortem mural thrombus (Option C): Mural thrombi form along the heart wall and appear as dry, friable, layered masses with lines of Zahn, different from postmortem clots.

Antemortem arterial thrombus (Option D): Arterial thrombi are pale, granular, usually occlusive and firmly attached to the vessel wall, not gelatinous.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page no. 112
question: During the autopsy of a 70-year-old man, a clot with a yellow, gelatinous appearance resembling "chicken fat" is observed within the heart chamber. Such a finding is characteristic of which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The main pulmonary artery bifurcates into the right and left pulmonary arteries at the level of the pulmonary hilum. Large emboli often lodge at this bifurcation, known as a saddle embolus, causing sudden obstruction and cardiopulmonary compromise.

Pulmonary vein (Option B): Pulmonary veins drain oxygenated blood to the left atrium and are not typical sites for emboli causing obstruction in the lungs.

Ascending aorta (Option C): The ascending aorta is a systemic artery, and emboli causing pulmonary obstruction do not lodge here.

Descending aorta (Option D): The descending aorta supplies systemic circulation to the lower body, not relevant to pulmonary embolism.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page no. 114
question: A 60-year-old woman, recently hospitalised after a hip fracture surgery, suddenly develops severe dyspnea and hypotension. Autopsy reveals a large embolus blocking the main vascular bifurcation at the level of the lungs. In which vessel is this embolus most likely located?

correctAnswer: A. Characterized by the presence of Aschoff bodies
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is a chronic sequel of acute rheumatic fever (ARF), which follows infection with Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). Its hallmark is Aschoff bodies in the myocardium - distinctive granulomatous lesions that confirm rheumatic carditis.

  • It develops as a complication of untreated or inadequately treated acute rheumatic fever (ARF), which is caused by an abnormal immune response to an infection with Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus bacteria. (Option B ruled out)
  • The bacteria trigger an immune response that leads to chronic inflammation and scarring of heart valves, commonly affecting the mitral valve.
    • Order of valves affected in RHD: Mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonary.

Manifests only as myocarditis (Option C): RHD involves all three layers of the heart (pancarditis) - endocarditis (valvulitis), myocarditis (Aschoff bodies), and pericarditis (“bread-and-butter” appearance).

Associated with aortic valve rupture (Option D): Chronic RHD causes valvular fibrosis and stenosis, most often mitral stenosis, not rupture. Aortic valve involvement causes regurgitation, not rupture.



Reference:

Robbins & Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Pages 561

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The histopathology findings given show Reed-Sternberg cells suggestive of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

  • Hodgkin lymphoma is staged using the Ann Arbor staging system with Cotswolds modification.

  • Certain suffixes are added to provide additional prognostic information.

  • The suffix “X” denotes Bulky disease.

  • Bulky disease means:

    • A large tumor mass

    • Usually, a mediastinal mass >1/3 of the thoracic diameter

    • Or nodal mass >10 cm.

  • Bulky disease is associated with higher tumour burden, worse prognosis and need for more aggressive therapy.

  • It is especially important in pediatric and mediastinal Hodgkin lymphoma.

  • The “X” suffix helps guide:

    • Radiation decisions

    • Chemotherapy intensity.

question: A patient with myocardial infarction shows changes of coagulative necrosis, loss of nuclei and neutrophil infiltration at:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, especially UV-B (280-320 nm), causes direct DNA damage. The hallmark lesion is the formation of pyrimidine dimers, mainly:

  • Thymine-thymine dimers
  • Cytosine-containing dimers

UV light induces covalent bonding between adjacent pyrimidine bases in DNA. These dimers distort the DNA helix and interfere with:

  • DNA replication
  • Transcription

If unrepaired, mutations accumulate, leading to carcinogenesis.

  • Normally, these lesions are repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.
  • Defective NER is seen in xeroderma pigmentosum, causing extreme UV sensitivity and high skin cancer risk.
  • UV-induced mutations commonly affect tumour suppressor genes, such as TP53
  • Therefore, pyrimidine dimer formation is the primary initiating molecular event in UV carcinogenesis.

Increase in cyclins (Option B): Cyclins regulate the cell cycle and may be altered in cancers.

Inhibition of TP53 (Option C): TP53 mutations can occur secondary to UV-induced DNA damage. However, UV light does not directly inhibit TP53 initially.

Increase in NF-κB (Option D): NF-κB is involved in inflammation and cell survival signalling.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathological Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 289

The given features, tall stature, long limbs (arachnodactyly), and joint hypermobility, suggest a diagnosis of Marfan Syndrome, caused by FBN1 mutations that weaken connective tissue by affecting fibrillin-1.

Genetics

Defect on chromosome 15, involving the FBN1 gene → defective fibrillin-1 protein.

Pathophysiology

  • Impaired elastin formation
  • Dominant negative effect
  • Loss of regulation of TGF-β

Clinical features

  • Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP - M/c Cardiac abnormality)
  • Aortic Dissection (M/c cause of death)
  • Retinal Detachment
  • Freely moveable Joint (M/c : Thumb joint)
  • Arachnodactyly (long/spider fingers)

• Mitochondrial inheritance follows a maternal inheritance pattern, meaning that only the mother passes mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) to her offspring.

Inheritance Pattern

  • Threshold effect: Minimum percentage of mutated mtDNA required for disease manifestation. In the presence of heteroplasmy, the threshold effect leads to variability in clinical expression across different tissues and mtDNA mutations.

  • Arterial dissection is a structural mechanical injury involving a tear in the tunica intima that allows blood to enter and separate the layers of the arterial wall. It represents mechanical failure rather than functional endothelial dysfunction.

Endothelial Dysfunction:

  • Definition:
    • Functional impairment of endothelial cells leading to reduced vasodilation, increased leukocyte adhesion, and enhanced thrombogenicity.
  • Mechanisms:
    • Decreased nitric oxide production
    • Increased reactive oxygen species
    • Upregulation of adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, VCAM-1)
    • Increased procoagulant activity
  • Clinical Consequences:
    • Contributes to atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes-related vascular damage, and thrombus formation.

Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) (Option A): Promote oxidative stress, reduce nitric oxide bioavailability, and activate inflammatory pathways, particularly in diabetes.

Atherosclerosis (Option B): Endothelial dysfunction is an early initiating event in atherosclerosis; established atherosclerosis further propagates endothelial dysfunction through chronic inflammation and disturbed flow.

Inflammatory cytokines (Option D): Cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1 induce adhesion molecule expression and promote a pro-thrombotic endothelial phenotype.

  • Clinical features:

    • In the kidneys, it leads to nephrosclerosis → diffuse ischemia and glomerular scarring.

Cholesterol plaque deposition (Option A): Atherosclerosis affects large arteries, not arterioles, and involves lipid-laden plaques rather than homogeneous hyaline thickening.

Immune complex-mediated inflammation (Option C): Vasculitis causes inflammatory damage and fibrinoid necrosis, not hyaline deposition.

explanationHtml:
This clinical presentation is typical of secondary achalasia caused by Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis).

  • The disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, which infects and destroys the Auerbach (myenteric) plexus of the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Loss of the myenteric plexus results in:
    • Failure of esophageal peristalsis
    • Impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES)
    • Progressive dilation of the esophagus (megaesophagus)
  • Chagas disease can also affect other regions containing the myenteric plexus, including the colon (megacolon) and occasionally the duodenum and ureters.

Chagas Disease

  • Cause: Trypanosoma cruzi infection
  • Transmission: Triatomine (“kissing”) bug
  • Mechanism: Destruction of Auerbach (myenteric) plexus
  • Major GI manifestations:
    • Megaesophagus
    • Megacolon

Degeneration of nitric oxide-producing neurons (Option A): Seen in primary achalasia.

Autoimmune destruction of inhibitory neurons (Option B): Proposed in idiopathic achalasia.

Smooth muscle fibrosis (Option D): Seen in systemic sclerosis (hypotensive LES).

Explanation:

Crooke hyaline change is the characteristic pituitary histologic finding in hypercortisolism. Excess glucocorticoids cause accumulation of cytokeratin intermediate filaments in corticotroph cells, producing pale, homogeneous cytoplasm.

[[figure-1]]

Cushing’s syndrome- Morphology:

  • Pituitary: Crooke hyaline change in corticotroph cells (paler cytoplasm from keratin filament accumulation).
  • Adrenal Glands:
    • Exogenous steroid use: Bilateral cortical atrophy (zona fasciculata/reticularis), normal zona glomerulosa.
    • Endogenous Cushing:
      • Diffuse hyperplasia: Bilateral, thickened cortex with vacuolated lipid-rich outer layer and compact lipid-poor zona reticularis.
      • Macronodular hyperplasia: Nodules 10-30 mm; admixture of lipid-poor and lipid-rich cells.
      • Micronodular hyperplasia: 1-3 mm pigmented nodules (lipofuscin), atrophic intervening cortex.
      • Adenoma/Carcinoma:
        • Adenomas: Yellow, encapsulated, <30 g, resemble zona fasciculata.
        • Carcinomas: Large, unencapsulated, >200-300 g, malignant features; contralateral cortex atrophic.

Corticotroph hyperplasia (Option B): May occur in chronic CRH stimulation but is not the classic histologic change caused by glucocorticoid excess.

Basophil hyperplasia (Option C): Corticotrophs are basophils, but the typical change in Cushing syndrome is Crooke hyaline change rather than simple hyperplasia.

Pituitary acidophil hyperplasia (Option D): Involves GH or prolactin-secreting cells and is unrelated to Cushing syndrome.

question: A 55-year-old male presents to the gastroenterology clinic with complaints of persistent abdominal pain, nausea, and unintentional weight loss over the past three months. His medical history is significant for peptic ulcer disease and he is a former smoker. An upper endoscopy reveals multiple gastric lesions, and a biopsy is taken for histological examination. The results indicate the presence of gastric adenocarcinoma, and positive for Helicobactor pylori. Which protein produced by Helicobacter pylori is primarily associated with this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Gastric adenomas most commonly arise in a background of chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia, which predisposes to dysplasia and carcinoma.

Gastric Adenoma:

  • Benign neoplastic polyp with dysplasia
  • ~10% of gastric polyps
  • Usually arises in the background of:
    • Chronic gastritis
    • Atrophy
    • Intestinal metaplasia
  • Exception: Germline APC or MUTYH mutations

Acute erosive gastritis (Option B): Acute gastritis causes superficial mucosal injury and inflammation, usually due to NSAIDs, alcohol, or stress, but it does not predispose to gastric adenoma formation.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (Option C): GERD primarily affects the esophagus and may lead to Barrett esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma, but it is not associated with gastric adenomas.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (Option D): This condition involves gastrin-secreting tumours (gastrinomas), causing excess gastric acid and recurrent peptic ulcers. It does not predispose to gastric adenoma development.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 705

Hepatitis C (HCV) is primarily a blood-borne virus. Transmission occurs when the blood of an infected person enters the body of someone who is not infected.

Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Transmission:

  • Primary Routes:

question: A patient is diagnosed with Bourneville disease after evaluation of the characteristic skin and systemic findings. Which mode of inheritance is typically seen in this disorder?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HBx is the key oncogenic HBV protein that activates proliferative signalling pathways, inhibits p53, and alters epigenetic regulation, promoting hepatocellular carcinoma.

  • Chronic infection with the hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a major global cause of HCC.
  • The HBV X protein (HBx) is implicated in promoting cancer development.
  • HBx influences DNA methylation and histone modification, altering gene expression without changing DNA sequence
  • HBx shifts cellular balance toward survival and proliferation.
  • It may impair apoptosis (programmed cell death) and promote cell cycle dysregulation.

HBsAg (Surface Antigen) (Option A): Primarily serves as the envelope protein for viral entry and immune decoys. While its accumulation in "ground-glass hepatocytes" indicates chronic infection, it is not the primary driver of the multi-pathway signalling disruptions listed.

HBcAg (Core Antigen) (Option B): This is the structural protein that forms the viral capsid. It is a major target for the host immune response but lacks the transactivating properties of HBx.

HBeAg (Envelope/Secreted Antigen) (Option C): A marker of high viral replication and infectivity. It acts as an immune tolerogen to help the virus evade the host's immune system, but it does not directly trigger the intracellular oncogenic pathways described.



Reference:
  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4197427/
  2. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 293, 757

Explanation:

[[figure-2]]

Tubular adenoma (Option B): Displays dysplastic epithelium with nuclear hyperchromasia and pseudostratification.

[[figure-3]]

Sessile serrated polyp (Option D): Shows full-length crypt serration, crypt dilation, and lateral crypt growth, predominantly occurs in the right colon.

[[figure-4]]

question: A 4-year-old child presents with painless rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy reveals a pedunculated rectal polyp. Histologic examination shows findings as shown, along with an inflamed lamina propria. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presentation is classic for Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome (PJS).

  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant (Statement 1 ruled out)
  • Gene: STK11 - tumour suppressor, loss-of-function mutation (Statement 3)
  • Clinical features:
    • Multiple hamartomatous polyps (mainly jejunum, also stomach/colon)
    • Mucocutaneous pigmentation – dark macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms, genitalia, perianal area
    • Complications: Intussusception, ↑ risk of GI, pancreatic, breast, ovarian, uterine cancers (~40%)
  • Histology: Arborising pattern of smooth muscle, lamina propria, and glands with normal epithelium (Statement 4).

Congenital retinal pigmentation (Statement 2) is not a feature of PJS.



Reference:

Robbins & Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Page 809,810

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The features of a rapidly enlarging uterine mass with perimenopausal bleeding and malignant smooth muscle histology are diagnosed as Leiomyosarcoma.

Origin

Arise from the myometrium or endometrial stromal precursor cells

Genetics
  • Tumor suppressor/oncogene mutations: TP53, RB, PTEN
  • MED12 mutations → mostly in uterine smooth muscle tumors.

Morphology
  • Bulky, fleshy masses invading the uterine wall
  • Polypoid masses projecting into the uterine lumen

Microscopy

  • Tumor cells are irregular in size and have hyperchromatic nuclei.
  • Mitotic figures

Clinical features
  • Occurs before and after menopause, peak 40-60 years
  • Rapidly enlarging uterine mass, abnormal bleeding
  • Frequently recurs after surgery

Leiomyoma (Option A) is a benign, slow-growing smooth muscle tumor, not the malignant lesion in question.

Endometrial carcinoma (Option B) arises from glandular endometrium, not smooth muscle tissue.

Adenomyosis (Option C) causes diffuse uterine thickening and is benign, unlike a discrete tumor.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran, and Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 921-922.
question: A 45-year-old female presents with a rapidly enlarging uterine mass accompanied by perimenopausal bleeding. Histopathological examination reveals a malignant smooth muscle tumor. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario points towards ependymoma. In adults, the spinal cord is the most common location, CSF dissemination is uncommon, and posterior fossa ependymomas often present with hydrocephalus due to progressive obstruction of the fourth ventricle.

Ependymoma

Definition

Glial tumor arising from ependymal lining of ventricles or central canal

Common Age

Children and young adults

Common Sites
  • Floor of the fourth ventricle in posterior fossa in children (Option 2 ruled out)
  • Spinal cord in adults (Option 1)

Association

Neurofibromatosis type 2

Clinical Features

Headache, vomiting, ataxia, hydrocephalus; spinal lesions cause pain, weakness, sensory symptoms (Option 4)

Gross

Usually well-circumscribed and may arise in the fourth ventricle or spinal cord

Histology

Perivascular pseudorosettes and true ependymal rosettes

WHO Grade

Usually Grade 2; anaplastic ependymoma is Grade 3

Spread

CSF dissemination is uncommon (Option 3)

Prognosis

Depends on location, grade, and extent of resection

Treatment

Surgical excision with radiotherapy in selected cases.


Reference:

Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 1180.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. It results from a deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), leading to hyperuricemia, neurological symptoms, self-mutilation (lip injuries), and characteristic nail deformities.

Autosomal dominant (Option A): Autosomal dominant disorders typically affect both males and females equally and do not usually present with the classic features of this condition.

Autosomal recessive (Option B): Autosomal recessive disorders require two mutated gene copies and manifest differently than this syndrome.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes that appear as round, intensely eosinophilic (acidophilic) cytoplasmic bodies with condensed or fragmented nuclei.

  • They represent hepatocytes undergoing programmed cell death (apoptosis) due to hepatocellular injury.
  • Classically described in → Yellow fever (a characteristic histopathological finding). (Statement 3)
  • Seen in viral hepatitis (acute and chronic), where similar apoptotic hepatocytes are often termed acidophil bodies. (Statement 1 and 4)
  • Histopathological Examination:
    • Pyknosis → Nuclear chromatin condensation
    • Karyorrhexis → Nuclear fragmentation
    • Acidophilic/Councilman bodies → Deeply eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocytes.

Autoimmune hepatitis (Statement 2): The characteristic histologic features include interface hepatitis, lymphoplasmacytic portal inflammation, and hepatocyte necrosis, rather than Councilman bodies.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 749

question: A 46-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes undergoes a liver biopsy for persistently elevated transaminases. Histology is suggestive of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Which of the following histologic features is not typically seen in NASH?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hepatitis B infection is not typically associated with hepatic steatosis. While it causes chronic hepatitis, inflammation, and cirrhosis, it does not characteristically produce fatty change.

  • Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) refers to the accumulation of triglycerides within hepatocytes.
  • It most commonly occurs due to metabolic abnormalities, alcohol use, toxins, or certain metabolic diseases that disrupt normal lipid metabolism in the liver.

Important Causes of Hepatic Steatosis:

  • Chronic alcohol use (Option A):
    • Alcohol metabolism increases NADH, impairing fatty acid oxidation and promoting triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes.
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus (Option B):
    • Strongly associated with hepatic steatosis due to insulin resistance, which increases hepatic lipid accumulation and contributes to metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease.
  • Wilson disease (Option C):
    • Caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to copper accumulation in the liver.
    • Fatty change may occur early in the disease, so it can be associated with hepatic steatosis.
  • Obesity
  • Metabolic syndrome
  • Hepatitis C (especially genotype 3)
  • Drugs: Methotrexate, Amiodarone, Valproic acid, Tamoxifen, Tetracycline
  • Acute fatty liver of pregnancy / HELLP syndrome
  • Starvation / Total parenteral nutrition


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2620

question: Which of the following statements regarding secondary hemochromatosis is not true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hereditary hemochromatosis markedly increases the risk of HCC, especially in patients with cirrhosis. Iron-induced oxidative DNA damage predisposes to malignant transformation.

Clinical Features:

  • Triad:
    • Cirrhosis
    • Diabetes mellitus
    • Skin pigmentation
  • Hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, cardiac dysfunction
  • Atypical arthritis, hypogonadism
  • More common in males (5-7:1).
  • Symptoms usually appear after 40 years (earlier in men; delayed in women due to menstruation).

Major Complication: Hepatocellular carcinoma

  • Risk is ~200-fold increased
  • Risk persists even after iron reduction

Acute liver failure (Option B): Hereditary hemochromatosis typically causes chronic progressive liver injury leading to fibrosis and cirrhosis, rather than acute liver failure. Liver damage develops gradually due to progressive iron accumulation and oxidative injury.

Splenic rupture (Option C): Splenic rupture is not a recognised complication of hereditary hemochromatosis. Although mild splenomegaly may occur secondary to portal hypertension in advanced cirrhosis, spontaneous rupture is not associated with this condition.

Autoimmune hepatitis (Option D): Autoimmune hepatitis is an immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease characterised by autoantibodies and interface hepatitis.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 773
question: Which of the following is the major life-threatening complication of hereditary hemochromatosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Hereditary Hemochromatosis, and the gene responsible (HFE) is located on Chromosome 6.

Hereditary Hemochromatosis:

  • Caused by mutations affecting hepcidin regulation:
    • HFE gene (the most common cause)
    • TFR2 (transferrin receptor 2)
    • HAMP (hepcidin gene)
    • HJV (hemojuvelin) → juvenile hemochromatosis
  • Mutations in HFE, HJV, HAMP, or TFR2 → Reduced hepcidin synthesis → Increased ferroportin activity → Increased intestinal iron absorption → Systemic iron overload
  • Most Common Genetic Cause:
    • HFE mutation C282Y (cysteine → tyrosine at position 282)
      • Present in ≥70% of cases
      • Homozygosity frequency ≈ 1 in 220
      • Low penetrance
    • H63D mutation → milder, worldwide distribution


Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6660136/
question: A 42-year-old man presents with fatigue, skin hyperpigmentation, and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus. Laboratory studies show elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation. The gene responsible for this condition is located on which chromosome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct diagnosis is Hereditary hemochromatosis, because iron deposition begins in periportal hepatocytes, appears as Prussian blue-positive hemosiderin, and progresses to micronodular cirrhosis with minimal inflammation.

Hemochromatosis - Morphology:

  • Liver:
    • Earliest deposition in periportal hepatocytes
    • Golden-yellow hemosiderin granules
    • Prussian blue positive
    • Inflammation is typically minimal.
    • Progression → micronodular cirrhosis
    • Late stage → small, shrunken, dark brown liver
  • Other organs:
    • Pancreas → fibrosis → diabetes mellitus
    • Heart → cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias
    • Skin → slate-grey pigmentation
    • Joints → pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition)
    • Pituitary/testes → hypogonadism

Wilson's disease (Option A) involves copper accumulation. Copper is stained with Rhodanine or Orcein stains, not Prussian blue. It also typically presents at a younger age.

Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) (Option B) is an autoimmune destruction of the bile ducts. It typically presents with itching (pruritus) and elevated alkaline phosphatase, mainly in women.

α1-antitrypsin deficiency (Option D) shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant pink globules in the hepatocytes, not iron-positive granules.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 771-773

question: Which of the following findings is wrong regarding the diagnosis of Wilson's disease?

correctAnswer: C. Targeted genetic testing for the familial ATP7B mutation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, resulting in impaired biliary copper excretion and accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues.

  • When a specific pathogenic ATP7B mutation has already been identified in the affected patient (proband), the most appropriate method for screening asymptomatic first-degree relatives is targeted genetic testing for the known familial mutation.
  • This allows early identification of affected individuals before clinical manifestations develop and enables timely initiation of therapy.
  • The diagnosis of Wilson's disease is usually based on biochemical findings such as:
    • Decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels
    • Increased hepatic copper content (the most sensitive and accurate test)
    • Increased urinary copper excretion (the most specific test)
    • Demonstration of Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination
  • However, ATP7B mutation analysis is useful for confirming the diagnosis and for screening family members, particularly when the familial mutation is already known.

Serum ceruloplasmin measurement (Option A): Often decreased in Wilson disease and used in biochemical screening, but levels may be normal in some patients or altered by liver injury.

24-hour urinary copper excretion (Option B): A highly specific diagnostic test, commonly used in the evaluation of suspected Wilson disease, but less definitive for screening when the familial mutation is known.

Slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings (Option D): Helpful supportive finding, especially in patients with neurologic disease, but rings may be absent in early or asymptomatic cases.



Reference:
  1. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 774
  2. https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/liver-disease/wilson-disease/diagnosis

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Valproate classically causes microvesicular steatosis due to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired β-oxidation.

Drug-liver injury associations:

  • Acetaminophen (Option A) → Confluent necrosis
  • Halothane → Confluent hepatic necrosis (halothane hepatitis)
  • Nitrofurantoin → Portal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation
  • Oral contraceptives (OCPs) (Option C) → Budd–Chiari syndrome
  • Anabolic steroids → Bland cholestasis; peliosis hepatis; hepatic adenoma
  • Alcohol → Steatosis; Mallory hyaline; pericellular (“chicken-wire”) fibrosis
  • Valproate → Microvesicular steatosis
  • Tetracycline → Microvesicular steatosis

question: Which of the following drug-liver injury associations is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Prothrombin time reflects hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (especially factors I, II, V, VII, X).

Hepatocyte Synthetic Function:

  • Serum Measurements:
    • Proteins secreted into the blood:
      • Serum albumin (Decreased in liver disease)
    • Coagulation factors (PT and PTT; factors I, II, V, VII, X) (Decreased)
  • Hepatocyte metabolism:
    • Serum ammonia (Increased in liver failure)
    • Aminopyrine breath test (hepatic demethylation) (Decreased)

Hepatocyte Integrity:

  • Cytosolic hepatocellular enzymes:
    • AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase)
    • ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase) (Option A)
    • LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase)
  • Expected Change in Disease: Increased

Biliary Excretory Function:

  • Substances normally secreted in bile:
    • Serum bilirubin (Option D) (Total = conjugated + unconjugated; Direct = conjugated only)
    • Urine bilirubin & serum bile acids

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) has the highest likelihood of progressing from acute infection to chronic hepatitis among the hepatitis viruses.

Hepatitis C (HCV):

  • Virology:

  • Treatment:
    • Direct-acting antivirals (NS3, NS5A, NS5B inhibitors)

Hepatitis A virus (Option A): Hepatitis A virus is a non-enveloped RNA virus transmitted by the fecal–oral route, typically through contaminated food or water. HAV causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and does not lead to chronic infection.

Hepatitis B virus (Option B): Hepatitis B virus is a DNA virus transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and perinatal exposure. Although HBV can cause chronic hepatitis, only about 5–10% of infected adults develop chronic infection, which is much lower than the chronicity rate seen with HCV.

Hepatitis E virus (Option D): Hepatitis E virus is a fecal–oral transmitted RNA virus that usually causes acute hepatitis, particularly in regions with poor sanitation. Chronic infection is rare and mainly occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as transplant recipients.

The histology image given shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). This is suggestive of Barrett’s esophagus.

  • Barrett’s esophagus is a condition in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium. This is an example of metaplasia.

  • It occurs due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

  • Barrett’s esophagus commonly affects the distal esophagus/gastroesophageal junction.

  • It is a premalignant condition for esophageal adenocarcinoma.

  • Diagnosis requires:

  • The presence of goblet cells is the key diagnostic feature.

Squamous cell CA (Option C): Malignant tumour composed of atypical squamous cells. Histology may show keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Usually occurs in the upper/middle esophagus.

[[figure-2]]

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The biopsy findings of homogeneous, pink hyaline thickening of the arteriolar walls and luminal narrowing are characteristic of hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Chronic hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis resulting from chronic hemodynamic stress, causing plasma protein leakage and increased smooth muscle matrix synthesis.

Hyaline Arteriolosclerosis:

  • Morphology: Homogeneous, pink hyaline thickening of arteriolar walls with luminal narrowing.

[[figure-1]]

  • Mechanism: Leakage of plasma proteins across injured endothelium + increased smooth muscle matrix synthesis.
  • Clinical features:
    • More severe in hypertension and diabetes.
    • In the kidneys, it leads to nephrosclerosis → diffuse ischemia and glomerular scarring.

Amyloidosis (Option A): While amyloidosis also shows pink, amorphous deposits on H&E, it typically appears more "waxy" and extracellular. More importantly, amyloid is identified by Congo Red staining with apple-green birefringence under polarised light, rather than the simple hyaline thickening of hypertension.

[[figure-2]]

Hypercholesterolemia (Option C): This is primarily associated with atherosclerosis, which affects large and medium-sized muscular arteries (like the renal artery or aorta) by forming intimal plaques containing cholesterol crystals and foam cells, rather than the diffuse hyaline thickening of small arterioles.


Vasculitis (Option D): Arteriolar vasculitis (like polyarteritis nodosa) typically presents with fibrinoid necrosis (a shaggy, bright red appearance) and an inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall, rather than the smooth, homogeneous hyaline thickening described here.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 448
question: A 65-year-old patient presents with slowly progressive renal insufficiency. A kidney biopsy shows arterioles with homogeneous, pink hyaline thickening of the walls and associated luminal narrowing. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these vascular changes?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The hallmark vascular lesion seen in severe (malignant) hypertension is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

Hyperplastic Arteriolosclerosis:

  • Morphology: Concentric, laminated “onion-skin” thickening of arteriolar walls with luminal narrowing.

[[figure-1]]

  • Composition: Smooth muscle cells + reduplicated basement membrane.
  • Severe cases: Malignant hypertension → fibrinoid necrosis of vessels.

Hyaline arteriolosclerosis (Option A): Typically seen in chronic, mild to moderate hypertension or diabetes, not malignant hypertension.

Mönckeberg medial sclerosis (Option C): Medial calcification of muscular arteries without luminal narrowing; unrelated to blood pressure severity.

Atherosclerosis (Option D): Affects large arteries, driven by lipid deposition and plaque formation, not small arterioles in severe hypertension

Nephrotic syndrome:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • All listed mutations are associated with nephrotic syndrome, primarily through disruption of podocyte structure and slit diaphragm integrity.

NPHS1 (Nephrin):

  • Encodes nephrin, a vital component of the slit diaphragm.
  • Mutations lead to congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type.
  • Characterised by minimal change disease-like glomerulopathy and extensive foot process effacement.

NPHS2 (Podocin):

  • Encodes podocin, an intracellular protein associated with the slit diaphragm.
  • Mutations cause autosomal recessive FSGS, typically presenting as steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children.

ACTN4 & INF2:

  • Encode actin-binding proteins α-actinin-4 and inverted formin-2.
  • Associated with autosomal dominant FSGS.
  • Features an insidious onset with a high risk of progression to renal insufficiency.

TRPC6:

  • Found in families with adult-onset FSGS.
  • Mutations are thought to disrupt podocyte function by increasing calcium flux in the cells.

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 831
question:
Which of the following mutations are associated with nephrotic syndrome?

  1. Nephrin
  2. Podocin
  3. ACTN4
  4. INF2
  5. TRPC6

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The liver increases the synthesis of fibrinogen and other coagulation factors to compensate for the low plasma oncotic pressure.

  • Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by massive urinary loss of plasma proteins due to increased glomerular permeability. In response to reduced plasma oncotic pressure, the liver increases synthesis of several proteins, including:
    • Fibrinogen
    • Other coagulation factors
    • Lipoproteins
  • Elevated fibrinogen levels contribute to the hypercoagulable state seen in nephrotic syndrome, increasing the risk of venous thrombosis (e.g., renal vein thrombosis).

Antithrombin III (Option A): Lost in the urine and decreased in plasma, contributing to thrombosis risk.

Albumin (Option B): Lost in large amounts in urine. Although hepatic synthesis increases, plasma albumin levels remain low (hypoalbuminemia).

Immunoglobulin G (Option D): Lost in urine, leading to decreased plasma levels and increased susceptibility to infections.



Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9453016/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Minimal change disease is a distinct primary podocytopathy characterised by diffuse foot process effacement without segmental sclerosis. It is not classified under FSGS.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS):

Classification:

  • Primary: Idiopathic
  • Secondary:
    • Viral & Toxic Injury: Caused by infections (HIV, SARS-CoV-2), heroin addiction, sickle cell disease (Option B), or other direct toxicities.
    • Adaptive Changes:
      • Reduced renal mass (nephrectomy, reflux nephropathy (Option A), agenesis)
      • Obesity, advanced CKD
      • Mechanism: glomerular hypertension → podocyte loss → sclerosis
    • Inherited Forms: Uncommon mutations in slit diaphragm- and actin cytoskeleton-associated proteins.
      • NPHS1 (nephrin) → congenital nephrotic syndrome (Finnish type)
      • NPHS2 (podocin) → steroid-resistant childhood nephrotic syndrome
      • ACTN4 (Option C) → autosomal dominant FSGS
      • INF2 → autosomal dominant FSGS
      • TRPC6 → adult-onset FSGS
    • APOL1 Risk Alleles
    • Secondary Scarring:
      • IgA nephropathy
      • ANCA-associated vasculitis


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 831
question: A 40-year-old man presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis. You are reviewing conditions associated with secondary FSGS. Which of the following is not associated with FSGS?

correctAnswer: B. Tip lesion variant - Best; Collapsing variant - Worst
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tip lesion variant is associated with the best prognosis.
    • It often responds well to corticosteroid therapy and has more favorable renal outcomes.
  • Collapsing variant has the worst prognosis.
    • It is characterized by collapse of glomerular capillary loops with podocyte proliferation and is associated with rapid progression to renal failure.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS):

  • Focal: some glomeruli
  • Segmental: part of tuft
  • Primary podocytopathy → podocyte loss → sclerosis
  • Clinical features:
    • Nephrotic syndrome (often nonselective proteinuria)
    • Hematuria, hypertension, ↓ GFR are common
    • Poor steroid response
    • ~50% → ESKD in 10 years
    • 25–50% recurrence post-transplant
  • Variants:
    • Collapsing glomerulopathy (poor prognosis)
    • Cellular variant
    • Hilar lesion
    • Tip lesion (better prognosis)
    • Not otherwise specified (NOS)


Reference:
  1. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 831
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2342

α2-macroglobulin is increased in nephrotic syndrome.

  • In nephrotic syndrome, there is massive urinary loss of low molecular weight proteins such as albumin and IgG.
  • In response to decreased oncotic pressure, the liver increases the synthesis of various proteins.
  • α2-macroglobulin is a very large molecule that:
    • Is not filtered through the damaged glomerulus
    • Is retained in plasma
    • Increases in concentration
    • Produces a rise in the α2-globulin fraction on serum electrophoresis

Serum electrophoresis in nephrotic syndrome:

[[figure-1]]

  • Pattern:
    • ↓ Albumin
    • ↑ α2-globulin fraction
    • ↓ γ-globulin (IgG)

Escherichia coli is the most common cause of urinary tract infections and acute pyelonephritis. It is an enteric gram-negative bacillus with P-fimbriae that facilitate adherence to urothelial cells.

Pyelonephritis: Infection-induced inflammation of renal tubules, interstitium, and pelvis

  • Usually associated with UTI
  • Acute → bacterial infection
  • Chronic → recurrent acute episodes (often due to reflux or obstruction)

Common Causative Organisms:

  • >85%: Enteric Gram-negative bacilli
    • Escherichia coli (most common)
    • Proteus
    • Klebsiella
    • Enterobacter
  • Others:
    • Streptococcus faecalis, staphylococci, fungi

Proteus mirabilis (Option B): Urease-producing organism associated with struvite stones and complicated UTIs; less common than E. coli.

question: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever, flank pain, dysuria, and urinary frequency. Urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites. Urine culture is sent. Which of the following is the most common causative organism of acute pyelonephritis?

explanationHtml:

  • Chronic Pyelonephritis leads to progressive cortical scarring and parenchymal loss, producing small, irregular, and asymmetrically contracted kidneys, rather than enlargement.

Conditions causing an enlarged kidney:

  • Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (1):
    • In the early stages, kidneys are typically normal to enlarged due to severe glomerular inflammation, crescent formation, and interstitial edema.
  • Amyloidosis (2):

correctAnswer: A. Medial degeneration with elastic fibre fragmentation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Marfan syndrome is caused by defective fibrillin-1, leading to abnormal TGF-β signalling. The hallmark histology is medial degeneration with elastic fibre fragmentation.

Medial Degeneration (Cystic Medial Degeneration):

  • A nonspecific weakening of the aortic media characterised by structural breakdown of elastic tissue and smooth muscle cells, commonly seen in aortic aneurysms.
  • Histological findings:
    • Elastic fibre fragmentation
    • Smooth muscle cell (SMC) loss
    • Mucoid (myxoid) extracellular matrix accumulation
    • Thinning of the media
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Occurs due to an imbalance between ECM synthesis and degradation
      • ↑ Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) → elastin & collagen breakdown
      • Medial ischemia (e.g., hypertension, vasa vasorum compromise)
      • Abnormal TGF-β signalling in genetic disorders

Atherosclerotic plaque formation (Option B): Seen in atherosclerosis, typically affecting the abdominal aorta in older individuals.

Transmural neutrophilic inflammation (Option C): Suggests acute infectious or inflammatory arteritis.

Granulomatous vasculitis (Option D): Seen in large-vessel vasculitis (e.g., giant cell arteritis), not Marfan syndrome.

question: An 18-year-old tall male with long limbs and lens dislocation develops progressive ascending aortic dilation. Genetic testing confirms FBN1 mutation. Which histologic finding is most characteristic?

correctAnswer: A. Proximal straight tubule and thick ascending limb
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Ischemic acute tubular injury predominantly affects the proximal straight tubule (S3 segment) and the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, particularly in the outer medulla.

  • These regions:
    • Have high metabolic demand
    • Require significant oxygen for active transport
    • Are located in a relatively hypoxic environment
    • Are therefore most vulnerable to decreased renal perfusion

Acute Tubular Injury (ATI):

  • The most common cause (~50%) of acute kidney injury (AKI) in hospitalised patients
  • Characterised by acute renal failure with tubular epithelial injury
  • Often reversible
  • Types:
    • Ischemic ATI:
      • Due to ↓ renal perfusion (hypotension, shock)
      • Patchy necrosis
      • Affects:
        • Proximal straight tubule (PST)
        • Thick ascending limb (TAL)
      • Seen in:
        • Severe trauma
        • Acute pancreatitis
        • Sepsis
    • Nephrotoxic ATI:
      • Prominent in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)
      • Examples:
        • Mercury → acidophilic inclusions
        • Ethylene glycol → vacuolar degeneration + calcium oxalate crystals
      • Due to toxins/drugs:
        • Gentamicin
        • Radiographic contrast
        • Heavy metals (e.g., mercury)
        • Organic solvents (e.g., carbon tetrachloride)


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 847, 848

question: Which of the following statements regarding Wilms' tumour is incorrect?

correctAnswer: C. Mutation of TP53 leading to defective apoptosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The histological description of large hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei with abnormal mitotic figures indicates anaplastic Wilms tumour, an uncommon but clinically important variant associated with poor prognosis and resistance to chemotherapy.

  • Most cases of anaplastic Wilms tumour harbour mutations in the TP53 gene.
  • The p53 protein normally acts as a tumour suppressor by inducing cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage, including damage caused by cytotoxic chemotherapy.
  • When TP53 is mutated, this apoptotic response is impaired, allowing tumour cells to survive despite chemotherapy, resulting in treatment resistance and a worse prognosis.

Gain-of-function mutation in β-catenin (Option A): Mutations in the CTNNB1 gene (β-catenin) occur in a subset of Wilms tumours and contribute to tumour development through abnormal WNT signalling

Loss of the WT1 tumour suppressor gene (Option B): WT1 mutations are involved in the initiation of Wilms tumour and are seen in conditions such as WAGR syndrome and Denys-Drash syndrome

IGF2 overexpression due to an imprinting abnormality (Option D): IGF2 overexpression occurs in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to abnormalities at chromosome 11p15, contributing to tumour growth



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 438

question: A 4-year-old child undergoes nephrectomy for a Wilms tumour. Histology shows large hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei with abnormal mitotic figures. The tumour shows a poor response to preoperative chemotherapy. Which of the following best explains the chemotherapy resistance in this tumour?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The classic triphasic histology of Wilms tumour consists of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal components.

  • When this pattern occurs without anaplasia, it represents favourable histology, which is associated with a good response to therapy and an excellent prognosis.
  • Most children with favourable histology Wilms tumour have survival rates approaching 90% or higher with modern treatment.

[[figure-1]]

In contrast, several histological and genetic features are associated with poor prognosis:

  • Anaplastic histology (Option A):
    • This is the most important adverse prognostic factor in Wilms tumour.
    • Anaplasia is characterised by marked nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and abnormal mitotic figures, and is often associated with TP53 mutations and chemotherapy resistance.
  • Loss of heterozygosity at chromosomes 1p and 16q (Option B):
    • This genetic abnormality is associated with increased risk of relapse and poorer survival, and it is used in risk stratification in modern treatment protocols.
  • Gain of chromosome 1q (Option C):
    • Gain of 1q is one of the most common cytogenetic abnormalities in Wilms tumour and is also associated with higher relapse rates and worse outcomes.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 439

question: A 4-year-old child is diagnosed with Wilms tumour. Histology and genetic studies are reviewed to assess prognosis. Which of the following is not associated with poor prognosis in Wilms tumour?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most reliable criterion used to distinguish renal papillary adenoma from papillary renal cell carcinoma (pRCC) is the maximum tumour size.

  • According to the WHO classification, papillary renal tumours measuring ≤ 1.5 cm are classified as papillary adenomas, while lesions > 1.5 cm are considered papillary renal cell carcinomas.
  • Histologically and cytogenetically, these lesions are often very similar, suggesting that papillary adenomas may represent precursor lesions of papillary RCC.
  • Both papillary adenomas and papillary RCC show papillary architecture (Option A)
  • Both may exhibit low-grade nuclear features (Option B), so these characteristics cannot reliably distinguish the two.
  • Similarly, psammoma bodies (Option D) may be present in papillary tumours but are not specific for carcinoma.
  • Both papillary adenomas and papillary RCC frequently show similar cytogenetic abnormalities, particularly trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17 and loss of the Y chromosome, further supporting their biological relationship.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma is the second most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 15-20% of RCC cases.

  • Two major histologic patterns are recognised:
    • Type 1: Papillae lined by a single layer of small basophilic cells with low-grade nuclei.
    • Type 2: Larger eosinophilic cells with higher nuclear grade, generally associated with more aggressive behaviour and poorer prognosis.


Reference:
  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9394504/
