question: Which of the following most reliably differentiates renal papillary adenoma from papillary renal cell carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features described - recurrent pneumothorax, facial fibrofolliculomas, and renal tumours with an FLCN mutation are characteristic of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the FLCN gene (folliculin).

  • This syndrome is associated with a characteristic triad:
    • Skin lesions: fibrofolliculomas, trichodiscomas, and acrochordons
    • Pulmonary manifestations: lung cysts and spontaneous pneumothorax
    • Renal tumours: most commonly chromophobe RCC and hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe tumours

Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma (ChRCC):

  • Origin: Intercalated cells of the collecting duct
  • Cytogenetics: Multiple chromosome losses (e.g., 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17, 21)
  • Prognosis: Better than clear cell RCC
  • Histology:
    • Composed of pale eosinophilic cells
    • Prominent perinuclear halo
    • Arranged in solid sheets
    • Tendency for larger cells to cluster around blood vessels
    • Distinct cell borders → “plant cell-like” appearance
    • Cytoplasm may show reticular clearing

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (Option A): Most common sporadic RCC and classically associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease, not Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma (Option B): More commonly linked to Hereditary papillary renal carcinoma due to MET proto-oncogene mutations.

Collecting duct carcinoma (Option D): A rare, aggressive RCC subtype not characteristically associated with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.



Reference:
  1. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 863
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6942440/
question: A 50-year-old man with recurrent pneumothorax and multiple facial fibrofolliculomas is found to have bilateral renal masses. Genetic testing reveals an FLCN mutation. Which renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is most commonly associated with the most probable condition?

correctAnswer: D. Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma, because this subtype commonly occurs in children and young patients, shows nested, solid, or tubulopapillary architecture, and is defined by TFE3 gene rearrangements, leading to positive TFE3 immunostaining.

Xp11 Translocation Renal Cell Carcinoma (TFE3-Rearranged RCC):

  • Genetically distinct subtype of RCC characterised by TFE3 gene rearrangement.
  • Common in children and young adults
  • Genetics:
    • Translocation involving TFE3 gene at Xp11.2
    • Fusion with various partner genes
    • Leads to the overexpression of the TFE3 transcription factor
  • Morphology:
    • Variable (depends on fusion partner)
    • Patterns include:
      • Nested
      • Solid
      • Tubulopapillary

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (Option A): Associated with VHL gene mutation and chromosome 3p deletion. It typically shows clear cytoplasm with rich vascularity and is more common in adults.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma (Option B): Commonly associated with trisomy 7 and 17 and MET mutations. Although papillary architecture may be present, it lacks TFE3 rearrangement and usually occurs in older adults.

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (Option C): Characterised by pale eosinophilic cells with perinuclear halos and multiple chromosome losses; not associated with TFE3 translocation.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 864
question: A 13-year-old girl presents with painless hematuria. Imaging shows a renal mass. Biopsy reveals nested and tubulopapillary architecture. Immunostaining is positive for TFE3. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows bilateral adrenal haemorrhage, characteristic of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome:

  • This syndrome results from overwhelming septicemia with DIC, leading to massive adrenal haemorrhage and acute adrenal insufficiency.
  • It is classically caused by Neisseria meningitidis, but can also occur with other severe infections such as
    • Pseudomonas
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae, and
    • Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Key features:
    • Severe septicemia
    • Hypotension → shock
    • DIC with widespread purpura
    • Acute adrenocortical insufficiency
  • Morphology:
    • Adrenals replaced by clotted blood
    • Haemorrhage begins in the medulla and spreads to the cortex


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 1019

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Genotype 3 HCV is particularly associated with direct virus-induced hepatic steatosis. The virus alters lipid metabolism, causing more pronounced fatty infiltration compared to other genotypes.

  • Genotype 3 accounts for ~20 % of global HCV infections and is particularly prevalent in regions such as South Asia and parts of Europe.
  • Characteristics:
    • Steatosis (fatty liver): More frequent and severe compared to other genotypes; associated with altered lipid metabolism.
    • Fibrosis & Progression: Faster progression of liver fibrosis and potential quicker advancement to cirrhosis.
    • Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC): Genotype 3 carries a higher risk for HCC and liver‑related mortality.

Genotype 1 (Option A): The most common HCV genotype worldwide. Hepatic steatosis may occur, but it is typically associated with metabolic factors such as obesity or insulin resistance rather than direct viral effects.

Genotype 2 (Option B): Less commonly associated with hepatic steatosis and does not have a strong link with virus-induced lipid metabolism abnormalities.

Genotype 4 (Option D): More prevalent in North Africa and the Middle East. Although it can cause chronic hepatitis, it does not show the strong association with hepatic steatosis seen with genotype 3.

Explanation:

  • Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a rare form of chronic pyelonephritis characterised by foamy macrophages, mixed inflammatory infiltrate, association with Proteus infection and obstruction, and yellow-orange nodules that may mimic renal cell carcinoma.

Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis:

  • Rare form of chronic pyelonephritis
  • Characterised by:
    • Foamy macrophages
    • Mixed inflammatory cells (plasma cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils)
    • Occasional giant cells
  • Commonly associated with:
    • Proteus infection
    • Urinary tract obstruction
  • Grossly:
    • Large yellow-orange nodules
    • May mimic renal cell carcinoma

Renal cell carcinoma (Option B): While it can appear as a yellow mass (especially the clear cell type), it would show malignant epithelial cells and a distinct vascular pattern, not a diffuse infiltration of foamy macrophages and mixed inflammatory cells typical of a chronic infection.

Acute pyelonephritis (Option C) presents with fever, chills, and flank pain, but the pathology shows neutrophilic abscesses and "white cell casts" rather than chronic, yellow-orange granulomatous nodules.

Chronic glomerulonephritis (Option D) is a bilateral, diffuse kidney disease resulting in shrunken, scarred kidneys and eventually renal failure. It does not present as a focal, yellow, mass-like lesion.

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 844
question: A 50-year-old woman with recurrent UTIs presents with flank pain. Imaging shows a mass-like renal lesion. Grossly, the kidney is shown in the image below. Histology reveals numerous foamy macrophages with mixed inflammatory cells. History of Proteus infection and obstruction. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical features of hypertension, hematuria and renal biopsy showing subepithelial hump-like deposits on electron microscopy are suggestive of Post-infectious glomerulonephritis.

[[figure-1]]

  • Post-infectious glomerulonephritis (PIGN) commonly occurs in children following:

    • Streptococcal throat infection

    • Skin infection

  • Classic presentation includes:

    • Hematuria (“cola-colored urine”)

    • Hypertension

    • Edema

    • Oliguria

  • Pathogenesis: Immune complex deposition after infection.

  • Diagnosis:

    • Serum C3 levels are decreased due to complement consumption.

    • Electron microscopy: Subepithelial hump-shaped immune complex deposits

    • Immunofluorescence shows: Granular (“lumpy-bumpy/starry sky”) deposition of IgG and C3 along GBM and mesangium.

    • Light microscopy: Hypercellular glomeruli with neutrophilic infiltration

[[figure-2]]

  • Most children recover completely with supportive treatment.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) (Option B): ANCA-associated vasculitis causing lung involvement, rapidly progressive GN. Typically shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. Complement levels are usually normal.

[[figure-3]]

Membranous glomerulonephritis (Option C): Commonly presents with nephrotic syndrome in adults. Shows subepithelial deposits - “Spike and dome” appearance. C3 is usually not markedly decreased. Basement membrane thickening/spike formation is best seen on a silver stain.

[[figure-4]]

Basement membrane thickening/spike formation

Minimal change disease (Option D): Most common nephrotic syndrome in children. Electron microscopy shows foot process effacement. Immunofluorescence is usually negative.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathological Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 823, 824.
question: A 12-year-old child presents with hypertension, hematuria, and decreased serum C3 levels. Renal biopsy shows subepithelial hump-like deposits on electron microscopy. Direct immunofluorescence findings are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation is classic for Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS), a rare genetic disorder characterized by accelerated aging in children.
  • HGPS is caused by a de novo point mutation in the Lamin A (LMNA) gene.
  • This mutation leads to the production of an abnormal, toxic protein called Progerin.
  • Progerin disrupts the nuclear membrane architecture (causing nuclear blebbing) and leads to premature cellular senescence.
  • This results in the clinical features of growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, alopecia, and accelerated atherosclerosis, leading to death from myocardial infarction or stroke in the teenage years.

WRN gene (Option B) is mutated in Werner Syndrome, which is an adult-onset progeria. Patients typically appear normal until puberty, with signs of aging (cataracts, graying hair, skin atrophy) beginning in their 20s.

C-KIT gene (Option C) is a proto-oncogene that encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase. Gain-of-function mutations are associated with various cancers, most notably Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST).

TP53 gene (Option D) mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome associated with a high risk of developing multiple types of cancers at a young age.



Reference:

Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome

question: Which of the following is most likely associated with basaloid vulvar carcinomas?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Mild Factor VIII deficiency, prolonged APTT, and an abnormal ristocetin test suggest a von Willebrand factor (vWF) defect. Hemophilia A has low Factor VIII but a normal ristocetin test.

Von Willebrand Disease or vWD (Pseudohemophilia)

Cause

Deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF)

von Willebrand factor (vWF)

Source: Endothelial cells (Weibel-Palade bodies), megakaryocytes, liver.

Functions:

  • Platelet adhesion via Gp Ib/IX
  • Carrier protein for Factor VIII
    • Factor VIII half-life alone: ~2.4 hours
    • vWF-Factor VIII complex half-life: ~12 hours

Laboratory findings
  • Platelet adhesion defect → Bleeding time ↑
  • Factor VIII deficiency → aPTT ↑
  • PT normal

Clinical features

Superficial (platelet-type) bleeding > deep tissue bleeding

Treatment

Cryoprecipitate

Hemophilia A (Option A) shows a normal ristocetin test, so it does not explain the platelet function defect.

Glanzmann thrombasthenia (Option C) has a platelet aggregation defect, but von Willebrand factor is normal, unlike in this case.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome (Option D) involves a defective GP Ib receptor and low platelet count, which is not seen in this patient.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran, and Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 606-607.
question: A patient with a bleeding disorder has a Factor VIII level of 50%, an abnormal ristocetin test, normal PT, and prolonged APTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Accounts for 85% of thyroid cancers
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common thyroid cancer, representing approximately 85% of cases.

Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC):

  • Most common thyroid cancer (~85%)
  • Age: 25-50 years
  • Strongly associated with prior ionising radiation (Option A)
  • Morphology:
    • Gross: Solitary/multifocal, cystic, may calcify
    • Microscopic: Branching papillae, Orphan Annie nuclei, nuclear grooves, pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies, lymphatic invasion common

[[figure-1]]

  • Clinical features:
    • Usually asymptomatic nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy
    • Advanced: hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, dyspnea
  • Diagnosis:
    • FNA cytology reliable
    • Cold nodule on scintigraphy (Option B)
    • Molecular testing for indeterminate cytology
  • Prognosis/Management:
    • 10-year survival >95% (Option D)
    • Lobectomy for low-risk; total thyroidectomy + radioactive iodine for high-risk
    • Recurrence 5-20%; distant metastases 10-15%
    • Poor prognosis: age >55, extrathyroidal extension, metastases


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 989, 990
question: A 35-year-old patient is diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following statements about papillary thyroid carcinoma is true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a psammoma body, characterised by concentric lamellated calcification. Psammoma bodies are a characteristic feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and are commonly found within papillary structures or adjacent stroma.

  • The clinical presentation of a midline neck swelling that moves with tongue protrusion suggests a thyroglossal cyst, which may contain ectopic thyroid tissue.
  • Papillary carcinoma can arise in this ectopic thyroid tissue

Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC):

  • Most common thyroid cancer (~85%)
  • Age: 25-50 years
  • Strongly associated with prior ionising radiation
  • Microscopic features:

[[figure-1]]

  • Branching papillae with fibrovascular cores
  • Orphan Annie eye nuclei (clear nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin)
  • Nuclear grooves and intranuclear pseudoinclusions
  • Psammoma bodies (concentric calcifications)
  • Lymphatic invasion is common, vascular invasion is uncommon
  • Clinical features:
    • Usually asymptomatic thyroid nodule
    • May present with an enlarged cervical lymph node
    • Advanced disease: hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea

Follicular carcinoma (Option A): Characterised by follicular architecture with capsular and vascular invasion; lacks the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma.

Medullary carcinoma (Option C): Arises from parafollicular (C) cells and produces calcitonin; does not show papillary structures or characteristic nuclear features.

Anaplastic carcinoma (Option D): Highly aggressive, undifferentiated tumour in elderly patients; shows marked pleomorphism without papillary architecture or nuclear features.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 989, 990
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion. The swelling has been present since childhood but has recently increased in size. Surgical excision is performed. Histopathological examination reveals the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Papillary thyroid carcinoma (~85%) is the most common, whereas anaplastic carcinoma (<1%) is the least common and most aggressive thyroid cancer.

Thyroid Carcinomas:

  • Major Subtypes & Frequency:
    • Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) (~85% of cases)
    • Follicular or oncocytic thyroid carcinoma (~5-15% of cases)
    • High-grade differentiated and poorly differentiated carcinoma (~5%
    • of cases)
    • Anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinoma (~1% of cases)
    • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (a neoplasm of C cells) (<5% of
    • cases)

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 988
question: Which of the following correctly represents the most common and least common thyroid carcinomas, respectively?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A solitary thyroid nodule is more likely to be neoplastic and has a higher risk of malignancy compared with multinodular goitre. However, most nodules are still benign, and the incidence increases with age and they are relatively common.

Solitary Thyroid Nodule:

  • A solitary thyroid nodule (STN) is a clinically palpable, discrete swelling in the thyroid gland, although many such nodules are actually part of multinodular disease on ultrasonography.
  • Present in up to 50% (autopsy studies) (Option C)
  • Incidence increases with age (Option B)
  • Clinical significance:
    • Primary concern: malignancy
    • Most nodules are benign (Option A) (multinodular goitre, cysts, thyroiditis, follicular adenoma)

question: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding a solitary thyroid nodule?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, suggested by a painful thyroid enlargement following a viral upper respiratory infection, with transient thyrotoxicosis (↑T3/T4, ↓TSH) and low radioactive iodine uptake, due to release of preformed thyroid hormones from damaged follicles.

Subacute Granulomatous Thyroiditis (de Quervain):

  • Age: 40-50 years
  • F:M = 4:1
  • Etiology:
    • Post-viral (URTI)
    • Viruses: Coxsackie, SARS-CoV-2, mumps, measles, adenovirus
  • Pathology:
    • Granulomatous inflammation
    • Multinucleated giant cells around colloid
    • Damaged/collapsed follicles
    • Later fibrosis
  • Clinical features:
    • The most common cause of painful thyroid
    • Transient thyrotoxicosis (2-6 weeks)
    • ↑T3/T4, ↓TSH
    • Low radioactive iodine uptake
    • May have a temporary hypothyroid phase
    • Recovery in 6-8 weeks

Hashimoto thyroiditis (Option A): Painless autoimmune hypothyroidism with lymphocytic infiltration and Hürthle cells.

Graves disease (Option B): Hyperthyroidism with diffuse goiter and increased radioactive iodine uptake.

Riedel thyroiditis (Option D): Extensive fibrosis producing a hard, fixed thyroid mass that may mimic carcinoma.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 983
question: A 45-year-old woman presents with painful enlargement of the thyroid following an upper respiratory infection. Laboratory tests show ↑ T3/T4, ↓ TSH, and low radioactive iodine uptake. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. It is an autoimmune disease characterised by destruction of thyroid follicles and the presence of anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.

Hypothyroidism:

  • ↓ thyroid hormone production due to dysfunction of the thyroid, pituitary, or hypothalamus
  • 10× more common in females
  1. Primary Hypothyroidism (Most common):
    • Due to intrinsic thyroid disease
    • Causes:
      • Hashimoto thyroiditis - most common in iodine-sufficient areas
      • Iodine deficiency
      • Post-ablative (thyroid surgery, radioiodine, irradiation)
      • Drugs: lithium, amiodarone, thionamides
      • Congenital defects
        • Thyroid agenesis/hypoplasia
        • Dyshormonogenesis
  2. Secondary (Central) Hypothyroidism:
    • Due to pituitary failure → ↓ TSH
  3. Tertiary Hypothyroidism:
    • Due to hypothalamic disease → ↓ TRH

Wolff-Chaikoff effect (Option B): The Wolff-Chaikoff effect refers to a temporary inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis following exposure to large amounts of iodine. Although it may cause transient hypothyroidism in certain situations, it is not the most common cause of hypothyroidism.

Pituitary failure (Option C): Pituitary failure leads to secondary (central) hypothyroidism due to decreased secretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). However, central hypothyroidism is much less common than primary hypothyroidism caused by thyroid gland disorders.

Thyroid agenesis (Option D): Thyroid agenesis is a congenital absence of the thyroid gland and is an important cause of congenital hypothyroidism, but it is rare and not the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the general population.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 980, 981, 983
question: Which of the following is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas?

correctAnswer: C. Fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule is characteristic of Riedel thyroiditis and is not seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis. In Hashimoto thyroiditis, fibrosis may be present but remains confined within the gland.

Hashimoto Thyroiditis - Morphology:

  • Thyroid gland: Diffusely enlarged, well-demarcated
  • Cut surface: Pale, yellow-tan, firm, slightly nodular
  • Microscopy:

[[figure-1]]

  • Dense mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate (Option D)
    • Lymphocytes
    • Plasma cells
    • Lymphoid follicles with germinal centres (Option A)
  • Atrophic thyroid follicles
  • Hürthle (Oncocytic) Cell Change: (Option B)
    • Follicular epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm
    • Represents metaplastic response to chronic injury
    • On FNAC: oncocytes + mixed lymphocytes → characteristic
  • Fibrosis:
    • Increased interstitial connective tissue
    • Does not extend beyond the thyroid capsule (unlike Riedel thyroiditis)


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 982

options.text: Fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule

question: Which of the following histopathological features is not typically seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis?

correctAnswer: A. Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Graves' disease accounts for approximately 85% of cases of hyperthyroidism and is the most common cause. It results from autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor, leading to increased thyroid hormone production.

Hyperthyroidism:

  • Hyperthyroidism: thyrotoxicosis due to thyroid gland hyperfunction
  • Common causes:
    • Graves' disease (~85%)
    • Toxic multinodular goitre
    • Toxic adenoma
    • Rare: TSH-secreting pituitary tumor
  • Other Causes (without ↑ hormone production):
    • Subacute thyroiditis
    • Painless thyroiditis
    • Struma ovarii
    • Factitious thyrotoxicosis
  • Clinical features:
    • Weight loss despite ↑ appetite
    • Heat intolerance, sweating
    • Warm, flushed skin
    • Tachycardia, palpitations, atrial fibrillation
    • Tremor, anxiety, insomnia
    • Hyperdefecation (Option D)
    • Lid lag, staring gaze
    • Proptosis (Graves disease)
  • Complications:
    • Osteoporosis (Option C)
    • Thyroid storm (life-threatening)
    • Apathetic hyperthyroidism in the elderly
  • Lab findings:
    • Primary: ↓ TSH, ↑ T4 (Option B)
    • T3 toxicosis: ↑ T3 only
    • Secondary: normal/↑ TSH


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 979, 980

Serum TSH levels are increased in primary hyperthyroidism.

question: Which of the following statements regarding hyperthyroidism is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pituitary carcinoma (metastatic PitNET) is defined only by the presence of metastasis to craniospinal or systemic sites, not by histologic features alone.

Pituitary Carcinoma:

  • Rare (<1% of pituitary tumours)
  • Defined by craniospinal or systemic metastasis
  • Usually functional tumors
  • Common hormones: Prolactin, ACTH
  • Course:
    • Metastasis occurs late
    • Often, after multiple local recurrences

High mitotic activity (Option A): Increased mitotic activity may indicate an aggressive pituitary tumour, but it does not establish carcinoma in the absence of metastasis.

Cellular atypia (Option B): Cytologic atypia can occur in benign pituitary tumors and is not sufficient to diagnose carcinoma.

Large tumour size (Option D): Large tumours are classified as macroadenomas, but size alone does not indicate malignant behaviour.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 976

explanationHtml:
• Meningiomas are common extra-axial tumors that arise from the meninges and are often characterized by the presence of psammoma bodies, which are concentrically laminated calcifications.
  • These tumors are typically slow-growing and can cause symptoms due to compression of adjacent brain structures.
  • The association of vestibular schwannoma with meningioma is seen in Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), a genetic disorder that predisposes individuals to multiple nervous system tumors, including bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas.


Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM (Option B): GBM is the most aggressive primary brain tumor, typically arising from astrocytes. It is characterized by pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation, not psammoma bodies. Unlike meningioma, which is well-circumscribed and extra-axial, GBM is an infiltrative intra-axial tumor.

Pilocytic Astrocytoma (Option C): This is a low-grade astrocytoma, most commonly seen in children and often located in the cerebellum. It is histologically characterized by Rosenthal fibers, which are eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped inclusions, but it does not show psammoma bodies. Additionally, pilocytic astrocytomas are not associated with vestibular schwannomas.

Oligodendroglioma (Option D): These tumors arise from oligodendrocytes and are commonly associated with calcifications and a "fried egg" appearance of tumor cells due to perinuclear clearing. However, unlike meningiomas, they do not contain psammoma bodies. Oligodendrogliomas are also intra-axial tumors, meaning they arise from within the brain parenchyma, whereas meningiomas are extra-axial.



Reference:

Robbins Basic Pathology, 11th Edition, Page no: 345

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

While the duodenum is the most common overall site of peptic ulcer disease, the most common site of gastric peptic ulcers is along the lesser curvature at the body-antrum junction, not the antrum itself.

Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD):

  • Chronic mucosal ulcer of:
    • Duodenum (most common) (Option A)
    • Stomach
  • Major causes:
    • Helicobacter pylori (most common) (Option B)
    • NSAIDs
    • Cigarette smoking
  • Pathogenesis: Imbalance between acid injury and mucosal defence (usually on a background of chronic gastritis).
    • H. pylori (antral gastritis) → ↑ Gastrin → ↑ Acid → Duodenal ulcer
    • NSAIDs → ↓ Prostaglandins → ↓ Mucus & bicarbonate
  • Gastric atrophy (↓ acid) → protects against duodenal ulcers. (Option C)
  • Common sites:
    • Duodenum: proximal, near pylorus
    • Stomach: lesser curvature (body-antrum junction)
  • Complications:
    • Bleeding (most common)
    • Perforation (most fatal)
    • Obstruction


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 701, 702

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A treatment-resistant nipple eczema with histology showing large pale intraepidermal malignant cells (Paget cells) is diagnostic of Mammary Paget's disease. It typically presents as a unilateral eczematous lesion of the nipple and is usually associated with underlying DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma.

Mammary Paget Disease:

  • Rare manifestation of breast cancer (~1-4% of cases).
  • Clinical features:
    • Unilateral erythematous, scaly crusted lesion of the nipple
    • Pruritus common
    • Often mistaken for eczema
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Malignant Paget cells spread from ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) through lactiferous ducts/sinuses into the nipple epidermis (Option B)
    • Tumour cells disrupt the epithelial barrier, causing serous fluid exudation on the nipple surface.
  • Associated lesions:
    • DCIS (most common) (Option A)
    • Invasive ductal carcinoma
  • IHC:
    • Positive: CK7 (Option C), HER2/neu, EMA, CEA
    • Negative: S100
  • Diagnosis:
    • Nipple biopsy


Reference:
  • Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 952
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK563228/

question: A 58-year-old woman has a eczematous lesion of the nipple not responding to treatment. Histopathology is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has a persistent unilateral erythematous, scaly, crusted lesion of the nipple with pruritus that does not respond to eczema treatment, which is classic for Paget disease of the breast.

  • The next step in management is a nipple biopsy to identify Paget cells within the epidermis, which confirms the diagnosis.

Paget’s disease of the nipple:

  • Rare manifestation of breast cancer (~1-4% of cases).
  • Clinical features:
    • Unilateral erythematous, scaly, crusted lesion of the nipple
    • Pruritus common
    • Often mistaken for eczema
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Malignant Paget cells spread from underlying ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) through lactiferous ducts/sinuses into the nipple epidermis
    • Tumour cells disrupt the epithelial barrier, causing serous fluid exudation on the nipple surface.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Nipple biopsy
    • Cytology of nipple discharge/exudate

Repeat topical corticosteroids (Option A): Persistent unilateral nipple eczema unresponsive to treatment requires biopsy, not further topical therapy.

Fine-needle aspiration of the breast mass (Option B): FNA is useful only if a palpable mass exists, but diagnosis of Paget disease requires biopsy of the nipple lesion.

Reassurance and follow-up (Option D): Inappropriate because the lesion may represent underlying breast carcinoma.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 952

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

p63 is a nuclear myoepithelial marker used to distinguish ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) from invasive carcinoma.

  • Myoepithelial cells normally surround ducts and lobules and maintain basement membrane integrity.
    • In DCIS, the myoepithelial layer is preserved → p63 shows continuous nuclear staining around ducts.
    • In invasive carcinoma, the myoepithelial layer is lost → absence of p63 staining supports invasion.
  • However, p63 should not be used in isolation, as focal positivity may occasionally be seen in invasive lesions.
  • Therefore, interpretation is done in conjunction with morphology and a panel of myoepithelial markers.

Myoepithelial Markers in Breast Lesions:

  • P63
  • Calponin
  • α-Smooth Muscle Actin (α-SMA)
  • Smooth Muscle Myosin (SMM)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nonproliferative fibrocystic changes are associated with low breast cancer risk. Florid hyperplasia is a proliferative lesion with significant epithelial overgrowth → higher risk of breast cancer.

Nonproliferative Breast Changes (Fibrocystic Changes):

  • Common breast alterations in women aged 30–50, often linked to hormonal changes during menstruation.

Principal Morphologic Features:

  • Cysts:
    • Formed by lobular dilation, may coalesce into larger cysts.
    • Contain turbid, brown/blue fluid (“blue-dome cysts”).
    • Lined by flattened atrophic epithelium or apocrine metaplasia.
    • Apocrine change (Option A): abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, resembling sweat gland epithelium.
    • Calcifications are common.
    • Solitary, firm cysts may mimic tumours; diagnosis confirmed by fnac.
  • Fibrosis: (Option B)
    • Occurs when cysts rupture, releasing secretory material into the stroma.
    • Leads to chronic inflammation and palpable nodularity.
  • Adenosis: (Option C)
    • Increase in acini per lobule.
    • Lined by columnar epithelial cells.
    • Calcifications may be present.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 947, 948

The image shows gynecomastia, the most common benign lesion of the male breast, characterized by subareolar enlargement due to proliferation of ductal tissue. Classical seminomas are non–hormone-producing germ cell tumors

  • Gynecomastia results from an increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio:
    • Estrogens → stimulate breast tissue growth
    • Androgens → inhibit estrogenic effects
  • Associations:

    • Drugs:
      • Alcohol, Marijuana & Heroin
      • Antiretroviral therapy
      • Anabolic steroids
    • Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY)
    • Functioning testicular tumors
      • Leydig cell tumor
      • Sertoli cell tumor

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most common cause of bloody nipple discharge (especially when it is spontaneous and coming from a single duct) is intraductal papilloma.

Intraductal Papilloma:

  • Benign papillary tumour arising within a dilated breast duct
  • Composed of multiple branching fibrovascular cores
  • Associated changes:
    • Usual ductal hyperplasia
    • Apocrine metaplasia
  • Large Duct Papilloma (Central):
    • Located in the lactiferous sinuses near the nipple
    • Usually solitary
    • >80% cause nipple discharge
      • Often bloody (due to stalk torsion and infarction)
      • May be serous
  • Small Duct Papillomas (Peripheral):
    • Occurs in the peripheral ductal system
    • Often multiple
    • Usually clinically silent
    • May present as:
      • Small palpable mass
      • Mammographic density or calcification

Mammary duct ectasia (Option B): Usually causes thick, sticky green or brown nipple discharge, not typically bloody.

Fibrocystic change (Option C): Presents with breast pain, nodularity, and cysts, not bloody discharge.

Sclerosing adenosis (Option D): A proliferative breast lesion without atypia that may mimic carcinoma but rarely causes nipple discharge.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 948

Adenosis is one of the three principal morphologic features of non-proliferative breast change, defined as an increase in the number of acini per lobule.

  • Non-Proliferative Breast Changes:
    • Cysts
    • Fibrosis
    • Adenosis
  • Proliferative Breast Disease Without Atypia:
    • Usual ductal hyperplasia
    • Sclerosing adenosis (Option A)
    • Radial scar (complex sclerosing lesion) (Option B)
    • Intraductal papilloma
  • Proliferative Breast Disease With Atypia:

question: Which of the following is not a proliferative breast lesion?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

>90% of cases of squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (periductal mastitis) occur in smokers. Smoking may cause relative vitamin A deficiency, leading to abnormal squamous differentiation of duct epithelium and keratin plugging.

Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts (Periductal mastitis, Recurrent subareolar abscess, Zuska disease):

  • A condition involving keratinising squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts leading to duct obstruction, inflammation, and recurrent abscess formation.
  • Painful erythematous subareolar mass
  • May mimic a bacterial abscess
  • Recurrent cases → fistula tract opening near the areola
  • Nipple inversion due to inflammation and scarring
  • Occurs in women and occasionally in men
  • Major risk factor: Smoking (>90% of cases)
  • Morphology:

  • Keratinising squamous metaplasia of lactiferous duct epithelium
  • Keratin plugs in the ducts
  • Duct dilation and rupture
  • Chronic granulomatous periductal inflammation


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 946
question: A 36-year-old woman presents with a painful subareolar mass and recurrent nipple discharge. Examination reveals nipple inversion, and histology shows keratinising squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts with keratin plugging. Which of the following is the most important risk factor for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Large duct (subareolar/lactiferous duct) involvement is seen in mammary duct ectasia, large duct papilloma, and Paget disease of the nipple.

  • Mammary duct ectasia: Dilatation of major ducts near the nipple with periductal inflammation and fibrosis → presents with nipple discharge and subareolar mass
  • Large duct papilloma (central papilloma): Benign tumor arising in major ducts → commonly causes serous or bloody nipple discharge
  • Paget disease of nipple: Intraepidermal spread of malignant ductal cells from underlying DCIS via lactiferous ducts

Atypical lobular hyperplasia: Proliferative lesion arising from the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU); associated with increased breast cancer risk.

Sclerosing adenosis: TDLU lesion characterized by increased acini per lobule with stromal fibrosis; may mimic carcinoma.



Reference:
  • Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 948

question:
Which of the following conditions involves the large ducts of the breast?

  1. Mammary duct ectasia
  2. Large duct papilloma
  3. Paget disease of the nipple
  4. Atypical lobular hyperplasia

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mammary duct ectasia primarily involves large subareolar ducts near the nipple, not the terminal duct lobular unit. It is characterised by dilatation of major ducts with periductal inflammation and fibrosis, often presenting with nipple discharge and subareolar mass. Therefore, it does not originate from the TDLU.

Terminal Duct Lobular Unit (TDLU):

  • Formed by the terminal duct + lobule.
  • It is the structural and functional unit of the breast.

Conditions Arising from the Terminal Duct Lobular Unit (TDLU):

  • Non-Proliferative Breast Changes (Fibrocystic Changes):
    • Cysts
    • Apocrine metaplasia
    • Fibrosis
    • Adenosis
    • Lactational adenoma
  • Proliferative Breast Disease Without Atypia:
    • Usual ductal hyperplasia
    • Sclerosing adenosis (Option B)
    • Radial scar (complex sclerosing lesion)
    • Intraductal papilloma (Option C)
  • Proliferative Breast Disease With Atypia:
    • Columnar cell lesions
    • Flat epithelial atypia
    • Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH)
    • Atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH)
  • Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) (Option A)
  • Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 944, 947, 949, 953

This region is also clinically significant because tumors here may present with early axillary lymph node involvement due to proximity to lymphatic drainage pathways.

Distribution of Breast Carcinoma

Explanation:

Colorectal carcinoma is not a classic cancer associated with BRCA2 mutations. It is more commonly linked to:

  • Lynch syndrome (MMR genes)
  • APC mutations (FAP)

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes involved in homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Mutations lead to genomic instability and increased cancer risk.

BRCA2-associated cancers

  • Male breast cancer (strong association; hallmark)
  • Ovarian carcinoma
  • Pancreatic carcinoma
  • Prostate carcinoma

BRCA1-associated cancers

  • Breast carcinoma (often triple-negative)
  • Ovarian carcinoma (higher risk than BRCA2)
  • Also associated with pancreatic and prostate cancers (less prominently)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most common stromal malignancy of the breast is Breast angiosarcoma, a rare malignant vascular tumour arising from endothelial cells.

Angiosarcoma of the Breast:

  • Most common malignant stromal tumour of the breast.
  • Primary (Sporadic):
    • Occurs in the breast parenchyma
    • Young women (mean age ~35 years)
    • Poor prognosis
  • Secondary (Therapy-related):
    • Occurs in older women
    • Associated with:
      • Radiation therapy
      • Stewart–Treves syndrome (chronic lymphedema)
    • MYC amplification in >90%
    • Incidence after radiation: ~0.3%
    • Develops 5-10 years after treatment

Fibrosarcoma (Option A): Extremely rare in the breast and not the most common stromal malignancy.

Liposarcoma (Option C): Occurs very rarely in the breast and is less common than angiosarcoma among stromal malignancies.

Leiomyosarcoma (Option D): A rare smooth muscle tumour of the breast and not the most frequent stromal malignancy.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 968, 969
question: Which of the following is the most common stromal malignancy of the breast?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most probable diagnosis is Phyllodes tumour, a fibroepithelial breast tumour characterised by leaf-like stromal projections lined by epithelium.

  • Phyllodes tumours commonly show local recurrence, especially borderline and malignant tumours, and margin status is the most important predictor of recurrence.

Phyllodes tumour:

  • Fibroepithelial tumour arising from intralobular stroma (Option C)
  • ~2.5% of fibroepithelial breast lesions
  • Mutations: MED12, RARA; additional TERT, TP53, RB
  • Morphology:

[[figure-1]]

  • Large palpable breast mass
  • Leaf-like stromal projections lined by epithelium
  • May form cystic spaces
  • Clinical features:
    • Peak age: ~6th decade (later than fibroadenoma)
    • ~75% benign (Option A)
    • Local recurrence is common; margin status predicts recurrence
  • Metastasis:
    • Lymphatic spread rare → no axillary dissection
    • Malignant tumours metastasise hematogenously (~1/3)
    • Metastases contain only the stromal component (Option B)


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 968

question: 60-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging breast mass. Histology shows findings as shown. Which of the following statements regarding the most probable condition is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Tumours that express estrogen receptors (ER-positive) generally have a better prognosis and respond well to endocrine therapies such as tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors.

  • ER positivity is therefore considered an important, favourable prognostic and predictive marker in breast cancer.

Breast cancer - Prognostic factor:

Disease factors that influence prognosis

Histologic Subtypes
  • Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC): Prognosis varies by grade and molecular markers.
  • Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC): Intermediate prognosis.
  • Tubular and Mucinous Carcinomas: Best prognosis.
  • Basal-like Breast Cancer (Option D): Aggressive, triple-negative, no targeted treatments.
  • Other Subtypes: Medullary, cribriform, papillary, adenoid cystic, and metaplastic carcinomas, vary in prognosis.

Tumour Size & Lymph Node
  • Larger tumours (>2cm) and positive lymph nodes = worse prognosis.

Molecular Markers
  • Hormone Receptors (ER, PR): ER-positive = better prognosis.
  • HER-2 Status: HER-2 positive = aggressive (Option A) but treatable with targeted therapies.

Patient factors that influence prognosis

Age

Younger, particularly premenopausal women, may have higher local recurrence rates post-surgery, but radiation therapy can reduce this risk.

BRCA Mutation

(Option C)

Associated with aggressive phenotype

Family History

A strong family history may indicate inherited susceptibility and potentially worse prognosis.


Reference:
  • Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 828, 829, 831, 832, 835, 839, 847, 851
  • Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 942

  • B: Faint incomplete staining → Score 1+

question: Which of the following IHC requires confirmation with fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) for HER2 gene amplification?

correctAnswer: D. Prominent neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A breast carcinoma classified as T4d corresponds to inflammatory breast carcinoma, which is characterised by tumour emboli within dermal lymphatic vessels leading to lymphatic obstruction.

  • Despite the term inflammatory, true inflammatory cell infiltrates are usually absent

Inflammatory Breast Carcinoma (IBC):

  • Often no discrete palpable mass

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Occult breast carcinoma (OBC) is a breast malignancy that presents with metastatic disease (most commonly axillary lymph node metastasis) without a detectable primary tumour in the breast on clinical examination or imaging.

  • Most common presentation: Isolated axillary lymphadenopathy due to metastatic carcinoma.

      • Ultrasound

Bloody nipple discharge (Option C): Seen in conditions with a primary ductal lesion such as intraductal papilloma or carcinoma, not in occult breast carcinoma.

Diffuse breast skin thickening resembling peau d’orange (Option D): Characteristic of inflammatory breast carcinoma with overt breast involvement, not occult disease where the primary tumor is not detectable.

• The child’s features (transverse palmar crease, cardiac defect, mild intellectual impairment) suggest Down syndrome (Trisomy 21).
  • Mosaicism (1% of cases) occurs due to a post-zygotic mitotic error, leading to a mixture of normal and trisomy 21 cells.
    • This results in a milder phenotype with better cognitive and physical outcomes compared to full trisomy 21.

Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21):

Key Features:

  • Facial & Physical Features: Flat facies, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, incurved 5th finger, wide gap between 1st & 2nd toes.
  • GI & Cardiac Anomalies: Duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, congenital heart defects (e.g., ASD, AVSD).
  • Neurological & Hematological Risks:
    • Intellectual disability (most common genetic cause).
    • Early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (chromosome 21 codes for APP).
    • Increased risk of AML (<5 years) & ALL (>5 years).
  • Ophthalmologic: Brushfield spots (whitish spots on the iris periphery).

Genetic Causes:

  • 95% cases: Meiotic nondisjunction, most often in meiosis I, linked to advanced maternal age.
  • 4% cases: Robertsonian translocation, typically t(14;21).
  • 1% cases: Mosaicism (post-zygotic mitotic error).

Diagnosis:

  • Prenatal Screening:
    • First-trimester USG: ↑ nuchal translucency, hypoplastic nasal bone.
    • Serum Markers:
      • ↑ hCG, ↑ Inhibin A
      • ↓ AFP, ↓ Estriol

Other Associations:

  • Umbilical hernia (incomplete umbilical ring closure).
  • Mnemonic: "5 A’s":
    1. Advanced maternal age
    2. Atresia (duodenal)
    3. Atrioventricular septal defect
    4. Alzheimer’s disease (early-onset)
    5. AML/ALL


Tetralogy (Option A):
This likely refers to Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), a congenital heart defect. While TOF is seen in some syndromes (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome/22q11.2 deletion), it is not the defining chromosomal abnormality here.

Haploid (Option B):
Haploidy refers to a single set of chromosomes (23, n), which is not compatible with survival.

Monosomy (Option C):
Monosomy refers to the loss of an entire chromosome, such as Turner syndrome (45,X)

question: A 12-year-old girl presents for a regular health maintenance visit. There are no active complaints, and she has been feeling well. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Renal papillary necrosis (RPN) refers to ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae, usually resulting from impaired blood supply to the renal medulla. The renal papillae are particularly vulnerable because the medulla normally has low oxygen tension and relatively poor blood supply, making it susceptible to ischemic injury.

Several conditions are classically associated with renal papillary necrosis:

  • Diabetes mellitus (1): Diabetes is one of the most common causes of RPN. Diabetic microangiopathy and increased susceptibility to infections contribute to medullary ischemia and papillary necrosis.
  • Sickle cell trait (2): The renal medulla has low oxygen tension and high osmolarity, which promotes sickling of red blood cells, leading to vascular occlusion and ischemic injury of the papillae.
  • Urinary tract obstruction (3): Obstruction increases intratubular pressure and reduces medullary blood flow, predisposing the papillae to ischemia and necrosis.
  • Renal tuberculosis (4): Tuberculous infection of the kidney can cause destruction of renal papillae and cavitation, resulting in papillary necrosis.
  • Analgesic abuse (5): Chronic use of analgesics (especially older phenacetin-containing drugs and prolonged NSAID use) causes analgesic nephropathy, characterised by chronic interstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis.

A commonly used mnemonic for causes of renal papillary necrosis is POSTCARDS:

  • P - Pyelonephritis
  • O - Obstruction
  • S - Sickle cell disease/trait
  • T - Tuberculosis
  • C - Cirrhosis
  • A - Analgesic abuse
  • R - Renal vein thrombosis
  • D - Diabetes mellitus
  • S - Systemic vasculitis/shock


Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5453664/

question: In patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which of the following laboratory findings is uncommon?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation suggests Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, which is characterized by drug-induced hemolysis (e.g., after antimalarial therapy) with bite cells on peripheral smear. G6PD deficiency follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.

  • G6PD deficiency causes oxidative damage to RBCs due to impaired protection against reactive oxygen species.
  • Exposure to oxidant drugs (e.g., primaquine) triggers acute intravascular hemolysis, presenting with:
    • Cola-colored urine (hemoglobinuria)
    • Back/flank pain
    • Jaundice
    • Bite cells on peripheral smear
  • It predominantly affects males, while female carriers are usually asymptomatic.

Autosomal dominant (Option A) disorders occur due to a mutation in one copy of an autosomal gene and affect both sexes equally. Examples: Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease, Familial hypercholesterolemia.

Autosomal recessive (Option B) recessive disorders require two defective copies of an autosomal gene for disease manifestation and affect both sexes equally. Examples: Cystic fibrosis, Phenylketonuria, Sickle cell disease.

X-linked dominant (Option C) disorders result from a mutation in one copy of an X-linked gene, affecting both males and females. Examples: Rett syndrome, Hypophosphatemic rickets.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 581-582.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. MRI reveals the following findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Elevated C-peptide indicates endogenous insulin production, helping differentiate insulinoma from exogenous insulin administration.

Insulinoma:

  • Insulinoma is the most common functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.
  • β-cell tumor → excess insulin
  • Causes hypoglycemia (<50 mg/dL)

    • ↑ Insulin

Increased insulin levels (Option A): Elevated insulin levels may occur in both insulinoma and exogenous insulin administration, so insulin alone cannot confirm endogenous production.

Increased glucagon levels (Option C): Glucagon is secreted by pancreatic α-cells and is not used to diagnose insulinoma.

Increased proinsulin levels (Option D): Proinsulin may be elevated in insulinoma, but C-peptide is the key marker used to confirm endogenous insulin secretion.

question: Which of the following statements regarding a sporadic juvenile polyp is correct?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Myelophthisic anemia

Explanation:

  • Myelophthisic anemia results from bone marrow replacement by metastatic cancer, granulomas, or fibrosis. In this case, the firm prostate nodule suggests prostate carcinoma with marrow infiltration, while tear-drop cells, nucleated RBCs, and immature myeloid cells on smear indicate a leukoerythroblastic picture, which is classical for this condition.

Incorrect Options:

Myelodysplastic syndrome (Option A): Causes cytopenias with dysplastic marrow cells; smear shows abnormal morphology, not tear-drop cells or leukoerythroblastic picture.

Primary myelofibrosis (Option C) also shows tear-drop cells and a leukoerythroblastic picture, but the marrow fibrosis is due to a myeloproliferative neoplasm, not metastatic tumor, and there is no prostate nodule in this condition.

Prior exposure to radiation (Option D): Includes CML, PV, ET, PMF; causes abnormal blood counts but not typically due to marrow replacement by metastasis.

question: A 72-year-old male complains of increasing tiredness and generalised weakness. On examination, a firm 1-cm nodule is palpated in the prostate gland. Laboratory studies show anemia with a normocytic, normochromic blood picture. Peripheral smear demonstrates occasional myelocytes, tear-drop erythrocytes, and about 2 nucleated red cells per 100 leukocytes. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?

correctAnswer: B. Secondary deposits from malignant tumours
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Secondary deposits from malignant tumours

Explanation:

  • The most common cause of myelophthisic anemia is bone marrow infiltration by metastatic cancers (commonly breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid), which replace normal hematopoietic tissue and lead to anemia or pancytopenia. Disrupted marrow function produces characteristic blood smear findings such as teardrop cells and immature precursors (leukoerythroblastosis).

Incorrect Options:

Granulomatous disorders (Option A) cause marrow infiltration by inflammatory granulomas but are less common than tumour metastases.

Myeloproliferative disorders (Option C) can cause marrow fibrosis leading to anemia, but rarely cause the marrow replacement seen in myelophthisic anemia.

Prior exposure to radiation (Option D): Radiation can damage bone marrow and cause aplasia, but does not typically cause the marrow replacement pattern seen in myelophthisic anemia.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 601.
question: Myelophthisic anemia typically arises when normal bone marrow is replaced by abnormal tissue. Among the following, which is the leading cause?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - 1, 2, 4

Explanation:

Parvovirus B19 infection, Thymoma, and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia are known to cause pure red cell aplasia (PRCA).

  • Parvovirus B19 infection: Parvovirus B19 is the most common viral cause, destroying erythroid precursors and leading to transient or chronic PRCA, particularly in immunocompromised patients or those with chronic hemolytic anemia.
  • Thymoma: Tumors of the thymus are strongly associated with PRCA, possibly due to autoimmune mechanisms where abnormal T cells attack red cell precursors.
  • Chronic neutrophilic leukemia: It is not a known cause of PRCA.
  • Diamond–Blackfan anemia: This is a congenital (inherited) pure red cell aplasia affecting children, characterized by failure of erythroid progenitors from birth.
  • Rifampicin use: Drug-induced PRCA is rare but recognized with certain medications; rifampicin is not commonly implicated.


Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 601.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - 1, 5

Explanation:

Aplastic anemia can evolve into acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) due to clonal evolution of hematopoietic stem cells or as a consequence of immunosuppressive therapy.

  • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML): Aplastic anemia can evolve into AML, particularly after immunosuppressive therapy, as clonal evolution of hematopoietic stem cells leads to malignant transformation.
  • Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): MDS is a clonal bone marrow disorder characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis and risk of progression to AML. It can develop in patients previously diagnosed with aplastic anemia, representing a clonal evolution.

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL): These lymphoid or chronic myeloproliferative leukaemias are not typically reported secondary transformations of aplastic anemia.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 599-600.

2. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia

4. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Drugs

Explanation:

Some drugs, such as antibiotics (like chloramphenicol), anti-inflammatory drugs, and chemotherapy agents, can damage the bone marrow and lead to aplastic anemia.

  • This is the most commonly identified cause when a specific cause is found, but overall, many cases are idiopathic (unknown cause).

Incorrect Options:

Autoimmune disorders (Option B): The autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells is a common underlying cause of aplastic anaemia, particularly in idiopathic cases, and often responds to immunosuppressive therapy.

Infections (Option C): Viral infections such as hepatitis, EBV, HIV, and parvovirus B19 may cause aplastic anemia.

Radiation exposure (Option D): High doses of ionising radiation can cause bone marrow aplasia, usually seen in cancer therapy or radiation accidents.

Correct Option B - The anemia may present as normocytic and normochromic

Explanation:

  • Anemia of chronic disease (ACD) typically presents as a mild to moderate normocytic, normochromic anemia, especially early in the disease. It may become microcytic over time.

Incorrect Options:

Both serum iron and tissue iron are within normal limits (Option A): In anemia of chronic disease (ACD), serum iron is low due to hepcidin-induced iron sequestration, but total body iron stores (tissue iron) are normal or increased.

Hepcidin production is suppressed (Option C): Hepcidin production is increased in ACD, causing decreased iron absorption and release from macrophages.

Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is increased (Option D): TIBC decreases in ACD since transferrin (the main iron-binding protein) synthesis is suppressed by inflammatory cytokines.

Considering the type of anemia associated with chronic inflammatory states, which of the following statements is correct?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Type III antibody targets haptocorrin

Explanation:

  • Haptocorrin binds vitamin B12 in the stomach to protect it from acid degradation, but is not the target of autoimmune antibodies in pernicious anemia.

Incorrect Options:

Binding of cobalamin to haptocorrin in the stomach (Option A): Type I antibody (“blocking antibody”) can be detected in serum and gastric secretions and prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to intrinsic factor.

Transport of cobalamin via transcobalamin II (Option B): Type I antibody inhibits vitamin B12 from binding to intrinsic factor, preventing intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex formation.

Interaction of vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor (Option C): Type II antibody (“binding antibody”) binds to the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex and blocks its uptake in the terminal ileum.

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 594.

question: With respect to antibodies associated with pernicious anemia, which of the following descriptions is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Cubilin receptor–mediated uptake in the terminal ileum

Explanation:

  • Vitamin B12 absorption occurs mainly in the terminal ileum, where the intrinsic factor–vitamin B12 complex binds to the cubilin receptor on the ileal enterocyte surface for absorption. Extensive ileal resection, as in Crohn’s disease surgery, impairs this step, leading to B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Binding of cobalamin to haptocorrin in the stomach (Option B): Binding of vitamin B12 to haptocorrin occurs in the stomach; this step is unaffected by ileal resection.

Transport of cobalamin via transcobalamin II (Option C): Transcobalamin II transports vitamin B12 in the plasma after absorption; this process is not impaired by ileal resection.

Interaction of vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor (Option D): Vitamin B12 binds intrinsic factor in the duodenum; this early step remains intact in ileal resection.

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 593.

question: A 28-year-old woman who underwent ileal resection for Crohn’s disease presents with features of megaloblastic anemia. Which step in vitamin B12 absorption and transport is most likely impaired in her case?

explanationHtml:
Option D: Reduced Serum Vitamin B12

  • Megaloblastic Anaemia is caused by a deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid.
  • Vitamin B12 or methylcobalamin is required for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine by methionine synthase.
  • In this reaction, methylcobalamin recovers a methyl group from N5-
  • methyltetrahydrofolate (N5 -methyl FH4), which is the principal form of folic acid in plasma.
  • N5- methyl FH4 is converted to tetrahydrofolic acid (FH4) during this process.
  • Tetrahydrofolic acid is crucial for DNA synthesis because its derivative N5,10-methylene FH4 is required to convert deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP).
  • The "methyl tetrahydrofolate trap" hypothesis has been proposed to explain the cause of impaired DNA synthesis in vitamin deficiencies.
  • Folic acid deficiency can occur due to vitamin B12 deficiency due to an impairment of methionine synthase resulting in the trapping of folate as methyltetrahydrofolate whereby methyl THFA accumulates in serum leading to folate trap phenomenon and increased urinary excretion of folate.
  • Conversion of methyl FH4 [tetrahydrofolate] to FH4 requires Vitamin B12.
  • Hence in Vitamin B12 deficiency, this conversion is impaired & most of the folate remains trapped as methyl FH4 ("folate trap").
  • Methylene FH4 required for the synthesis of dTMP is thus not generated (functional folate deficiency), ultimately leading to defective synthesis of DNA.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: Normal Serum Tetrahydrofolate

  • In "the folate trap," most of the folic acid is trapped in the form of methyltetrahydrofolate, as its conversion to tetrahydrofolate requires vitamin B12 during the conversion of homocysteine to methionine.
  • The serum levels of tetrahydrofolate would therefore be reduced in vitamin B12 deficiency.

Option B: Reduced Serum Methyltetrahydrofolate

  • Vitamin B12 is required to convert methyltetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate during the reaction involving the conversion of homocysteine to methionine.
  • Serum methyltetrahydrofolate levels would be increased in vitamin B12 deficiency because of the trapping of the folic acid as methyltetrahydrofolate.

Option C: Normal Serum Vitamin B12

  • Megaloblastic Anaemia is characterised by a "folate trap" secondary to vitamin B12 deficiency.
  • The serum levels of vitamin B12 would therefore be reduced than normal.


Reference:

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10th edition, page 653

explanationHtml:
• The patient's presentation, with a history of piles and a peripheral smear showing anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and target cells, along with the microcytic nature of the anemia, strongly suggests iron deficiency anemia (IDA) due to chronic blood loss.
  • Serum ferritin is a key marker for diagnosing IDA.
  • In IDA, ferritin levels decrease as iron stores are depleted. Levels below 30 ng/mL are indicative of depleted iron stores.

Investigations for IDA

Iron Study

Interpretation in Iron Deficiency Anemia

Serum Ferritin

Low (< 30 ng/mL) indicates depleted iron stores.

Serum Iron (Fe)

Low levels are seen in iron deficiency anemia.

question: A female patient presented with fatigue and a history of piles. Routine complete blood count analysis showed a hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, an MCV of 65 fL, and an RBC count of 3.2 million and RDW is increased. A peripheral smear is given below. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?

explanationHtml:
• Given the context of anaemia, the other findings, along with the peripheral smear showing fragmented red blood cells such as schistocytes, the most likely diagnosis is microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, which could be seen in conditions like mechanical heart valves or hemolytic uremic syndrome.
  • Mechanical heart valves can cause intravascular hemolysis due to the turbulence of blood flow around the valve, leading to red blood cell fragmentation, hemoglobinuria, increased bilirubin, and elevated LDH.

[[figure-1]]

Schistocytes in Peripheral smear

Splenomegaly (Option A) is commonly associated with chronic hemolytic anaemias. However, in this case, the key features are hemoglobinuria, increased bilirubin, and elevated LDH, which point more toward mechanical hemolysis and typically don't cause splenic enlargement.

Increased HbA2 (Option C) is a hallmark of beta-thalassemia, a genetic disorder of haemoglobin production, where the production of normal beta-globin chains is reduced, leading to an increase in the relative amount of HbA2. However, beta-thalassemia does not cause hemoglobinuria or the other signs of acute hemolysis described in this case.

Goitre (Option D) refers to an enlarged thyroid gland, and it is typically associated with thyroid disorders. The patient’s symptoms and lab results point toward a haematological problem, specifically hemolysis, which would not be linked to a thyroid disorder like goitre.



Reference:
  • Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Pages 566, 637,
  • Medscape Link
question: An elderly patient presents with anemia and hemoglobinuria. Investigations reveal increased bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase. The peripheral smear image is given below. Which of the following is associated with this?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation described, with recurrent chest infections, abdominal pain, delayed growth, bone problems, icterus, and mild splenomegaly, points towards a hemoglobinopathy, and the peripheral smear showing target cells is also consistent with Beta-thalassemia.
  • Thalassemia is a genetic disorder affecting haemoglobin production and causing microcytic, hypochromic anemia.
  • Hemoglobin consists of two alpha (α) and two beta (β) chains, and mutations in the genes responsible for these chains lead to alpha or beta thalassemia, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
  • Beta thalassemia is caused by mutations in the HBB gene on chromosome 11, affecting β chain production. The severity depends on whether one or both β genes are mutated:
    • Beta Thalassemia Trait (β-thalassemia minor) (1 mutated gene)
    • Beta Thalassemia Intermedia (2 mutated genes with partial function)
    • Beta Thalassemia Major (β0-thalassemia) (2 mutated genes, with complete absence of β chain production)

Beta Thalassemias

Major (Transfusion-dependent)

Intermedia (Non-transfusion-dependent)

Minor (Trait or Carrier)

Genotype

Homozygous:

  • β⁰/β⁰
  • β⁰/β⁺
  • β⁺/β⁺

Variable:

  • β⁰/β⁺ or β⁺/β⁺ or β⁰/β or β⁺/β

Heterozygous:

  • β⁰/β or β⁺/β

Laboratory Findings

Severe microcytic anemia with target cells (Hb 3–4 g/dL)

Moderate microcytic anemia

Mild microcytic anemia

Hemoglobin Electrophoresis
  • HbA₂ (5% or more);
  • HbF (up to 95%); No HbA
  • HbA₂ (4% or more);
  • HbF (up to 50%)
  • HbA₂ (4% or more);
  • HbF (up to 5%)

Incorrect options:

HbC disease (Option B) results in mild hemolysis splenomegaly and usually presents with milder symptoms compared to beta-thalassemia. Electrophoresis in HbC disease would reveal elevated levels of HbC, not HbA, and affected individuals generally experience normal growth and development.

Sickle cell disease (Option C) is caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene, leading to the production of HbS (sickle haemoglobin). The electrophoresis in this condition would show a predominant HbS peak.

Acute coronary disease (Option D) is a cardiovascular condition that primarily affects adults. This condition would present with chest pain, shortness of breath, and EKG changes rather than jaundice, splenomegaly, and bone deformities. The patient described here is a child, making ACS an unlikely diagnosis.

Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Pages 644 - 647

question: A patient presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia (MCV: 70–79 fL) and a Mentzer index of 11 with increased RBC count. Peripheral blood smear reveals target cells. Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate for establishing the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:

  • Thalassemia major predominantly causes:

    • Extravascular hemolysis
  • RBC destruction mainly occurs in the bone marrow and spleen

Features of thalassemia major:

Iron overload (statement 2)

  • Patients with β-thalassemia major often require repeated blood transfusions. Chronic transfusions lead to progressive iron accumulation in tissues. In addition, ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin, increasing intestinal iron absorption.
  • Iron overload affects the heart, liver and endocrine glands
  • Complications include: Cardiomyopathy, cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus

Ineffective hematopoiesis (statement 3)

  • β-globin chain deficiency leads to excess unpaired α-globin chains. These precipitate in erythroid precursors, causing intramedullary destruction. As a result, erythropoiesis becomes ineffective.
  • Bone marrow expands markedly, causing skeletal deformities and a crew-cut skull appearance.
  • Extramedullary hematopoiesis may also occur.

Hepcidin level changes (statement 4)

  • Hepcidin is the major regulator of iron metabolism.
  • In β-thalassemia major, hepcidin levels are typically decreased.
  • Low hepcidin increases intestinal iron absorption.
  • This contributes significantly to iron overload even before multiple transfusions.


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathological Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 586, 587.

Kawasaki disease causes bilateral non-purulent conjunctival congestion. The presence of purulent conjunctivitis suggests bacterial or viral conjunctivitis.

Diagnosis is made when there is:

  • Fever for ≥ 5 days (essential criterion)
    PLUS

  2. Oral mucosal changes

explanationHtml:
• Bruton’s X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA) is caused by a BTK gene mutation, leading to B cell maturation failure and very low levels of all immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE).
  • It presents in infancy (after 6 months) with recurrent bacterial infections, especially with Staphylococcus and encapsulated bacteria.
  • B cells are absent or very low, but T-cell function remains normal, explaining the normal skin reaction to environmental antigens.


Bruton’s agammaglobulinemia or hypogammaglobulinemia:

  • X-linked recessive, most commonly seen in boys.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Failure of pre-B cells to differentiate into immature B cells in the bone marrow - due to the absence of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) enzyme.
    • As a result, there is a total absence of B cells and plasma cells in the circulation, with depressed serum levels of all classes of immunoglobulins.
    • However, Pre-B cells are found in normal numbers in bone marrow and the T cell-mediated responses are also normal.
    • The B cell maturation stops at pre-B cell stage; after the synthesis of heavy-chain without forming the light chains.
    • Hence the cytoplasm of pre-B cell may have incomplete immunoglobulins
  • Clinical features:
    • Recurrent bacterial infections.
    • Infections do not develop until 6 months of age (when maternal antibodies are no longer active).
  • On examination:
    • Tonsils may be difficult to visualize.
    • Cervical/inguinal lymph nodes may not be palpable.
  • Laboratory findings and other features:
    • Marked reduction or absence of B cells in the peripheral circulation.
    • Immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgM, and IgA) are low or undetectable.
    • Plasma cells are absent throughout the body.
    • T-cell-mediated reactions are normal.
  • Management:
    • Immunoglobulin replacement therapy.
    • Antibiotics to treat infections.
    • Live vaccines are contraindicated


DiGeorge Syndrome (Option B): DiGeorge syndrome results from 22q11.2 deletion, leading to T-cell deficiency due to thymic hypoplasia, whereas this case has a B-cell deficiency.

Hyper IgM Syndrome (Option C): Characterized by high IgM with low IgG, IgA, and IgE due to a CD40L mutation, but this case shows low levels of all immunoglobulins.

Common Variable Immunodeficiency (Option D): CVID also causes low immunoglobulins, but it typically presents later in life (teens or adulthood), whereas XLA appears in infancy.

• Mucinous carcinoma, also known as colloid carcinoma, is a rare subtype of invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, typically occurring in postmenopausal women.
  • It is characterized by tumor cells floating in abundant extracellular mucin, which is a hallmark feature seen on microscopic examination.
  • It shows chicken wire blood vessels.
  • Clinically, it presents as a slow-growing, well-circumscribed breast mass, often with a favorable prognosis due to its lower likelihood of metastasis compared to other invasive breast cancers.


Incorrect options:

Lobular Carcinoma of the Breast (Option B):

  • Lobular carcinoma is characterized histologically by single-file infiltration of tumor cells due to loss of E-cadherin expression.
  • It typically presents with a diffuse, ill-defined mass rather than a well-circumscribed mucinous appearance.

Medullary Carcinoma (Option C):

  • Medullary carcinoma is a rare subtype of breast cancer that is associated with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, poorly differentiated cells, and a syncytial growth pattern.
  • It lacks the mucin pools seen in mucinous carcinoma.

Phyllodes Tumor (Option D):

  • Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial neoplasms that can be benign, borderline, or malignant.
  • Histologically, they show leaf-like stromal projections with stromal overgrowth, which differentiates them from mucinous carcinoma. Unlike mucinous carcinoma, they do not have mucin-filled spaces.

explanationHtml:
• CML is the most common myeloproliferative neoplasm.
  • It is caused by a reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 & 22 [t(9;22)], giving rise to shortened chromosome 22, which is referred to as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph chromosome).
  • CML progresses in three phases:

  • 1) Chronic phase:
    • Leukocytosis, < 10% blast cells, basophils <20% and monocytosis < 3%

    2) Accelerated phase:
    • 10%-19% blasts, ≥ 20% basophils in the peripheral blood or bone marrow
    • Persistent or increasing WBC (>10 × 10^9/L) and splenomegaly, unresponsive to therapy
    • Persistent thrombocytosis (>1000 × 10^9/L), unresponsive to therapy
    • Persistent thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10^9/L) unrelated to therapy
    • This phase often leads to the terminal blast crisis within 6-12 months

    3) Blast Crisis:
    • ≥20% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow
    • In 50% of patients, the blast crisis occurs abruptly without an accelerated phase
    • Extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs to compensate for CML and leads to significant splenomegaly
    • Transformation into AML is more predominant than ALL
  • Patient present with hyperleukocytosis, massive splenomegaly
  • Bone marrow is hypercellular with granulocytic hyperplasia. Sea-blue histiocytes can be seen.
  • After a variable period, some patients may transform into an accelerated phase or blast crisis.
  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the drug of choice, e.g., Imatinib, Dasatinib, etc.
Generation Drugs Activity
1st generation Imatinib BCR-ABL inhibitor
2nd generation Dasatinib, Nilotinib, Bosutinib More potent, used in resistance
3rd generation Ponatinib Active against T315I mutation

Option A: Philadelphia chromosome is present in a minority of cases

  • CML is caused by the reciprocal translocation between long arms of chromosomes 9 & 22 [t(9;22)], giving rise to shortened chromosome 22, which is referred to as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph chromosome).
  • It is present in more than 90% of patients with CML.
  • The presence of the Philadelphia chromosome confirms CML.

Option C: Most cases present in the blast phase

  • Some patients with CML progress to blast crises in which the CML acts as acute leukaemia.
  • It is the terminal phase of CML.
  • Most patients with CML present with splenomegaly and are in the chronic phase of the disease.

Option D: Methotrexate is the drug of choice for AML

  • Methotrexate is a nucleotide synthesis inhibitor.
  • It is used for the treatment of psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, breast cancer, and certain acute leukaemias.


Reference:

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10th ed pgs 622, 623

Multiple myeloma characteristically involves the axial skeleton, with the vertebral column being the most commonly affected site.

  • Vertebral involvement frequently leads to back pain and compression fractures, which are common presenting features.
  • Bone destruction in myeloma occurs due to:
    • Increased osteoclast activity (via RANKL and cytokine stimulation)
    • Suppressed osteoblast function (mediated by inhibitors such as DKK1)
  • This imbalance produces the classic “punched-out” lytic lesions seen on radiographs.
  • Commonly affected bones include the vertebrae, ribs, skull, pelvis, and proximal long bones.
