question: A 67-year-old man presents with back pain and anaemia. Skull radiograph shows multiple punched-out lytic lesions. He is diagnosed with multiple myeloma. Which of the following is the most common location of lytic bone lesions in multiple myeloma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In multiple myeloma, bone destruction results from an imbalance between osteoclast activation and osteoblast suppression. Neoplastic plasma cells produce MIP-1α (macrophage inflammatory protein-1 alpha, also known as CCL3), which is a key mediator of osteoclast differentiation and activation.

  • MIP-1α stimulates osteoclast precursors and enhances osteoclast formation, leading to increased bone resorption and the characteristic punched-out lytic lesions.
  • The resulting bone breakdown also contributes to hypercalcemia.
  • Although additional factors such as RANKL (from stromal cells) and DKK1 (which inhibits osteoblast differentiation) participate in myeloma bone disease, MIP-1α is a principal osteoclast-activating factor produced directly by myeloma cells.

Interleukin-2 (Option A): Primarily promotes T-cell proliferation and is not involved in osteoclast activation in multiple myeloma.

Erythropoietin (Option C): Stimulates erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow and does not mediate bone resorption.

Transforming growth factor-β (Option D): Involved in tissue remodelling and fibrosis, but is not the primary mediator of osteoclast-driven bone destruction in multiple myeloma.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 553

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

IgG3 is the immunoglobulin subtype among the given options most strongly associated with hyperviscosity in multiple myeloma.

  • Hyperviscosity syndrome results from markedly elevated levels of monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein), which increases plasma viscosity and impairs microcirculation.
  • In multiple myeloma, hyperviscosity is most commonly associated with IgA myeloma because IgA forms dimers and polymers that significantly increase serum viscosity.
  • However, since IgA is not listed in the options, IgG3 is the best answer among those provided.
  • IgG3 has a long hinge region and a greater tendency for self-aggregation, increasing its effective molecular size and its contribution to plasma viscosity compared to other IgG subclasses.
  • Clinical features of hyperviscosity include:
    • Headache
    • Blurred vision
    • Mucosal bleeding
    • Retinal venous engorgement
    • Neurological symptoms

IgG (Option B): Although IgG is the most common immunoglobulin subtype in multiple myeloma overall, it is less strongly associated with hyperviscosity compared to IgG3.

IgM (Option C): IgM is the classic cause of hyperviscosity in Waldenström macroglobulinemia, not multiple myeloma.

IgG2 (Option D): Does not demonstrate the aggregation tendency seen with IgG3 and is less associated with hyperviscosity.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 554
question: Excessive production of which of the following proteins is most commonly associated with hyperviscosity in multiple myeloma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

IgD myeloma is most commonly associated with a higher risk of renal insufficiency.

  • IgD myeloma characteristically produces large amounts of free light chains (Bence Jones proteins).
  • These light chains are filtered by the kidneys and precipitate within renal tubules, leading to light chain cast nephropathy (myeloma kidney).
  • Tubular obstruction and inflammation result in progressive renal dysfunction.
  • IgD myeloma is rare but often presents with high tumour burden and advanced renal impairment at diagnosis.
  • Renal injury in multiple myeloma is primarily mediated by excessive free light chain production.

IgG myeloma (Option A): Most common subtype of multiple myeloma; renal failure may occur, but is not disproportionately associated compared to IgD myeloma.

IgA myeloma (Option B): Second most common subtype; can cause renal involvement but is less frequently associated with severe renal insufficiency compared to IgD myeloma.

IgE myeloma (Option D): Extremely rare subtype and not classically associated with a higher incidence of renal failure.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9727151/

Pseudo-Gaucher cells are macrophages with cytoplasm resembling true Gaucher cells, seen in conditions associated with high cell turnover, particularly chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).

  • In CML, rapid myeloid proliferation leads to increased breakdown of leukocytes, resulting in the accumulation of glucocerebroside within marrow macrophages.
  • Unlike true Gaucher cells, these cells occur without β-glucocerebrosidase deficiency.
  • They are termed “pseudo” because they resemble Gaucher cells morphologically but do not represent a lysosomal storage disorder.

Hairy cell leukaemia (Option C): Characterised by TRAP-positive B cells, marrow fibrosis, and “fried-egg” appearing cells; pseudo-Gaucher cells are not a typical feature.

Multiple myeloma (Option D): Although rare pseudo-Gaucher-like cells have been reported in high cell turnover states, multiple myeloma is primarily characterised by clonal plasma cell proliferation, not by classic pseudo-Gaucher cells.

Lymphocytosis is not a feature of PCV because the disease arises from a myeloid progenitor, not the lymphoid lineage.

Polycythemia Vera (PCV):

  • Symptoms are mainly from erythrocytosis

    • JAK2 V617F mutation → constitutive JAK/STAT → growth factor-independent hematopoiesis

  • Morphology:

    • ↑ basophils (Option B), giant/abnormal platelets
    • Mild organomegaly; fibrosis & extramedullary hematopoiesis in spent phase

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Primary myelofibrosis disrupts normal marrow architecture due to progressive marrow fibrosis, leading to a leucoerythroblastic blood film characterised by nucleated RBCs, tear-drop cells (dacrocytes), and early myeloid precursors in the peripheral blood.

[[figure-1]]

Leucoerythroblastic Blood Film / Anaemia:

  • Presence of immature blood cells in peripheral blood - nucleated RBCs along with early myeloid precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes).
  • Significance:
    • Pathological in adults; indicates marrow infiltration, fibrosis, or severe marrow stress.
    • It may clinically resemble leukaemia due to circulating immature cells and splenomegaly, though marked leukocytosis is more typical of leukaemia.
  • Common causes:
    • Marrow infiltration: metastatic carcinoma, myelofibrosis
    • Severe systemic stress: sepsis, severe infections (e.g., tuberculosis)
    • Other marrow stress: acute blood loss, severe haemolysis, marrow recovery phase

Iron deficiency anaemia (Option A): Causes microcytic, hypochromic RBCs but does not disrupt marrow architecture; therefore, a leucoerythroblastic blood film is uncommon.

Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option B): Causes megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. Although severe cases may show occasional nucleated RBCs, a true leucoerythroblastic picture with myeloid precursors is not typical.

Thalassemia (Option D): Shows microcytosis, target cells, and marked erythroid hyperplasia. Severe forms may show nucleated RBCs, but true leucoerythroblastosis with early myeloid precursors is uncommon, as the marrow is hyperactive rather than infiltrated.

  • The presence of the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR::ABL1 fusion) establishes a diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and therefore excludes chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML). According to WHO 2022, CMML requires exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive CML and other defined myeloproliferative neoplasms.

CMML (WHO 2022) - Diagnostic Criteria:

Prerequisite Criteria (all must be present):

  • Persistent peripheral blood monocytosis (Option A)
    • Absolute monocyte count ≥ 0.5 × 10⁹/L
    • Relative monocytes ≥ 10% of leukocytes
  • Blasts < 20% in peripheral blood and bone marrow (Option B)
  • Does not meet criteria for:
    • Chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR::ABL1-positive)
    • Other myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs)
    • Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and defining gene rearrangements (e.g., PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2)

Supporting criteria:

  • Dysplasia in ≥1 myeloid lineage (Option D)
  • Acquired clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality
  • Abnormal distribution of peripheral blood monocyte subsets

Requirements for Diagnosis:

  • If absolute monocytosis ≥ 1 × 10⁹/L:
    • At least one supporting criterion (dysplasia, clonal abnormality, or abnormal monocyte subsets) must be present.
  • If absolute monocytosis 0.5-<1 × 10⁹/L:
    • Both dysplasia and an acquired clonal cytogenetic/molecular abnormality must be demonstrated.

Subtyping Based on WBC:

  • MD-CMML (Myelodysplastic type): WBC < 13 × 10⁹/L
  • MP-CMML (Myeloproliferative type): WBC ≥ 13 × 10⁹/L

Subgrouping Based on Blasts (including promonocytes):

  • CMML-1:
    • <5% blasts in peripheral blood
    • <10% in bone marrow
  • CMML-2:
    • 5-19% blasts in peripheral blood
    • 10-19% in bone marrow


Reference:

https://www.mll.com/en/myelodysplastic-myeloproliferative-neoplasm-mds-mpn/chronic-myelomonocytic-leukemia-cmml

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In classic Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple genetic alterations converge to cause constitutive activation of NF-κB, the central pathogenic driver of Reed-Sternberg cell survival.


NF-κB Activation (Central Event): Promotes RS cell growth & survival.

  • Mechanisms:
    • EBV (LMP-1) - mediated activation
    • Loss-of-function mutations in:
      • IκB
      • TNFAIP3 (A20)
    • REL proto-oncogene (2p) copy gain


Loss-of-function mutation of IKBα (NFKBIA) (Option A): IKBα is a negative regulator of NF-κB. Its loss leads to NF-κB activation, but this is a mechanism causing the central event, not the event itself.

Loss-of-function mutation of TNFAIP3 (A20) (Option C): TNFAIP3 is another negative regulator of NF-κB. Mutation results in increased NF-κB signalling, but it is one of several contributing genetic alterations.

Copy number gain of the REL proto-oncogene (Option D): REL enhances NF-κB activity. Its amplification contributes to pathway activation but is not the defining central event.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 557

TNFAIP3 (Option A): Located on chromosome 6; loss-of-function mutation (not amplification) increases NF-κB activity.

NFKBIA (Option B): Encodes IκBα, a negative regulator of NF-κB; typically inactivated, not amplified.

Explanation:

  • Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is characterised by true Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells, not Reed-Sternberg-like cells.

  • In contrast, Reed-Sternberg-like cells (RSLC) are large atypical cells that resemble RS cells morphologically but occur in other conditions and lack the typical cellular milieu of cHL.

  • They may also be seen rarely in certain solid tumours.
  • These cells often express CD30, but their overall immunophenotype varies depending on the underlying disease, which helps distinguish them from true RS cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

The mantle zone consists of tightly packed small naïve B lymphocytes that form a ring around the germinal center and are pushed outward by it.


Germinal Centre: (Option A)

Round/oval zone containing pale-staining cells surrounded by darker cells

  • Most common site: Gastrointestinal Tract - specifically the stomach, followed by the small and large bowel.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lymph node biopsy shows diffuse sheets of small lymphocytes with scattered pale nodular aggregates of larger activated cells, and the Peripheral smear shows smudge cells.
  • The clinical presentation described (65-year-old male, lymphadenopathy, lymphocytosis, and smudge cells) is classic for Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL) / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL).
  • Proliferation centres are pathognomonic for Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma.

[[figure-1]]

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (CLL/SLL):

  • Lymph node findings:
    • Diffuse effacement of lymph node architecture
    • Predominantly small lymphocytes (6-12 µm)
      • Round to slightly irregular nuclei
      • Condensed (clumped) chromatin
      • Scant cytoplasm
    • Proliferation centres (pseudofollicles) present:
      • Aggregates of larger activated lymphocytes
      • Contain mitotically active cells
      • Pathognomonic for CLL/SLL

Smudge cells (Option A): These are fragile lymphocytes seen on peripheral smear in CLL, but they are not specific and therefore not pathognomonic.

Diffuse lymph node effacement (Option B): Although seen in CLL/SLL, diffuse effacement can occur in many other lymphomas, so it is not diagnostic.

Bone marrow involvement (Option D): Bone marrow infiltration is common in CLL/SLL, but it is not unique to this disease and therefore not pathognomonic.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 543
question: A 65-year-old man presents with lymphadenopathy and lymphocytosis. Lymph node biopsy & peripheral smear findings are as shown. Which feature is pathognomonic for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is Nodular sclerosis.


Nodular Sclerosis Hodgkin Lymphoma (NSHL):

  • Most common subtype (65–70%)
  • Histology:

  • Lacunar Reed–Sternberg cells
  • Collagen bands → nodular appearance
  • Mixed inflammatory background
  • Immunophenotype markers:
    • Positive: PAX5, CD15, CD30
    • Negative: CD45, other B/T markers
  • Clinical:
    • Adolescents & young adults
    • Equal M:F
    • Cervical, supraclavicular, mediastinal nodes
  • EBV: Uncommon association
  • Prognosis: Excellent


Lymphocyte-rich (Option A): Uncommon subtype; characterised by predominance of reactive lymphocytes with few classic Reed–Sternberg cells; very good prognosis.

Mixed cellularity (Option B): Second most common (20–25%); diffuse pattern with numerous RS cells; frequently EBV-associated; more common in older males.

Lymphocyte-depleted (Option D): Least common (<5%); numerous pleomorphic RS cells with paucity of lymphocytes; associated with HIV, elderly patients, advanced stage; poorer prognosis.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 557
question: What is the most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma?

correctAnswer: C. May regress if inciting agent is removed
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Extranodal MALT lymphoma often develops in chronically inflamed tissues (e.g., H. pylori gastritis) and can regress if the triggering antigen is eliminated.

  • Extranodal MZL (MALToma):
    • Triggers: Chronic inflammation (autoimmune or infection)
      • Salivary gland – Sjögren syndrome
      • Thyroid – Hashimoto thyroiditis
      • Stomach – H. pylori gastritis
    • Features:
      • Localized disease for long periods (Option B)
      • May regress if trigger removed
    • Pathogenesis:
      • Reactive Phase: Begins as polyclonal lymphoid hyperplasia due to chronic antigenic stimulation.
      • Early Neoplastic Phase:
        • Emergence of a monoclonal B-cell population
        • Still antigen-dependent
        • Tumor may regress if antigen is removed
      • Antigen-Independent Phase: (Option A)
        • Chromosomal translocations (t(11;18), t(14;18), t(1;14))
        • These upregulate BCL10 or MALT1
        • Activation of NF-κB pathway → promotes B-cell survival and proliferation
      • Advanced Disease:
        • Systemic spread
        • Possible transformation to Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)


Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 548, 549

Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is B. Sézary syndrome. It presents with the triad of generalized erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells (Sézary cells) with cerebriform nuclei in peripheral blood (leukemic phase).


Sezary syndrome:

  • Generalized exfoliative erythroderma
  • Leukemia of Sézary cells (cerebriform nuclei)

[[figure-1]]

  • Generalized lymphadenopathy
  • Skin lesions rarely form tumors
  • Prognosis:
    • More aggressive than MF
    • Poorer survival (minority alive at 5 years)


Mycosis fungoides (Option A): Typically presents with patch/plaque/tumor stages confined mainly to skin early; leukemic involvement is not a defining early feature.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (Option C): Usually presents with nodal/systemic disease without characteristic erythroderma and circulating Sézary cells.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (Option D): Associated with HTLV-1 infection and commonly presents with hypercalcemia and systemic disease rather than classic erythroderma with Sézary cells.

question: A 62-year-old man presents with generalized exfoliative erythroderma and intense pruritus. Examination reveals diffuse lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood smear shows findings as shown. Skin biopsy demonstrates dermal infiltration by atypical CD4⁺ T cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Sézary syndrome. It presents with the triad of generalized erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells (Sézary cells) with cerebriform nuclei in peripheral blood (leukemic phase).


Sezary syndrome:

Sézary syndrome is an aggressive leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) characterized by malignant CD4⁺ T lymphocytes (Sézary cells) involving the skin, blood, and lymph nodes. It is considered a distinct entity from mycosis fungoides, although the two are closely related.

Classical Triad

  1. Erythroderma (>80% body surface area)
  2. Generalized lymphadenopathy
  3. Circulating Sézary cells in peripheral blood (cerebriform nuclei)

Clinical Features:

  • Diffuse erythema (erythroderma), scaling, severe pruritus
  • Alopecia
  • Ectropion
  • Palmoplantar keratoderma with nail dystrophy (image below)
  • Edema, hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent infections

Peripheral Blood Finding

  • Sézary cells
    • Large atypical lymphocytes

  • Cerebriform (brain-like, convoluted) nucleus

ltrastructural
features of a typical cerebriform nucleus.

  • Malignant CD4⁺ helper T cells
  • Sézary cells are usually CD3+, CD4+, CD7– and CD26– T cells
  • CD4:CD8 ratio is increased (often >10:1)

Diagnosis

  • Skin biopsy
  • Peripheral blood smear showing Sézary cells
  • Flow cytometry (loss of CD7/CD26)
  • T-cell receptor clonality studies
  • Lymph node biopsy when indicated

Treatment

  • Extracorporeal photopheresis
  • Interferon-α
  • Retinoids (e.g., bexarotene)
  • Phototherapy (PUVA)
  • Systemic chemotherapy (advanced disease)
  • Monoclonal antibodies (e.g., mogamulizumab, alemtuzumab in selected cases)
  • Allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in selected fit patients

Prognosis

  • Aggressive disease
  • Frequently presents as advanced (Stage IV) because blood involvement is present at diagnosis.
  • Common causes of mortality include infection due to impaired skin barrier and immunosuppression.


Mycosis fungoides (Option B): It is the most common type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), which typically presents with patch/plaque/tumor stages confined mainly to skin early. It's due to the monoclonal proliferation of predominantly CD4+/CD45R0+ helper T cells and the loss of mature T-cell antigens in the skin and other involved organs. Histopathological features seen are epidermotropism and Pautrier's microabscess.


Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (Option C): Primarily presents as an aggressive nodal lymphoma with generalized lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms. It lacks the characteristic erythroderma and circulating cerebriform Sézary cells.


Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (Option D): Associated with HTLV-1 infection. Patients commonly have hypercalcemia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and circulating malignant T cells.



Reference:
  1. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 551, 552
  2. Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 140.18-140.27
question: A 62-year-old man presents with generalized exfoliative erythroderma and intense pruritus. His general physical examination reveals diffuse lymphadenopathy. A peripheral blood smear was performed and shows findings as given below. His skin biopsy demonstrates dermal infiltration by atypical CD4⁺ T cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Large granular lymphocytic (LGL) leukemia. It classically presents in adults with rheumatoid arthritis (Felty-like association), neutropenia, splenomegaly, and large granular CD3⁺ T lymphocytes with azurophilic granules on peripheral smear.


Large Granular Lymphocytic (LGL) Leukemia:

  • Types:
    • T-cell (CD3⁺) - more common, indolent
    • NK-cell (CD3⁻, CD56⁺) - more aggressive
  • Age: Adults
  • Key Mutation: STAT3 mutation (30–40%) → cytokine-independent activation
  • Morphology:
    • Large lymphocytes
    • Pale cytoplasm with azurophilic granules
  • Clinical features:
    • Neutropenia (common)
    • Anemia ± pure red cell aplasia
    • Splenomegaly
    • Strong association with autoimmune disorders (e.g., Felty syndrome)
  • Clonal cytotoxic T/NK-cell proliferation → prominent cytopenias + autoimmunity.


Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Option A): Characterized by small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells, not large granular cells.

Hairy cell leukemia (Option B): Shows cells with cytoplasmic “hairy” projections and marked pancytopenia with massive splenomegaly.

Sézary syndrome (Option D): Presents with erythroderma and circulating cerebriform T cells, not granular cytotoxic lymphocytes.

question: A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with recurrent infections. She has splenomegaly and neutropenia. Peripheral smear shows large lymphocytes with azurophilic granules. Cells are CD3⁺. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (EBV+ DLBCL).

  • The patient has an aggressive large B-cell lymphoma (CD20 positive) with strong EBER positivity, indicating EBV-driven disease. The activated B-cell phenotype and presentation in an older adult with B symptoms are characteristic.


Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (EBV+ DLBCL):

  • A subtype of Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).
  • Occurs in both elderly and younger patients
  • ~2–14% of DLBCL cases.
  • More common in older adults.
  • Slight male predominance.
  • Pathogenesis:
    • EBV infects B cells → viral proteins (e.g., LMP1) activate the NF-κB pathway.
    • Usually shows an activated B-cell (ABC) phenotype.
    • Most cases exhibit the EBV latency II pattern.
  • Clinical features:
    • Rapid lymphadenopathy.
    • B symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats).
    • Often advanced stage with extranodal involvement.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Lymph node biopsy.
    • EBV detection by EBER in situ hybridisation.
  • Treatment:
    • Treated with standard R-CHOP–based chemotherapy.
    • Response may be inferior to EBV-negative DLBCL.
  • Prognosis:
    • Generally poorer than EBV-negative DLBCL.
    • High EBV load may indicate a worse outcome.


Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (Option B): Reed–Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+), not diffuse CD20+ sheets.

Burkitt lymphoma (Option C): MYC translocation, starry-sky pattern, very high Ki-67.

Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (Option D): T-cell (CD3+) neoplasm, not B-cell.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK578250/

Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Richter syndrome (also known as Richter transformation).


An important factor affecting survival in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) is its ability to transform into a more aggressive malignancy.

  • Most common transformation:
    • Transformation to Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
    • Known as Richter syndrome
    • Occurs in approximately 5–10% of patients with CLL/SLL
  • Associated with rapid clinical deterioration (Most survive < 2 years)
  • Markedly worse prognosis compared to typical CLL


Progressive CLL (Option A): Shows gradual progression, not transformation to DLBCL.


Prolymphocytic transformation (Option C): Characterised by increased circulating prolymphocytes, not DLBCL.

question: A 70-year-old man with a 5-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia develops rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, fever, weight loss, and elevated LDH. Lymph node biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL).

  • The image showing large cells with horseshoe-shaped or kidney-shaped nuclei is the definitive morphological feature of ALCL.


Anaplastic large cell lymphoma:

  • Caused by ALK gene rearrangement (2p23) → ALK fusion protein
  • Constitutive tyrosine kinase activation → RAS & JAK/STAT signalling
  • IHC: ALK positive, CD30 positive
  • Morphology:
    • Large anaplastic cells
    • Characteristic “hallmark cells”:
      • Horseshoe / embryoid nuclei
      • Abundant cytoplasm
    • Tumour cells may cluster around venules
    • Can mimic metastatic carcinoma
  • Common in children & young adults
  • Often involves lymph nodes and soft tissues
  • Prognosis:
    • Good prognosis
    • Cure rate with chemotherapy: 75-80%
    • ALK inhibitors are effective in refractory cases


ALK-negative type:

  • Occurs in older adults
  • Worse prognosis
  • Also CD30 positive
  • Lacks ALK rearrangement


Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (Option A): Typically CD20 positive (B-cell markers) and ALK negative; lacks hallmark cells.


Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (Option B): CD30 positive but ALK negative; shows Reed-Sternberg cells.


Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (Option D): Associated with HTLV-1 infection and does not show ALK positivity or hallmark cells.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 551
question: A 15-year-old boy presents with painless lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows findings as shown. Tumour cells are CD30 positive and ALK positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Distinct cortex and medulla with germinal centres and sinuses
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Normal Lymph Node Histology:

  • A normal lymph node is divided into distinct regions known as the cortex and medulla.
  • Cortical Region: The cortex contains lymphoid follicles, which consist of densely packed B lymphocytes surrounding germinal centres. These germinal centres are sites of B cell proliferation and differentiation.
  • Paracortex: Located between the cortex and medulla, the paracortex contains high concentrations of T lymphocytes and is involved in initiating cellular immune responses.
  • Medullary Sinuses: The medulla contains medullary sinuses, which are spaces lined by endothelial cells and filled with lymph, serve as conduits for lymph drainage from the cortex to efferent lymphatic vessels.
  • Medullary Cords: Interspersed between the medullary sinuses are medullary cords, which contain plasma cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes. These structures filter lymph and remove foreign particles and antigens.
  • Afferent and Efferent Lymphatic Vessels: Lymph enters the lymph node through afferent lymphatic vessels and exits through efferent lymphatic vessels, allowing lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells to interact with antigens and participate in immune responses.

[[figure-1]]

Presence of large pleomorphic cells (Option A):

  • These cells often indicate malignancy or infection rather than normal lymph node architecture.

Disorganised architecture with fibrosis (Option B):

  • Disorganised architecture with fibrosis is typically associated with pathological conditions, such as chronic inflammation or lymphoproliferative disorders.

Distorted germinal centres and absence of sinuses (Option D):

  • Distorted germinal centres and absence of sinuses may suggest pathological changes, such as lymphadenitis or lymphoma, rather than normal histology.


Reference:

Robbin’s and Cotran Pathological Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page 587

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The strongest predictor of progression to chronic HBV infection is the age at exposure.

  • The risk of developing chronic Hepatitis B is inversely proportional to the age at which a person is infected.
  • This is primarily due to the immaturity of the neonatal immune system, which tends to develop "immune tolerance" toward the virus rather than mounting an effective cytotoxic T-cell response to clear it.
    • ~90% of infants infected perinatally develop chronic infection.
    • 20–30% of young children (<5 years) progress to chronicity.
    • 5–10% of adults progress to chronic infection.

Presence of HBsAg (Option B): While this indicates an active infection, it does not predict whether that infection will become chronic or be cleared. In an acute infection, HBsAg is present but usually disappears within 6 months.

Anti-HBs antibody positivity (Option C): This is a marker of immunity (either from a resolved natural infection or vaccination). If a newborn is anti-HBs positive, it usually means they are protected, not that they are progressing to a chronic state.

Elevated ALT during acute infection (Option D): Interestingly, a vigorous immune response (marked by high ALT and symptomatic jaundice) is actually a good prognostic sign for clearing the virus in adults. Newborns often have relatively normal ALT levels because their immune systems aren't attacking the infected hepatocytes, which paradoxically leads to chronicity.



Reference:
  1. Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 757

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The “chicken-wire” pattern of fibrosis refers to pericellular and perisinusoidal fibrosis surrounding hepatocytes, most prominently in zone 3 (centrilobular region) of the hepatic lobule. This pattern is a classic histologic feature of alcohol-associated steatohepatitis and may also be seen in metabolic steatohepatitis.

Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease - Morphology:

  • Begins in zone 3 (centrilobular) → spreads toward portal tracts
  • Steatosis (Earliest, Reversible):
    • Predominantly macrovesicular
    • Large fat droplets → nucleus pushed to the side
    • Gross: enlarged, yellow, greasy liver
    • Reversible with abstinence
  • Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis:
    • Ballooned hepatocytes (essential for diagnosis)
    • Mallory hyaline (keratin 8 & 18 aggregates)
    • Prominent neutrophils
    • Spotty necrosis ± confluent necrosis
  • Fibrosis progression:
    • Starts as pericellular (“chicken-wire”) zone 3 fibrosis
    • → Portal fibrosis
    • → Bridging fibrosis
    • → Micronodular (Laennec) cirrhosis

Chronic hepatitis B infection (Option B): Typically produces portal inflammation, interface hepatitis, and bridging fibrosis, not the characteristic chicken-wire pattern.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (Option C): Shows periductal “onion-skin” fibrosis involving bile ducts.

Hemochromatosis (Option D): Characterized by iron deposition in hepatocytes with progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis, rather than pericellular chicken-wire fibrosis.



Reference:

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 767,768
question: A 50-year-old man presents with jaundice. Liver biopsy shows pericellular, perisinusoidal fibrosis forming a characteristic “chicken-wire” pattern around hepatocytes in zone 3. In which of the following conditions is this pattern classically seen?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Laennec cirrhosis is the classic micronodular cirrhosis caused by long-term alcohol abuse, beginning with zone 3 injury and perivenular fibrosis.

Mechanism:

  • Long-term alcohol use → repeated hepatocyte injury (zone 3)
  • Steatosis → alcoholic hepatitis → perivenular fibrosis
  • Progressive fibrosis → micronodular cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis)
    • Associated vascular changes:
      • Phlebosclerosis
      • Veno-occlusive lesions

Chronic hepatitis B infection (Option A): Causes post-necrotic cirrhosis resulting from chronic viral hepatitis, not Laennec cirrhosis.

Autoimmune bile duct destruction (Option C): Seen in Primary biliary cholangitis, which produces biliary cirrhosis.

Chronic right-sided heart failure (Option D): Leads to congestive hepatopathy

Robbins, Cotran & Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Pages 767, 768

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with:

  • 56-year-old man
  • Dragging pain in the abdomen
  • Massive splenomegaly
  • Peripheral smear showing:
    • Leukocytosis
    • Myelocytes and metamyelocytes (left shift)
    • Basophilia

These findings are classical for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).

CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm caused by the Philadelphia chromosome, resulting from the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation. This creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, leading to uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)

Genetics

  • Myeloproliferative neoplasm
  • Philadelphia chromosome
  • Reciprocal translocation: t(9;22)(q34;q11)
  • Formation of the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene
  • Constitutively active tyrosine kinase → uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells

Clinical Features

Constitutional Symptoms

  • Fever
  • Fatigue
  • Weight loss
  • Night sweats

Organomegaly

  • Massive splenomegaly (most characteristic)
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Abdominal fullness or pain due to splenic enlargement

Hematological Findings

  • Marked leukocytosis (often >50,000/mm³)
  • Basophilia
  • Eosinophilia
  • Myeloid cells at all stages of maturation in peripheral blood

Diagnosis of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML):

  • CBC: Normal RBC + Elevated TLC + Elevated platelets
  • Peripheral smear:
    • Left shift with predominant segmented neutrophils, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes.
    • College girl/garden party appearance: Due to non-uniform appearance (every cell appears different).

[[figure-1]]

  • Bone marrow aspirate
    • Increased Myeloid: Erythroid ratio.
    • Dwarf megakaryocytes.
    • Sea blue histiocytes (blue-coloured cytoplasm)
    • Pseudo Gaucher cells

[[figure-2]]

  • NAP (Neutrophil Alkaline Phosphatase)/LAP score (Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase):
    • Decreased
    • Used to differentiate CML (low LAP) from a leukemoid reaction (high LAP)
    • Supportive test; not the investigation of choice for confirming CML.
  • FISH (IOC)
    • Confirms t(9:22) translocation.
    • Analysis to quantify Philadelphia chromosome-positive cells.
    • Estimates the tumour load.

[[figure-3]]

  • PCR
    • To quantify BCR-ABL-1
    • It can be a false negative or false positive
    • False negative: Early part of the disease

Management: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as Imatinib.

  • Fusion gene: RUNX1-RUNX1T1 (AML1-ETO).

t(15;17) (Option C)

  • Fusion gene: PML-RARA.
  • Classically presents with DIC and faggot cells.

t(8;14) (Option D)

  • Associated with Burkitt lymphoma.
  • Involves c-MYC translocation.
  • Presents with jaw mass (endemic) or abdominal mass (sporadic).

question: A 56-year-old man presents with dragging pain in the abdomen. On examination, there is a massive splenomegaly. A peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with increased myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and basophils. Which of the following translocations is seen in this condition?

The patient presents with:

  • 62-year-old man
  • Generalized lymphadenopathy
  • Splenomegaly
  • Small to medium-sized lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contours

These findings are characteristic of Mantle Cell Lymphoma (MCL).

The hallmark genetic abnormality is t(11;14), which juxtaposes the CCND1 (Cyclin D1) gene on chromosome 11 with the IgH gene on chromosome 14, resulting in Cyclin D1 overexpression and uncontrolled G1→S cell cycle progression.

SOX11 is another characteristic marker of mantle cell lymphoma and is especially useful in Cyclin D1-negative cases.

Mantle Cell Lymphoma (MCL)

Genetics

  • Mature B-cell Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
  • t(11;14)(q13;q32)
  • CCND1 (Cyclin D1)–IgH translocation
  • Overexpression of Cyclin D1 → G1 to S phase progression

Clinical Features

  • Elderly males
  • Generalized lymphadenopathy
  • Splenomegaly
  • Bone marrow involvement
  • Gastrointestinal involvement (multiple lymphomatous polyposis)

Immunophenotype

Positive:

  • CD19
  • CD20
  • CD5
  • Cyclin D1
  • SOX11

Negative:

  • CD10
  • CD23 (helps distinguish from CLL) (Statement 4)

CD200 (Statement 3) is more commonly associated with other lymphoproliferative disorders, such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), rather than mantle cell lymphoma.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The combination of cavitary lung lesions, granulomas with caseation, and systemic involvement strongly favours a diagnosis of histoplasmosis. Histoplasmosis is an important differential diagnosis of tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions.

  • Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus.
  • Patients commonly present with fever, weight loss, chronic cough and disseminated disease involving the liver/spleen
  • Lung involvement may produce cavitary lesions, granulomatous inflammation
  • Histology classically shows granulomas, caseous necrosis, and Langhans giant cells
  • Histoplasma survives within macrophages, producing a chronic granulomatous response.
  • Diagnosis is aided by PAS stain, silver stain (GMS stain), showing intracellular yeasts.

[[figure-1]]

Granuloma containing macrophages and several multinucleated giant cells

Sarcoidosis (Option A): Characterised by non-caseating granulomas. Langhans giant cells may be present, but caseous necrosis is typically absent. Cavitary lesions are uncommon.

GPA (Option C): Granulomatosis with polyangiitis causes necrotising granulomas and vasculitis involving the upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys. Usually associated with c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) positivity.

Aspergillosis (Option D): Typically causes aspergilloma (“fungus ball”), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. Histology shows septate, acute-angle-branching hyphae, not classic caseating granulomas.

question: A biopsy slide shows a granulomatous lesion in a patient with Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Which of the following cytokines is primarily responsible for the formation and maintenance of a granuloma by activating macrophages?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The case is diagnosed as Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), and imatinib is the treatment of choice because it specifically inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase caused by the t(9;22) translocation.

  • Translocation: t(9;22) → BCR-ABL fusion on Chr 22 (Philadelphia chromosome)
  • Effect: Constitutive tyrosine kinase activity → drives CML
  • Treatment: Imatinib mesylate (tyrosine kinase inhibitor)
  • Diagnostic test of choice: FISH for BCR-ABL.

Rituximab (Option B) is an anti-CD20 antibody used for B-cell malignancies, not CML.

IFN alpha (Option C) is an older therapy for CML, less effective than tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib.

Hydroxyurea (Option D) provides temporary cytoreduction but is not a targeted therapy against BCR-ABL.

Robbins, Cotran, and Kumar Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page 838-841.

question: Which genetic abnormality is classically associated with Burkitt lymphoma?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: D) Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura


Explanation:

  • It is a quantitative disorder of platelets caused by antibodies directed against platelet or megakaryocytic antigens.

  • Related to antibody-mediated immune destruction of platelets or their precursors.

  • The peripheral blood smear in ITP exhibits numerous large platelets, and the bone marrow shows a compensatory increase in megakaryocytes.

  • Clinical Features:

    • Petechia

    • Purpura

    • Hemorrhagic bullae

    • Gum bleeding

    • Hematuria

    • Melena

Classification of ITP: ITP is primarily classified by duration and cause.

  • By Duration:

    • Newly Diagnosed: Less than 3 months since diagnosis.

    • Persistent: Lasting 3 to 12 months from diagnosis.

    • Chronic: Lasting more than 12 months (more common in adults).

  • By Cause:

    • Primary ITP: Occurs in isolation without an underlying trigger (accounts for 80% of cases).

    • Secondary ITP: Associated with another condition, such as:

      • Infections: HIV, Hepatitis C, H. pylori.

      • Autoimmune diseases: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).

      • Malignancies: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL).

Treatment of ITP:

Phase Treatment Options Mechanism
First-Line Corticosteroids (Prednisone/Dexamethasone) Suppress immune destruction of platelets.
IVIG (Intravenous Immunoglobulin) "Distracts" the spleen from destroying platelets (fast-acting).
Anti-D IG Only for Rh-positive, non-splenectomized patients.
Second-Line TPO-RAs (Eltrombopag, Romiplostim) Stimulate the bone marrow to produce more platelets.
Rituximab Depletes B-cells that produce the auto-antibodies.
Splenectomy Surgical removal of the primary site of platelet destruction.
Emergency Platelet Transfusion + High-dose IVIG Used only in life-threatening bleeding (rarely used alone as the body destroys them quickly).

  • Thrombocytopenia may be observed in the other choices but is usually associated with other systemic signs and symptoms.

Option A: Anti-Phospholipid Antibody Syndrome

  • The antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is the most common form of acquired thrombophilia.

  • Antiphospholipid antibodies include lupus anticoagulant antibodies and anticardiolipin antibodies.

  • They can occur as a manifestation of various conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus and other rheumatic disease, infections, and drug reactions.

  • Women who sustain recurrent spontaneous abortions or a thromboembolic event during pregnancy should also undergo evaluation for the disorder

Option B: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a rare but serious condition that causes abnormal blood clotting throughout the body's blood vessels.

  • An infection usually follows it.

  • It can present with any of the following:

    • Bleeding at wound sites or from the nose, gums, or mouth

    • Blood in the stool or urine

    • Bruising in small dots or larger patches on the body

    • Chest pain

    • Pain, redness, warmth, and swelling of the leg

Option C: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome

  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a condition that affects the blood and blood vessels. It results in:

    • destruction of blood platelets (cells involved in clotting)

    • a low red blood cell count (Anemia)

    • kidney failure due to damage to the tiny blood vessels of the kidneys

  • However, in this case, the triad is not present



Reference:

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10th Edition Page No. 664-665
question: An 8-year-old girl has been brought to the pediatric clinic by her parents. She has been suffering from tiny cutaneous haemorrhages spread all over her body. She has been recovering for a week from a flu-like condition. Her Physical examination is unremarkable, and she is vitally stable. Her Laboratory investigations revealed a platelet count of 20,000/mL. The number of megakaryocytes in her bone marrow has increased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this girl?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario describes Reye’s Syndrome, a rare but severe condition typically occurring in children following a viral illness (like influenza or varicella) who were treated with aspirin (salicylates).

  • Reye syndrome causes mitochondrial dysfunction → impaired β-oxidation → diffuse microvesicular fatty change with minimal inflammation.

[[figure-1]]

Microvesicular steatosis:

  • Microvesicular steatosis is a distinct pattern of hepatic fat accumulation characterised histologically by numerous tiny fat droplets within hepatocytes, unlike the large single droplets seen in macrovesicular steatosis.
  • Associations:
    • Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
    • Reye’s syndrome
    • Jamaican vomiting sickness
    • Drug toxicities (e.g., valproate, high-dose tetracycline)
    • Urea cycle enzyme defects
    • Alpers syndrome

Macrovesicular steatosis (Option A): Seen in conditions such as alcohol-related liver disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes, where hepatocytes contain a single large fat vacuole displacing the nucleus.

Bridging necrosis (Option C): Characteristic of severe acute viral hepatitis or toxic hepatitis, where necrosis connects portal tracts and central veins.

Ground-glass hepatocytes (Option D): A classic histologic feature of Hepatitis B, caused by the accumulation of hepatitis B surface antigen within hepatocytes

http://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2177300/

correctAnswer: B. A 15-year-old male with progressive ataxia, enlarged heart, spinal curvature, and high-arched feet.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given pedigree chart shows an autosomal recessive disorder, as males and females are equally affected, and skip generations are present. The clinical scenario describing a 15-year-old male with progressive gait ataxia in adolescence with cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, and pes cavus describes Friedreich ataxia, which is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation (GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion) in the frataxin (FXN) gene on chromosome 9.

A teenage boy presenting with multiple hundreds of colorectal polyps throughout the colon (Option A): Describes Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), an Autosomal Dominant disorder, caused by to germline mutation in the APC tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 5q. It has a 100% risk of colon cancer if untreated and is associated with Gardner syndrome.

A toddler with rickets unresponsive to standard vitamin D therapy (Option C): This scenario describes X-linked Hypophosphatemic Rickets (Vitamin D-resistant rickets), an X-linked Dominant disorder, which is due to a mutation in the PHEX gene, which causes impaired phosphate reabsorption in renal tubules, causing hypophosphatemia, characterised by Short stature, bowing of legs and dental abscesses


An infant exhibiting small platelets, eczema, and frequent infections(Option D): This describes Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, an X-linked Recessive disorder caused due to a mutation in the WAS (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein) gene, leading to defective cytoskeletal reorganisation in leukocytes and platelets, causing immune dysfunction and thrombocytopenia.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The preservative used in stored blood is Citrate. In a massive blood transfusion, the patient's liver cannot metabolize the excess citrate quickly enough (citrate toxicity). Citrate acts as a chelating agent, binding rapidly to circulating ionized calcium. This chelation results in acute

Hypocalcemia, which is an immediate concern leading to potential cardiac and neuromuscular instability.

Hyperkalemia (Option A) is due to the passive leakage of potassium from aging red blood cells, not the preservative itself.

Metabolic acidosis (Option B) is typically a transient complication; the citrate in the blood is rapidly converted to bicarbonate in the liver, often leading to a rebound metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.

Hemolysis (Option C) is a reaction to incompatible blood, not a metabolic complication of the preservative.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Edema results when the normal balance of Starling forces is disturbed.

  • Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure (e.g., congestive heart failure, venous obstruction) promotes fluid movement out of the vasculature.
  • Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., hypoalbuminemia from nephrotic syndrome or liver disease) reduces the inward pull of fluid back into capillaries.

Both mechanisms lead to the accumulation of interstitial fluid and manifest as pitting oedema.

1 and 3 (Option A): Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure increases filtration, but raised plasma oncotic pressure does not favour oedema formation.

2 and 3 (Option B): Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure and increased plasma oncotic pressure both work to oppose fluid leakage and oedema.

2 and 4 (Option D): Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure opposes, rather than promotes, oedema.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 11th Edition, Page no. 101

The clinical presentation of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) forms the classic triad of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).

  • APS-1 is caused by a mutation in the AIRE gene, leading to failure of central T-cell tolerance and autoimmune destruction of multiple endocrine organs.

Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes:

  • APS-1:
    • Cause: AIRE gene mutation
    • Features:
      • Autoimmune adrenalitis
      • Hypoparathyroidism
      • Hypogonadism
      • Pernicious anemia
      • Mucocutaneous candidiasis
      • Ectodermal defects (skin, nails, dental enamel)
  • APS-2 - More common
    • Onset: 4th decade
    • Combination of:
      • Adrenal insufficiency
      • Autoimmune thyroiditis
      • ± Type 1 diabetes mellitus
    • No candidiasis or hypoparathyroidism
  • APS-4:
    • Adrenalitis + other autoimmune diseases
      • Gastritis
      • Vitiligo
      • Alopecia
      • Pernicious anemia
    • No thyroiditis or Type 1 DM

RET gene (Option B): Associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), particularly medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma, not autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome.

MEN1 gene (Option C): Associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), involving parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumours; not linked to APS-1.

TP53 gene (Option D): Associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, predisposing to various malignancies; not related to autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes.

Lipids are best visualised in frozen sections (cryostat technique) because routine paraffin embedding dissolves fats during tissue processing with organic solvents like xylene and alcohol.

In frozen sections, the tissue is rapidly frozen and cut without chemical processing, thereby preserving lipids for demonstration with fat stains such as:

  • Oil Red O
  • Sudan III / IV
  • Sudan Black B

Incorrect Options:

Paraffin-embedded section (Option B): Lipids are dissolved during routine processing, so they are not visualized.

Immunohistochemistry (Option C): Detects specific proteins, not lipids.

Electron microscopy (Option D): Can show lipid droplets ultrastructurally but is not the standard technique for routine lipid visualization.
